chapters.title: A Page in Pie
chapters.html:
Every four seconds, or thereabouts, a drop of water let go of a broken slate in the roof of Pargeter’s printing house, fell eleven feet through the brown dusk of the composing room, and struck the bottom of a copper preserving-pan with a small flat note, like a coin put down by a very patient creditor. The pan stood on the imposing stone for the purpose. Toby Mudge, who was thirteen and the printer’s devil, was made to empty it into the pail by the door every quarter of an hour, and had been so made since the first of May, which came to a great many quarters and had given him views on arithmetic. The household called the leak the Drip, and Mrs Hobday said grace over it, since it was present at every meal.

It was Wednesday the fifth of June, 1816, and the grates of London were lit. Nobody in Hand and Pen Court could have told you why the summer had failed to arrive, and the newspapers, which could generally tell you why anything had failed, were reduced to calling the weather a scandal. The wheat stood thin in the fields, the hay was rotting about Islington, a quartern loaf was a shilling and expected to be more, and the town, having nothing better to do indoors, was still chewing over Lord Byron, who had gone abroad in April and left a great deal to chew. The rain ran down the pump, through the brick arch and out into Paternoster Row, where it met the rain from every other court and made, at the corner of Ave Maria Lane, a river with opinions.

The reader who has never stood in a printing house on a wet evening is asked to furnish one as follows. Two rows of wooden frames, each holding its sloping cases of type like a lectern; a stone slab in the middle, under a skylight the colour of dishwater; a proofing press; a speaking-tube of japanned tin that climbed the wall and vanished through the ceiling towards a gouty man in bed. Make it colder than a church. Add the smell of lye, lamp-oil and wet wool, and under these the faint sweetness of lead, which compositors say they cannot smell. At the first frame, under the best of the lamps, stood Winifred Pargeter, who was twenty-six and five feet four, and square across the shoulders, and wore her dark hair pinned up with a brass composing rule thrust through the knot, so that from behind she looked as though she had been shot at with a very small arrow and had declined to notice. She smelt faintly of lye. Her left thumb was blue-black to the ball. It would not wash, and she had stopped asking it to.

At five by St Paul’s, which struck through the rain like a man with a cold, a boy came in under the arch with his hat held before him in both hands, as though it contained something hot. He was perhaps eleven, in a coat cut for a brother of fifteen, and he had been sent from Curzon Street by Mr Minton with orders to put his paper into the hands of a compositor and not a devil. It was a great deal for a boy to carry, and he delivered it all at once.

“Mr Minton’s compliments, and it’s the last of the Fashionable Intelligence, and it’s to go in tonight exactly as written, and I’m to give it to the lady and not to him.” He looked at Toby, who was eating a pie.

“I’m a devil,” said Toby, with dignity and some gravy. “It’s different.”

Winifred took the slip out of the hat. It was a half-sheet in a clerk’s fair hand, damp, as everything in London was damp, through no fault of its own. She did not as a rule read what she set, the sense being apt to get in the way of the work; but this once the copy pleased her, and she read it standing, aloud, because Mr Orme in his corner could not hear a word unless she did.

“’We are authorised to state that the report of an engagement between the Marquess of Stanmere and Miss Quarles, daughter of Sir Ephraim Quarles, Bart., is entirely without foundation, and that his Lordship is at present engaged to no lady whatever.’ Heavens. A gentleman has issued a bulletin on his own bachelorhood.”

“Eh?” said Orme.

“Lady Quarles,” she said, louder, “has told the town for a fortnight that her Verity is to be a marchioness, and the Marquess has written to the Gazette to say he never heard of it. Poor Miss Quarles. To be refused by a man who never asked, and at sevenpence.”

“Is it true,” said Toby, looking up from the gravy, “that gentlemen don’t eat pies? Only I’ve been told it and I can’t make it hold together.”

“It is true of this one. He lives, I am told, on alternate Thursdays.”

Orme had held out his hand for the slip. He was seventy-one, the Father of the Chapel, and had set type since before the American war, a line a minute, like a clock with a conscience. He took the half-sheet to arm’s length and read it from the bottom right-hand corner to the top left, as he read everything, and gave judgement. “Stop after Bart., miss.”

The whistle in the speaking-tube shrieked. Winifred pulled the cork, and a voice came down it like coals down a chute.

“Win! Is that the copy? Tell Toby the pan wants emptying, my dear fellow, I can hear it filling from here, it has a note like a bishop’s, and now what would happen if the toggle were set a trifle lower, I wonder, it would — no. Never mind. What is the copy?”

“The Fashionable Intelligence, Father. The Marquess of Stanmere is not to marry Miss Quarles.”

“A wiser man than most. Set it as written, Win. Underhill would find a comma in a coffin, and the Gazette has not printed a correction in nineteen years, and he is rather proud of it, so we shall not be the ones to spoil it. Toby! Are you eating? I can hear you not saying anything.”

“No, sir,” said Toby, swallowing.

She began to set. The stick in her left hand was her late mother’s, of brass, worn bright at the thumb-rest, and into it, upside down and in a looking-glass, her right hand dropped the letters one after another, nick uppermost, with a click like small rain on a tin roof. The click and the Drip kept time together, as a married couple do when they are not speaking. By six she had the Births and Marriages and the court news in the galley, and by seven the Marquess’s paragraph was half in the stick, and she talked to it the whole way, as she always did when the copy pleased her.

“’At present engaged to no lady whatever.’ That is a long line, it wants breaking. Mr Orme, if I were a marquess I should have it engraved on a plate.”

“Eh?”

“Nothing, Mr Orme.”

At the foot of the third column, where the eye of the Gazette’s reader never fell, stood three lines of her own, kept standing since Lady Day at a price she preferred not to dwell on: FAIR COPYING in a plain hand, for authors, lawyers and composers of music, and below it, centred, Miss W. Pargeter, of Paternoster Row. The capital W had a nicked left foot, an old wound in the Pargeter fount, and it printed with a hairline gap, a white thread across the leg, as though the letter wore one boot thinner than the other. She had meant to replace it since March. A new sort was fourpence; but fourpence is only fourpence when there is also an afternoon.

At eight the roof, which seemed to have no other occupation, began a second Drip. It found a new road through the slates above the first frame and fell, with the unerring malice of water, upon the slip where it hung from the copy-holder at the height of Winifred’s eyes, and struck it on the name-line. When she lifted the slip from the hook, the lower half had gone to a grey map of the Low Countries, with three words left standing on it like churches. She had set a good half of the paragraph and carried the rest in her head, having read it aloud, and she saw no reason for alarm. She laid the ruin on top of the case to dry.

“Two now,” said Toby, interested. “I shall have to be twice as quick.”

“You will have to be neither. Put the pail under the frame.”

In a better-regulated week the damage would have been mended at eleven, when the proof of the page went across to Pomfret Yard by a boy and came back marked by Mr Ingram, the Gazette’s reader, who had not in nine years let a comma pass without a hearing. But Mr Ingram was in bed with a quinsy and a mustard plaster. Mr Underhill, the editor, had sent word that proofs this week would be read by the compositors themselves, which Barnaby said was like asking the cat to be her own mouse; and by a rule of Mr Underhill’s older than the quinsy, no proof went to Pomfret Yard after midnight, an editor kept from his bed by a proof being, in his own opinion, an editor who will find an error in it out of spite.

At ten Mrs Hobday came up the cellar stair with a can of tea, a quarter of cold mutton and the stump of a candle, humming Rock of Ages in the key of a woman carrying a tray. She was sixty and wide, with forearms like hams.

“Cleft for me,” she sang, and cleft the mutton accordingly. “Man shall not live by bread alone, miss, and I notice he does not live by type either. Is it nearly done?”

“I have two columns to go.”

“The Lord made the world in six days,” said Mrs Hobday, “and did not have Mr Underhill.” She went down singing.

At eleven, with the Drip at its slowest and Winifred gone through to the press room to see about a roller that stuck, the first thing went wrong in Pargeter’s that night; and it went wrong, as most things do, with nobody looking.

Page two stood ready on the galley frame, tied in its cord: four columns of Long Primer, Fashionable Intelligence above the rule, advertisements below it, some thirty pounds of lead. Toby had been told to carry it to the stone, as he had been told on every Wednesday since Michaelmas, with both hands. He carried it with one, because the other held the last of the pie, and the cord, which Winifred had told him on Monday to knot afresh, was not knotted afresh. Brevier, the shop cat, a grey animal with a torn ear who had been named for a very small size of type when she was very small and had since outgrown it, came across the floor after a moth. It was never settled whether Toby tripped over the cat or the cat over Toby.

The page fell. A page of type falls all at once, with a noise like a dresser of cutlery pitched downstairs, and afterwards it lies on the floor in a state called pie: not a page, nor a word, nor properly a letter, but a drift of small grey sorts, some of the lines still holding hands in twos and threes where they went down, the rest scattered like a congregation at a fire. The pie lay on top. Both pies, in a sense; Mr Mutlow’s beefsteak, face down on the Fashionable Intelligence, which seemed a fair judgement.

Toby stood in the middle of it for as long as it takes to count three. Then he picked up Brevier, who was unhurt and affronted, and went out by the back door to the coal-hole, where he told her everything. She had been a party to the event and did not contradict him.

Orme slept on, with his chin on his chest and one hand curled round a stick that was not there.

Winifred came in at the noise and found the wreck, the sleeper, and nobody to blame, and supposed, as anyone would, that the cord had parted. It had been a loose cord. She had said so on Monday. “Heavens,” said Winifred, extremely politely, and Orme opened one eye.

In the doorway behind her Fairweather, enormous, looked at the floor and said “Aye.” Dick Sparrow, over his shoulder, whistled through the gap in his front teeth. Sparrow had lately taken to wearing a clean neckcloth, which the Chapel had remarked upon, as the Chapel remarks upon everything, and had not yet explained.

“Two hours,” said Sparrow, “for a page that wants three.”

“Then it wants two hours of me. Go away, Mr Sparrow, and whistle somewhere with a roof. The forme must be locked by one or the cart goes empty. Mr Orme, distribute the loose sorts, please. Everything that is not in a line.”

“Eh?”

“Everything that is not in a line!”

“Backwards, miss,” said Orme, rising, “it is perfectly plain.”

She did not ask what was.

The reader may suppose that she read as she worked. She did not. A compositor does not read; she sees letters, as a baker sees flour, and makes a line as a baker makes a loaf, by weight and look and ten thousand repetitions, with the sense going by overhead like weather. Sense is a luxury of those who read type the right way up. Winifred read it upside down and in a looking-glass, so fast that she had lost the knack of reading it any other way, and could have set a sermon in Hebrew without knowing whether it was a sermon.

By midnight she had the advertisements back, and the Births, whose lines had held together in the fall, and three lines of the Marquess’s paragraph, which had held as well. A fourth was in pieces. In the gap she wanted a line of the right measure, and the heap, which was much of a muchness, offered two, lying together on the stone like sisters in one bed: both began with Miss, both ended on a comma, both were spaced out to the same length. One was the end of the Marquess’s paragraph. One was her own advertisement. The first lay under the crust of the pie; the second lay on top, clean; and the slip, which might have told her, was a map. She had seen Miss W. Pargeter, of Paternoster Row every Gazette day for twelve weeks. It had long ceased to be a name and had become a piece of furniture, and a person no more reads her own name than she reads the shape of her own doorstep.

The rain had taken what it liked from the slip, and it had liked the negatives. The rest she supplied from her hands. In four years of Fashionable Intelligence the phrase that most often followed an engagement had been entirely well founded, and the one that most often followed engaged to was the lady; and the fingers know what the eye has not been asked.

At twenty to one Fairweather came and stood at the end of the stone. “Aye,” he said, which in the dialect of Pargeter’s meant that the Albion was inked, the paper was wet, and the Lord did not wait.

“A quarter of an hour.”

She planed the page down with the mallet, drew the quoins tight with the shooting-stick, and lifted one edge of the chase to see that nothing rose. It held, a slab of iron and lead as handsome as a ham. There ought to have been a proof. There was a proofing press at the end of the room and a boy to work it; but the boy was in the coal-hole, and the clock said a quarter to one, and the rule said midnight, and Mr Ingram was in bed with a mustard plaster. She looked at the forme once, as one looks at a child in a Sunday coat, and found it uncommonly clean.

The whistle shrilled in the wall.

“Win! Is it locked? Has Ingram’s boy been? My dear girl, there was a man called Ruddock in my day who proofed with his eyes shut and found more errors than any reader in London, I always said it was the dark —”

“Mr Ingram is ill, Father. The forme is locked.”

“Is it clean?”

“It is as clean a page as I have ever set.”

It was perfectly true, and she was to remember saying it.

The presses began at half past one. In the back room the Albion, which Barnaby’s cousin Ebenezer had forged for him in Clerkenwell in 1813 and which rival printers called Barnaby’s folly, drew down its platen with a long iron sigh under Fairweather’s hand, while Sparrow rolled the ink; and the Old Lady, who was oak and screw and built like a gallows, answered from the other wall with a groan, Orme laying on, Toby come back from the coal-hole in a straight paper hat to beat the ink-balls, and Winifred on the bar. The sheets came off one after another, glistening, and were hung on lines across the room like the washing of a family that wrote to the papers.

“You are very quiet, Toby.”

“Yes, miss.”

“It was the cord. I ought to have knotted it myself, and not told you.”

“Miss —” said Toby, and beat the ink-balls till they sang. “It’s only the ink, miss. It’s got in my eye.”

The last sheet came off at ten past four. Winifred sat down on a bale of paper and did not read a word of them.

At twenty to five Fairweather, who said “Aye” about eleven times in a working day and meant something different each time, planted himself in front of her with a heel of bread in one hand and in the other a sheet that had hung on the line since two.

“Aye,” he said. It meant Eat.

Daylight had come into the press room at some time after four, as it does in June even when nobody has asked for it, a grey wet light without a source. She took the bread in her right hand and the sheet in her left, and because her hands were full and her head was empty she did what she had not done since six o’clock the evening before. She read.

MARRIAGE IN HIGH LIFE.—We are authorised to state that the engagement between the Marquess of Stanmere and Miss W. Pargeter, of Paternoster Row, is entirely well founded, and that his Lordship is at present engaged to the lady.

She read it three times. The first gave her the Marquess. The second gave her the Row. The third gave her the W, which had printed as it always did, with its hairline gap in the left foot, white on black, like a crack in a plate; and after that there was no use in reading further, because there is only one Miss W. Pargeter of Paternoster Row, and she was standing in her own press room with a heel of bread in her mouth.

“Is the cart loaded?”

“Aye.”

“Is Sowerby on the box?”

“Aye,” said Fairweather, in a tone that added, And what is the matter with your face?

Winifred counted, which is what she did. Eleven hundred sheets, and the cart in the court to take them. She had only to say the word to Sowerby and he would stop, being a man who stopped. Then the forme must be unlocked and mended: half an hour, if the quoins did not stick. Fresh paper must be wetted and left to take the water: an hour, whatever one did. The two presses must run again at four hundred an hour, which was nearly three; and the cart that should leave at a quarter past five would leave at nine, and come into Pomfret Yard when the hawkers were already in the streets with nothing to cry. By Clause 6 a cart that came after six was a breach, and a second breach in any quarter voided the contract at the Proprietor’s option, which in practice meant Mr Underhill’s; the first had been on the eleventh of May, in a rain that floated the Row, and the quarter had not yet ended. Mr Underhill, who had been dined three times since Lady Day by Mr Hector Lovejoy of the Phoenix Press, had been heard to remark on the eleventh of May at some length.

And if the cart went, there was Clause 9. Any error of the press requiring a correction in a later number made the contract void and forfeited the bond of five hundred pounds. So she might escape the one clause only by breaking the other, and the contract that kept the roof over the Drip, and the Albion, and her father, was in either case a thing she could lose. The difference was this. If she stopped the cart, the loss was certain and it was hers, a late cart with her name upon it. If she let it go, the loss was only possible: it wanted a gentleman to be angry, and an editor to be brave, and a correction to be printed by a paper that had never printed one. She was twenty-six. She had known editors.

What she thought in the next quarter of an hour she was afterwards to tell once, plainly, to the one person with a right to it. The narrator will wait.

She went out into the court with the sheet in her hand and her mother’s stick knocking at her hip through the apron. The cart stood by the pump with its tilt up and the oilcloth roped down over the bundles, and the rain bounced on it. Sowerby sat on the box in his oilskin, a bent man with a face like an old saddle who had carried the Gazette for nineteen years behind a horse called Jehu, which had not driven furiously since the Peace of Amiens. Winifred walked across the cobbles and stood in the arch.

St Paul’s struck the quarter. Two floors above her, in a room she could not see, her father’s hand-bell began to ring, as it rang every morning at that hour, cheerfully and out of time, meaning tea, and what news of the Gazette. Sowerby clicked his tongue. Jehu leaned into the collar, and the cart came across the court and drew rein an arm’s length from her, and the horse blew.

“Morning, miss,” said Sowerby. “Wet. Is there anything the matter with the load?”

Winifred stood very still in the arch with the sheet in her hand, which is a thing compositors do well, standing being most of the trade, and she said nothing at all. The rain ran off the brim of Sowerby’s hat. The bell rang on, upstairs, in the dark.

“Miss?”

She stepped back against the brick. The wheel went by her skirt with the breadth of a hand to spare, and the cart went out into Paternoster Row, and Sowerby looked back once from the corner of Ave Maria Lane, and then the tilt was gone into the rain.

She had good boots and did not use them.

chapters.title: Cards on the Salver
chapters.html:
There is a way of carrying a silver salver that a butler learns at about thirty and does not afterwards forget: level, a little forward of the body, at the height of the third waistcoat button, with the wrists loose, as a man carries a sleeping child or a bad piece of news. Gantry, who was sixty and had carried both, bore the salver across the breakfast-room at Stanmere House at eight o’clock on the morning of Thursday the sixth of June, and set it down at his master’s left hand, and the cards slid on the silver in a long soft drift, like a trick performed by a conjuror who has been told that the audience is leaving.

“Yesterday’s, my lord,” said Gantry. “With the letters.”

“How many?”

“Nine, my lord. Of which three are letters.” He gave the figure in the voice of a man reporting the height of a river.

The Marquess of Stanmere did not look up. He was thirty-one, six feet one in his stockings and nearer six in the mornings, since he did most of his reading at a slant. He had sandy hair cut shorter than any hair in Mayfair, pale grey eyes, long hands spotted with ink, a nose that had been broken at Harrow in a dispute over the aorist of a Greek verb (he had been right, which was the whole trouble), and a small white notch in his left eyebrow where a cricket ball had once taken the other side. He had been up since five. Since five he had eaten a cold mutton chop, drunk two cups of tea he had not tasted, and worked through the Corn Returns for the Home Counties; and since seven, when the Morning Gazette came up from Pomfret Yard in the hand of a boy who had run the whole way and looked it, he had been reading that, with a pencil, because he could not be left alone with a printed page without improving it. He could not pass a tradesman’s signboard in Bond Street without correcting it under his breath, and the tradesmen of Bond Street, who had heard him do it, regarded him as a kind of weather. By eight he had mended a comma in the Births, a recieve in an advertisement from Bath, and the Gazette’s opinion of the Bey of Tunis. He was now on the second page.

He found the paragraph at the head of the second column, under a lost spaniel, and the narrator is in a position to say that for the first ten seconds it was a joke.

It was precisely the joke a newspaper makes when it does not know it is making one. His Lordship is at present engaged to the lady. It had the cadence of wit, and he was halfway into that cold pleasure which an exact man takes in a beautiful mistake when his eye reached the name in the middle of it, and for the next ten seconds it was not a joke at all.

Miss W. Pargeter, of Paternoster Row. He had read the word Pargeter at the foot of every proof for nine months. Printed by B. Pargeter, Hand and Pen Court: it was the imprint of the house that set A Kentish Farmer.

The reader ought now to be let into a secret that the Marquess had kept, since the fourteenth of September last, from the whole of London but one anxious man. At intervals of about a month there had appeared in the Gazette nine long letters upon the Corn Law, the poor-rate and the price of the labourer’s bread, and they were signed A Kentish Farmer, and nobody had found the Farmer out, though three noblemen had denounced him at dinner. His manuscripts went in a plain cover, carried by Mr Minton, to Mr Ingram the reader, who passed them to the Row; and the proofs came back by the same road, with the Farmer’s sentences corrected in a hand that was small, upright and entirely without respect, and initialled in the margin with two letters, W.P. He had supposed W.P. to be a man of sixty with a cold in the head.

He put his hand into his coat and found the pocket-book without looking, as one finds a tooth. It was small and bound in green morocco, and it held, cut from the margins of nine sets of proofs with a pair of nail-scissors (Minton, holding the lamp, had winced at every snip), some ninety queries, each pasted on its own leaf and dated in the Marquess’s hand. He opened it at random. You use “poor-rate” and “poor rates” within a page. I do not say which is right. I say choose. W.P. He turned a leaf. Delete “deplorable”. Your figures are deplorable enough without help. W.P. He turned another. A semicolon is not a courtesy. W.P.

He sat for some time with the pocket-book in one hand and the Gazette in the other, a man holding two kinds of evidence, until Gantry, who had not left the room and who knew from the set of his master’s shoulders that something was the matter, as a ship’s cat knows weather, said, “Mr Minton, my lord,” and Mr Minton came in.

Mr Ambrose Minton entered as a man enters a church in which he has dropped something. He was thirty-five and immaculate and grey about the mouth, with a pocket-watch already open in his left hand and, on the first finger of his right, a stain of ink that no pumice had ever shifted. He carried the Gazette at arm’s length, folded to the page, like a dead bird he had found on the step and could not decide whether to bury.

“My lord. I came the moment I saw it. I wish to say at once that I wrote, and your Lordship will recall that I wrote, ‘entirely without foundation.’”

“I recall it very well. It was a good sentence. I particularly liked ‘no lady whatever.’”

“It has come out, my lord, as—”

“As the exact opposite. Yes. There is a certain symmetry in it.” Julian turned his own copy upon the cloth and laid one long finger beside the offending line, as a man shows a bird in a hedge to someone with poor sight. “Mr Minton, I have been engaged for a little over an hour, and I find I am not good at it.”

Minton looked at his watch. It was four minutes past eight. He looked at it every four minutes, as other men breathe, and had never been known to be late or at ease. “I sent it straight to the Row, my lord. I did not take it by Pomfret Yard. Your Lordship was altering the last sentence until a quarter to four, and the counting-room shuts at four, and it seemed a saving of time. If I had taken it to Mr Underhill’s people, a clerk would have read it over, and I have been thinking since half past six that a clerk would have—”

“Copied it. Clerks copy. You were prompt, Minton. The division of labour in London is that the secretary is prompt and the printer is accurate, and it appears that on Wednesday night one of us kept to his side.”

“I shall write to Mr Underhill this minute demanding a correction in Saturday’s number. I have the first line. ‘Sir, the Marquess of Stanmere, having observed.’ I had got as far as ‘observed.’ I thought I should be guided by your Lordship as to whether it ought to run ‘regrets’ or ‘requires.’”

“In a moment,” said the Marquess.

Minton looked at his watch.

Lady Constance Dyer was announced in the sense that Gantry’s mouth had begun to open when her voice came through it. “I know he is at breakfast. I can see he is at breakfast. Do not take the dog.” She was sixty-four, tall and rigid in black bombazine with a purple ribbon at the throat, the widow of a general and the aunt of the house, and she carried a lorgnette on a chain, a tortoiseshell ear-trumpet in her reticule, and under her left arm a pug called Blücher, who had one eye, a flat opinion of everybody, and the look of a small old banker who has lent money to the wrong party. She did not need the trumpet. She had the hearing of a bat. She used it as other women use a fan, to put between herself and whatever she preferred not to be told, and she raised it now towards Minton, who had opened his mouth, and said “Eh?” in a tone that shut it.

“Who,” said Lady Constance, “is Miss W. Pargeter?”

“Good morning, Aunt Constance.”

“It is not a good morning. It is raining, and you are engaged. Who is she?”

“I am informed that she is of Paternoster Row.”

“That is an address. I asked for a person.” She let fall the lorgnette. “Count the salver, Gantry.”

“My lady, I have—”

“Count it again.”

Gantry counted it again, with his lips, and arrived at nine.

“Forty-one,” said Lady Constance, “on the Monday before Augusta Quarles began to talk. Nine yesterday, of which three are letters, which is to say three women who wish it known they had meant to call. It is a question of arithmetic. That was a rumour, Julian. Consider what a fact will do.”

“Which fact?”

“The one under your hand.”

A footman, who had been waiting for his turn at the door with the face of a man with a hot plate, came forward with a note on a second salver. It had been brought from Bankside, Gantry explained, by a brewery boy on a dray-horse; a very small boy, he said, on a very large horse, which was standing at the area railings and eating the geraniums. The seal was a plain red wafer. The hand was square and upright and without a flourish, the hand of a young woman who kept books, and it said: Thank you. V.Q.

“For what?” said Julian.

“For the first morning in a twelvemonth,” said Lady Constance, “on which her mother has not said your name over the toast. She is the only sensible Quarles. It is a pity about the brewery.” She set the pug upon a chair, where it regarded the Marquess with its single eye as it might have regarded a debtor.

It was at this point that Lord Rupert Tremayne strolled in, laughing, which was how he did most things, in a waistcoat of lemon silk that was slightly too beautiful for the hour. He was twenty-nine and lanky and russet-gold, with a long amused mouth, the Gazette folded to the page in one hand and in the other a guinea, which he tossed and caught, tossed and caught, as he had done to the knowledge of Mayfair since Lady Day without once being seen to spend it.

“My dear Stanmere. I came the moment I read it, which was the moment my man brought my chocolate, which was a quarter of an hour ago, and I have run the whole way. I met my tailor in Bond Street, and he bowed. A tailor who bows is a tailor about to sue, so I came round by the mews. Is she handsome?”

“Which?”

“The lady. Miss—” He consulted the page. “Pargeter. Is she handsome?”

“I have no idea.”

“Is she rich?”

“She is a printer, or her father is.”

“Is it true?” Rupert tossed the guinea. “I only ask so that I may know which of the three to congratulate you on.”

“I have not met her,” said Julian, and heard how it sounded, and laid his pencil down upon the cloth very precisely, parallel to his knife. “I have been engaged since seven o’clock this morning to a lady I have not met, cannot describe and can tell you nothing of except her trade, and I had it from the Gazette at sevenpence, like everyone else.”

“But, my dear fellow, it is the most romantic thing I ever heard. Lady Jersey will weep. Augusta Quarles will—” Rupert’s face lit like a lamp. “Has anyone told Augusta Quarles?”

“Only the Gazette.”

“Which is delivered in Brook Street at eight. She will have had it with her toast. Poor Verity. Poor Augusta. Well, you will write and put it right, of course. One does. ‘Sir, I observe—‘”

“I have the first line,” said Minton, from the corner.

“Minton,” said the Marquess.

“My lord?”

“In a moment.”

Lady Constance had said nothing for some while. She now raised the lorgnette and looked at her nephew through it, a thing which at close range was like being measured for a coffin by a woman who had views on the timber, and she went on looking for a full minute, which is a long time to be looked at through a lorgnette. In that minute she worked out the whole matter. She had known him thirty-one years and been wrong about him twice, both times agreeably. She saw that he had not known the girl; that the Gazette had blundered; that he, who ought at this moment to be dictating, was sitting with his pencil parallel to his knife, and was turning his ring. It was a heavy gold signet with the Stanmere griffin on it, and he turned it round and round his finger when he was thinking, and never knew that he did.

“You will not correct it,” said Lady Constance.

“I have not said I would.”

“No. You have been not saying it for ten minutes. It is how your father began.”

“Began what?” said Rupert.

“Eh?” said Lady Constance, and put the trumpet to him.

The cards lay on the salver. Minton’s watch ticked, with a sound of small dry insects. Blücher, on his chair, sighed through his flat face like a bellows with a hole in it.

“In ten years,” said Lady Constance, to nobody in particular and to the ceiling in general, “nothing has made Augusta Quarles leave a house with her hat crooked. I have sat in a room with that woman while the roof came in at Lady Jersey’s, in the year seven, and she went out by the door with the hat as she had put it on. I should like to see what this does.”

“You would like to see.”

“I said I should like to see it. I did not say I should arrange it. Arrangement is for people who cannot wait.” She gathered the dog. “I shall be at Hertford Street. I do not ask where you will be. I inform you that I am at home to nobody until I have thought, and that I think quickly, and that the name of the thing I am thinking about is Pargeter. Rupert, you will take me to my carriage and you will not tell me about your tailor. Come.”

“My dear Constance, I never tell anybody about my tailor. He tells them about me.” Rupert gave the Marquess a look of such pure delight that it was impossible to resent, and bowed himself out after the aunt with his guinea going up and down behind his back like a very small sun.

The door closed. The footman withdrew with the second salver. Gantry took up the first, and the cards slid on it with the sound of a pack being put away, and he went out also, with his face in perfect order.

“My lord,” said Minton, after some time. “The first line.”

Julian drew the Gazette to him. He found the paragraph, and under the words entirely well founded he laid his pencil flat across the page, like a bar across a gate. It was a good H pencil, sharpened with a penknife at five that morning. A single stroke in the margin, the proof-reader’s dele, with its curl like a pig’s tail, would have cancelled the whole line, and he had made that mark ten thousand times upon the work of other men without a qualm. The pencil lay where it was. Minton looked at his watch, and looked at it again, and found that four more minutes had gone by in which his employer had neither written nor spoken nor moved, except his thumb, which turned the ring.

It was not a decision. The Marquess of Stanmere had not decided to let the thing stand. He had only decided to look at it, which, as every printer knows, is how a great many things come to stand.

“Minton,” he said, “I should like to know everything there is to know about the firm of Pargeter.”

“The printers, my lord?”

“The printers.”

chapters.title: Articles of Agreement
chapters.html:
Mrs Hobday served breakfast as she served everything else, to music. She stood at the head of the long table in the basement kitchen at ten o’clock on Friday morning, which was the late breakfast of a house that would be at its frames again from six that evening until five the next day, with the bacon-fork in one hand and the hymn-book, which she did not need, open in the other, and she went round the company in the order of the verses: a rasher to Mr Orme at “Come, let us join our friends above,” a rasher to Mr Fairweather at “And can it be,” and to Toby, who was the youngest and visibly had the worst conscience, a rasher with an egg upon it and the whole of the fifth verse.

“Let me to thy bosom fly,” she sang, and let Mr Pargeter’s rasher fly to his plate. “While the nearer waters roll. And the waters are rolling, Mr Pargeter, in the front passage, from the same source as ever. The Lord is my shepherd. He is not, however, my plumber.”

Barnaby Pargeter sat at the foot of the table with his gouty foot in its flannel upon a stool and his spectacles on his forehead, where they had been for two days, and said, “Quite so, Mrs Hobday,” in the voice of a man who has not heard a word. He had been told on Thursday evening, in the parlour, with the door shut. Winifred said afterwards that he had taken it in three stages, as a man takes a tooth: a joke, then a silence, then a second helping. The joke had been, “My dear girl, I always said you would marry above the stone.” The silence had lasted from nine o’clock until St Paul’s struck ten, and in it he had looked at the ceiling, where the Drip came through. The second helping had been cold mutton, and he had eaten it all, and then he had taken her hand in both of his, which were ink to the wrists, and said, “Win. Whatever you did. I should have mended the roof,” which was not an answer to anything, and was the kindest thing she had ever heard him say.

At ten past ten a boy from Pomfret Yard came down the area steps with a letter in a hand that sloped like a man leaning into a gale.

My dear Pargeter,—Never in nineteen years has the Gazette been so asked for. We were sold out in the Strand by nine and I have been obliged to order six hundred more from your forme, which I trust is still standing; I have been stopped in Fleet Street by two bishops. As to Clause 9, which concerns errors of the press, I need hardly remind you that there has been none. The Marquess’s household authorised the paragraph; the Gazette printed what it was authorised to print; and the Gazette, as you know, does not retract. It has only to be right. I shall wait upon you and Miss Pargeter, and meanwhile am, with the liveliest sense of the honour, E. Underhill.

“Six hundred,” said Barnaby, after a pause. “My dear fellow, that is a second edition on a forme that has stood since Thursday. I should not like to say what the type thinks of it.” He read the letter again and held it up to the light. “He has put ‘the Marquess’s household authorised the paragraph’ and ‘there has been none’ in the same sentence and walked away from the collision. A very fine, safe man. He would find a comma in a coffin, and what a pity he has not the other thing, the thing for the sense.”

“It means,” said Winifred, “that so long as the engagement is not shown to be false, there is no error. And if it is shown to be false, there is.”

“Well, there it is.”

“There it is.” She had a letter of her own in her apron pocket, folded in four and sealed with a wafer, which she had written at five in the morning and meant to send by Toby to Curzon Street at noon. It said what she had to say in nine lines. She was fond of it.

Toby came down the stair at a run, with a pie in his mouth and his paper hat over one ear. “Miss! It’s bailiffs!”

“It is not.”

“It is, miss, there’s two, and they’ve brought their own umbrellas, and one’s got a broken nose, and they’re standing under the Drip!”

Winifred set down her cup. Bailiffs, in her experience, did not bring umbrellas; it was a point of their trade to be wetter than their prey. She went up the cellar stair with her sleeves still pushed above the elbow and her hand going, out of habit, to the rule in her hair.

In the composing room a tall man in a dark wet coat was standing with his head tilted back, looking at the roof. He had put his hat under his arm. Behind him, in the door, a second man, immaculate, held a second umbrella furled like a pike and consulted a watch. The tall one was stooped, as people are who read a great deal and have never been told to stop, and his nose had been broken at some time and set by someone in a hurry. He was following the line of the Drip upward, from the copper pan on the stone to the broken slate, with his eyes, and as she entered he said, without looking round, “Third slate from the ridge. Four inches by three.”

“I am aware,” said Winifred.

“You will want a plumber, and a man to lay on a ladder in the dry. There will not be any dry before October.” He lowered his eyes, and they were pale grey and tired and, she thought, slightly appalled at themselves. “Miss Pargeter. I am Stanmere. I ought to have written. I came instead, which I see is worse. This is Mr Minton, who is mine.”

“My lord. I wrote to you.” She took the letter out of her pocket. “I had better say it instead. I made it. My father did not. He was in bed with his foot, and I was at the frame, and the error is mine to the last letter.”

“Did you? Yes. I assumed so. I assumed it from the W.” He took the letter she held out and, because it was there and she was watching, broke the wafer, and read it.

She had seen men read proofs for ten years. She knew the look of a man whose hand has begun to move before his mind has been consulted, and she saw the pencil come out of his coat as if on its own account, and a small mark appear in the margin of her best letter, against the first line.

“That comma,” said the Marquess.

“I beg your pardon?”

“After ‘Lordship.’ ‘I beg leave to inform your Lordship, that the paragraph.’ It divides the verb from what is informed.”

“It is a comma of respect.”

“A comma is not a bow.”

“My lord, a comma is a courtesy. It goes where a gentleman would bow. I was taught so at my mother’s elbow, and she was the daughter of a compositor, and if she were alive she would bring it up with you personally.”

“A semicolon is a courtesy,” said the Marquess, strangely, and stopped. A look went over his face which she did not understand at all and which she was afterwards to understand perfectly. “I beg your pardon. It is a habit. I came to say I was sorry for your inconvenience, and I have begun by mending your punctuation.”

“It is generally held in the Row to be the shortest way into anyone’s good opinion.”

“It is the only way into mine,” said the Marquess; he said it as one mentions one’s height. Behind him Mr Minton looked at his watch, and Toby, in the door to the stair, removed the pie from his mouth in order to hear better.

“Miss Pargeter,” said Julian. “Who will be inconvenienced by a correction?”

“I?”

“You. Say how much. As a reader asks it. What does the Gazette do?”

She told him. She did not mean to tell him so much, but it was the first time since Wednesday that anyone had asked her a question that had an answer, and it went out of her like water from a cracked pan. Clause 9: any error of the press that required a correction in a later number voided the contract, and the bond of five hundred pounds was forfeit. The Gazette had never printed a correction in nineteen years. Mr Underhill kept the fact in front of him like a flag. The contract was three parts in five of the house’s bread; it paid the journeymen, and the paper, and the lamp-oil, and the slate which was not mended.

“So that if I were to write tomorrow to say that I did not mean it—”

“You would be believed. And it would be a correction. And Mr Underhill would be obliged by his own pride to put Pargeter’s out of Pomfret Yard before the ink was dry, in order that no one should say the Gazette had made a mistake.” She stopped. “That is the sum. I do not mean it to move you. It is only the figures.”

“And the cost of the error, to anyone? To me, for instance.”

“A fortnight of embarrassment, I should think.”

“A fortnight of peace,” said the Marquess. He walked three steps down the room and three back, which in that room was a considerable promenade, and stopped at the imposing stone, where the Drip fell into its copper pan with a small flat note. “I have been hunted since I was twenty-four. This morning, I am told, the salver fell from forty-one to nine in a week, and that was on a rumour. A fact will clear it. I should have the summer to myself, for the first time since I came into the title, and I have something I wish very much to do with a summer. Where the cost of mending a mistake is greater than the cost of the mistake, a careful reader does not mend it. He writes in the margin stet. Let it stand.”

“That is lying.”

“That is letting stand. It is the difference between a falsehood and a silence.”

“There is no difference in the Row.”

“There is a very great difference in the Gazette, which is the only place that it is heard.” He turned round. “I do not propose that you say anything. The Gazette has said it. I propose that neither of us contradicts it; until the end of the Season; and that the paper does the rest.”

She was outraged. It lasted, by the clock of St Paul’s, about nine seconds, and passed through three colours. Then she did what she always did, which was to count. She counted the bond, and the roof, and the six hundred copies standing in the type, and her father’s foot. She counted the bailiff she had not yet had at the door. She counted herself, one square-shouldered woman in an apron, with her thumb stained, and a Marquess in her composing room offering her the use of him as one offers the use of an umbrella. “I do not tell lies aloud,” she said at last. “It is a rule. I do not say it is a virtue. I say it is a rule, like not smoking over the type.”

“Then you need not.”

“Not the Season. Michaelmas. The twenty-ninth of September.”

“Why Michaelmas?”

“It is a Quarter Day. Everything in the trade falls due at Michaelmas, my lord.” Which was perfectly true, and not at all what she meant. “And at Michaelmas, I will have the sole right to end it. Not you. Me. You will be jilted.”

“I,” said the Marquess, with an expression of great interest, “shall be jilted.”

“By a printer’s daughter. I understand it is considered forgivable.”

“I should like it in writing.”

“My lord,” said Winifred, “I am a printer. I do not make a bargain that I cannot set in type.”

She set it standing at the case, without copy, as a man might talk to himself, and Julian stood at her elbow with his hands behind him and watched her hands.

He had not meant to watch them. He had meant to watch the type, in which, on a good day, a Marquess might have been expected to find something to correct. But the hands were doing a thing he had not seen done, and it held him as a juggler would have. They moved on the upper case and the lower case without her eyes going to either, and each letter went into the stick as though dropped by somebody who knew exactly where it would fall. They were a small woman’s hands, square, quick, light as a bird’s, with a blue-black stain on the ball and nail of the left thumb which was clearly permanent. The whole left hand held the brass stick against her apron. The stick was worn bright at the thumb-rest, and her thumb lay in the hollow of it as a head lies on a pillow.

These were the hands that had written, on nine sets of proofs, A semicolon is not a courtesy. He knew it as one knows the answer to a riddle, without a sense of having solved anything. It was not the smallest part of his wish to be gone that he could not for the life of him have said whether he wished it for her sake or his own.

“Article the first,” said Winifred, to the stick, and set it. “’The announcement in the Gazette of the sixth of June to stand as printed, and neither party to contradict it until Michaelmas Day.’ You are looking at my thumb.”

“I am looking at your spacing.”

“It is a very good thumb for spacing. Article two. You will call twice a week.”

“Twice a week.”

“At hours convenient to the press. And I shall appear with you on no fewer than six occasions. And at your table once.” She did not look up. “I do not say it for pleasure. A thing nobody sees does not stand.”

He dictated, after a while, where she let him. She would not allow affection and had no reason to give; she took out lady from his draft and put in Miss Pargeter, in a type that was larger. He proposed a clause by which a fund should be set up at Child’s for the benefit of the house, and she took it out of the stick with a flick of one finger, and set the third article in its place in a dozen letters. “’The Marquess shall not lend, give, advance or promise any money to Miss Pargeter or to Mr Pargeter, directly or by any third person.’ I will be paid for work. I will be paid for work at ordinary rates, as any customer pays. I will not be paid for being looked at.”

“I see.”

“You are going to tell me it is a point of pride.”

“I was about to say that I admire the placing of the second comma.” He had, in fact, been about to say a good deal else, and was astonished to find that it had left him, and that the article, as set, left no space in it for any other. It was a very good article. He signed away the right to be useful, in his head, and was aware of it as one is aware of a loose tooth: a small foreign matter of loss.

The fourth article was hers, and settled her conscience. “’Neither party shall be required to utter in their own voice any statement they know to be false; the Gazette shall be relied upon to speak for them.’” The fifth gave her the right to end it. The seventh limited the knowing of it to her father, to Mr Minton, who was standing by the door with his watch and the look of a man being measured for a rope, and to the Chapel, which was the whole of Pargeter’s, by custom and oath: and she read it aloud to Mr Orme, who had come from his corner to see what the noise was.

“The Chapel keeps it, Mr Orme.”

“Eh?”

“The Chapel keeps it!”

“The Chapel keeps everything, miss,” said Orme, with dignity. “It is what it is for.” Mr Fairweather, who had come in behind him with his arms folded across his chest like two bolsters, said “Aye.”

It was the sixth that she set last, without a word, and with a sort of gravity.

“What is that for?” said Julian.

“It is a point of order. I have set eleven novels in three volumes for the circulating libraries, my lord. I know what becomes of people who make a bargain.”

“What becomes of them?”

“The usual thing.”

“Ah,” said the Marquess. “That.”

By noon the forme was locked and the Albion drew down its platen on a single sheet of foolscap, with a long sigh like a church organ with a cold; and the shop stood about it as a household stands about a christening. Winifred pulled the proof herself. She looked at it, up and down, the first thing Pargeter’s had printed since Wednesday that any person had troubled to read, and she read it twice, once forwards and once backwards, with a pencil in her teeth, while the Marquess read it also, over her shoulder, with his own. They found nothing. It was an uncomfortable moment for them both, and in the silence the Drip said what it thought.

ARTICLES OF AGREEMENT, made at Hand and Pen Court, Paternoster Row, on the seventh day of June, 1816, between the Most Noble Julian, Marquess of Stanmere, and Miss Winifred Pargeter, printer.

I. The announcement in the Gazette of the 6th of June to stand as printed, and neither party to contradict it until Michaelmas Day, the 29th of September, 1816.

II. Miss Pargeter to appear in company with the Marquess on not fewer than six occasions, and at his table once; the Marquess to call at Hand and Pen Court twice in every week, at hours convenient to the press.

III. The Marquess shall not lend, give, advance or promise any money to Miss Pargeter or to Mr Pargeter, directly or by any third person.

IV. Neither party shall be required to utter in their own voice any statement they know to be false; the Gazette shall be relied upon to speak for them.

V. At Michaelmas Miss Pargeter shall have the sole right to end the engagement, and the Marquess shall bear all the blame.

VI. Neither party shall form an Attachment of the Affections.

VII. The truth shall be known to no persons beyond Mr Pargeter, Mr Minton, and the Chapel of Pargeter’s.

Printed by B. Pargeter, Hand and Pen Court, Paternoster Row.

At the foot she had set the imprint, as the law requires, and left the white space for two names. Julian saw that she had put her father’s, B. Pargeter, and that she had not hesitated over the initial.

Barnaby was fetched. He came down the stair backwards, one step at a time, with his foot in its flannel and Toby under his arm for a crutch, and stood in the composing room blinking at the Marquess of Stanmere through spectacles that were still on his forehead. “My dear fellow,” he said, “you will have to forgive the roof,” and shook his hand with a hand that left a perfect print on the glove. He was shown the sheet. He read it with one finger. “’The Marquess shall not lend, give—’ very proper, Win, very proper. ‘Neither party shall be required to utter—’ ha. ‘Neither party shall form an Attachment of the—‘” He read the sixth article aloud, in a thin voice like a clerk reading a will, and when he had reached the end of it he put the sheet down upon the stone, and sat down on the nearest stool, and wept. He wept with his whole body, from the spectacles down, and the Drip kept time. “Oh, Win,” he said. “Oh, my dear. A Marquess.”

“Father, you are to witness.”

“I shall, I shall.” He wiped his eyes with the flannel from his foot. “Where does he sign?”

The Marquess had taken up the pen. He held it, Barnaby remarked, as a bishop holds a hot potato; the thing wanted a firmer grip and, in his judgement, a little prayer. Julian looked at the sixth article. It lay on the damp paper in a plain Pica, among the sevens and the fives, among the rule of a gentleman’s money and the rule of a lady’s tongue, like a small stone in a good bread.

“I never fall in love,” he said, “it is a family trait,” and with a tolerable laugh he steadied the sheet with his left thumb, which had touched the forme an hour before, and signed. There were two counterparts, because a bargain wants a second copy as a man wants a second shoe; Fairweather pulled the second, in a single pull; and the second was signed also, and Winifred’s name followed his, upright and small, with a flourish nowhere, like a notice to quit.

At the street door Julian turned. He had his hat and his umbrella, and Minton had the other, and Toby, who had been allowed to hold the door, said all at once, “Are you really going to marry our Win?” and the whole room stopped.

“I am assured,” said the Marquess, “that it is in the Gazette.”

Winifred, at the stone, heard it. She looked at him, and she looked at the sheet, and something happened at the corner of her mouth. She was twenty-six years old, and had been engaged for twenty-nine hours, and she had just been handed the best sentence she had ever heard, and she took it, as a compositor takes a good sort that has fallen out of somebody else’s case, and put it in her own.

When the door had shut and the umbrellas had gone out under the arch like two large black flowers, she went and lifted the second counterpart from the line where it had been hung to dry. It was her own, to keep. She meant to put it flat in the lid of her mother’s brass stick-case, where it would not curl. On the margin, beside the sixth article, the Marquess of Stanmere’s left thumb had left a perfect inky print, whorls and all, as a witness might leave one who had not been asked. A clean rag lay within reach. She did not take it.

chapters.title: Lady Constance Inspects the Goods
chapters.html:
The morning-room at Hertford Street was so cold, and so full of stuffed birds, that Winifred Pargeter, who had been admitted by a butler with the manner of a man conducting her to the scaffold, felt she had been shown into an expensive larder. There were one hundred and forty birds. The late General Sir Hugh Dyer had shot them in four countries and had them stuffed in all of them, and they stood upon every shelf and bracket and in a great glass case by the window: kites, bustards, a griffon vulture with the expression of a landlord, two flamingoes that had been pink in Portugal and had since gone the colour of old soap. A fire was lit in the grate and gave out, as far as she could judge, the sentiments of a candle in a cathedral.

It was a quarter past eleven on Monday the tenth of June. She had been sent for. The note had said, in a hand like a row of railings, Lady Constance Dyer will receive Miss Pargeter at eleven on Monday. She is not asked whether she is free; and Winifred, who had read the note on the stone, upside down and from a distance of nine feet, had replied that she would be free until three, when the copy came.

“Sit,” said Lady Constance.

Winifred sat. A pug the size of a muff came across the carpet, regarded her left ankle with its one eye, and set his chin upon it, where he stayed. “That is Blücher,” said Lady Constance. “He is judging you. He has judged a bishop and found him wanting. Fell, the tea.”

A thin woman in grey rose from the shadow of the vulture and poured. She was past forty, long in the neck, with her hair going to silver in one white streak at the left temple, and she wore mittens, though it was June, indoors, and the pot was no hotter than the room. She handed Winifred a cup with a small stoop, and then, as the pot gave a dribble, said to it in a soft voice, “I beg your pardon,” and set it down.

“Miss Fell,” said Lady Constance, “has been in this house twelve years and has never repeated anything, because nobody has ever asked her anything. You may speak before her. Now. Do you dance?”

“I am able to do country dances, my lady. My aunt in Hackney had a fiddle.”

“Which dances?”

“Sir Roger de Coverley. The Dashing White Sergeant. Another, which she called Ruth, I think, in honour of a former tenant.”

“French?”

“I read it. I set a menu in French once, for a Mr Beauchamp of Cheapside who wished to impress his brother-in-law. I corrected his accents, and he did not speak to me for a month.”

“Horse?”

“No.”

“Music?”

“The Old Hundredth,” said Winifred, “and a good deal of the Chapel’s songs, which I should not sing in the presence of your birds.”

“Do you read?”

“My lady, I read for my living. Upside down, as a rule, and backwards, and when I am rested I can do it in the proper direction.” She added, because the old woman had brought up the lorgnette and was staring at her through it like an inspector of cattle, “I will show you if you like. Anything. At a distance.”

“The desk,” said Lady Constance.

It stood by the window across the room, a writing desk of walnut with a leather top, and on its slope, among the pens and the pounce-pot and a heap of tradesmen’s accounts, lay a letter with the seal broken and the cover turned towards the room. It was a good nine yards. Winifred looked at it as she looked at all print, in pieces, and let the pieces come. “The top bill is from a poulterer in Leadenhall Market. It is two pounds, eleven, for a goose and a hen pheasant, and it has been sent twice. The one under it is the sweep. And a cover with a Tuscan postmark, a ring with FIRENZE round the edge of it, and the direction in a lady’s hand, running uphill: Lady Constance Dyer, Hertford Street, and then a line beneath that begins, My dear—”

Lady Constance’s hand went out, with no hurry at all, and turned the letter face down.

It made no noise. A letter being turned over seldom does. But the room, which had been cold, became suddenly a degree colder, as if one of the flamingoes had opened a window; and from somewhere behind her Winifred heard Miss Fell’s cup go gently into its saucer; and she knew, by some trade instinct older than manners, that she had read something that was not hers to read, and that the Row’s rule, which is set what you are given and do not read it, had been a good rule after all.

“That will do,” said Lady Constance. “Very good. Where were you taught?”

“By my mother, my lady. She was a compositor’s daughter. She is dead.”

“I am sorry for it.” She was not looking at the desk. She was looking at the fire. “I have known since eight o’clock on Thursday morning,” she said, “that my nephew is not engaged to you.”

Winifred put down her cup.

“I knew it because he did not tell me first. I knew it because no Dyer has ever announced anything in a newspaper, or been announced in one; our births have been known, and our deaths, and the rest has been the business of the family. I knew it because Julian could no more have found a printer’s daughter than he could have found Timbuktu without a map and a sponsor. And I knew it because he sat for ten minutes with a pencil on the page and did nothing, which is the way his father did all his worst things. I do not know what has been agreed. I do not ask. Julian has not told me, and has not denied it, which with a Dyer is a deposition. I shall not ask you. I inform you that it will be done well.”

“My lady, I have not said that it is not true.”

“No. You have said very little. I observe that you do not lie aloud.”

“I do not.”

“What do you say,” said Lady Constance, “when you are asked if you are engaged?”

It was a fair question and Winifred had thought about it for three days, between the proofing of a draper’s bill and the casting off of a sermon on the Deluge, and had not got further than a certain tightness in the chest. She heard her own voice say, for the first time out loud and in a cold room, “It is in the Gazette.”

The ear-trumpet came up, and went down. “Again.”

“It is in the Gazette.”

“A little pause before the Gazette, as though it were a bishop. Again.”

“It is in the—Gazette.”

“Better. It will be taken for reserve. Reserve is the only fashionable thing a woman can do for nothing. It is also, I observe, perfectly true, which is more than can be said for most of what is said in drawing-rooms.” Lady Constance regarded her niece-to-be, so to speak, as a banker regards a draft on a house in whose solvency he does not entirely believe, but whose handwriting he admires. “You will want gowns.”

“I have a grey merino and a black silk.”

“You will want eight.”

“My lady, I thank you. I will not take them.”

“I did not say I should give them.”

“You were about to. I could see it in the ribbon.”

Miss Fell gave a very small sound which in any other person would have been a laugh and in her was an apology for one. Lady Constance turned her whole head. “Fell,” she said. “Go on pouring.”

“I will not wear a silk bought with the Marquess’s money,” said Winifred. “It is in the Articles. I mean—” She stopped; it was a thing she had not meant to say. “It is a principle. I will earn what I wear, my lady, or I will wear the grey.”

Lady Constance looked at her for rather longer than was comfortable. Then she took from the desk, without rising, a printed sheet in a small close type, which she held out at arm’s length, as a tradesman’s bill is held. “The Society for the Relief of Distressed Gentlewomen,” she said, “of which I am a patroness, and which wishes to circulate this appeal to fifteen hundred persons of property. I have been to Bond Street for it, and the man there is a fool and has misspelt distressed. The work is to be done at ordinary rates by a printer who can spell. You will put your price upon it. It will come to six pounds ten, I imagine, with the paper. And what you do with six pounds ten, once you have earned it, is no concern of mine.” She swung the lorgnette upon its ribbon. “If you were to spend it upon a gown, I should not even hear of it.”

“I could do it for six pounds.”

“Six pounds ten. I will not have a tradesman who undersells. It is vulgar and it deranges the trade.” She said it with an air of such exquisite annoyance, and was so evidently delighted, that Winifred understood, as one understands a thing in a language in which one has no vocabulary, that she had just been admitted.

The lessons followed. They were four, and they were given in a voice like a drill-sergeant’s. The first was on gloves. “They exist,” said Lady Constance. “I observe your left hand. I do not ask what it is. It is blue. You will wear gloves, at all times and in all company, and you will take them off at table when a lady takes off hers and not before, and you will keep the hand at your side. You will not hide it. A hidden hand is looked at. A gloved one is merely a hand.”

The second was on the word Marchioness. “You will not use it. Not in jest, not in reverie, not in the dark of your own bed. It is the one word in the language that tells everyone what you hope, and what you hope you must never say. If you are asked, you will say that you have not thought of titles. If you are pressed you will say it as one speaks of a distant relation’s disease.”

The third was on dancing: “You will not.” The fourth was on being looked at. “A woman who is looked at must have something to do with her face. Choose a point and rest your eyes on it. Look at the person with whom you are about to disagree. Do not smile at anyone, until you mean it. They will take that for a weapon. They will be right.”

“My lady?” said Winifred, rising at last, with the pug’s chin gently removed from her boot. “Why are you doing this?”

“Because I am sixty-four,” said Lady Constance, “and I have been asked to nothing worth attending in twenty years. And because he will behave like a man who intends to be jilted.” She said it flatly. “Do not let him enjoy it.”

It had left off raining, which was an event, and she walked.

She took the long way, down through the wet green of the Park railings and into St James’s Street, because the pavement there was clean and the clubs had their shutters back, and because the rain had stopped and that happened so seldom in that June that it seemed to require an answer. She had on her good grey, and the glove two sizes too small, and the six pounds ten shillings in her mind, laid out already as silk, a plain blue-grey at four and six the yard from a man in Cheapside she knew. She was almost cheerful. At the bottom of the street, where the shops begin to run to prints and seals, there was a small crowd on the pavement, five or six persons and a boy, standing before a window with their heads together and the look of people who have found a dead mouse in a drawer and are not sorry.

It was Mr Treacher’s. She had set his handbills. She stopped behind a clergyman and looked over his hat.

The print was hand-coloured and very good. It showed a long, lean Marquess with a face like a heron, in a coat the colour of a wet pavement, correcting the figure of Venus on a pedestal with a pencil the length of a walking-stick; and riding at him from the left of the plate, on a gigantic copy of the Morning Gazette that had been drawn as a sort of flying carpet, came a short, broad girl in an apron and a pair of sabots, with a brass composing stick couched in her arm like a lance. Her hair was down. It had the look of a mop. The Marquess, looking round, had an expression of mild alarm, and in a balloon over his head, as Mr Treacher’s artist had it, were the words, My dear Madam, a semicolon! The title was across the foot, in an inscription of cheerful capitals: THE MISPRINT. Beneath, a smaller line read, Entirely Well Founded. Price One Shilling Plain, Two Coloured.

She laughed. It rose up in her before she had decided, a short helpless snort, at the pencil and at the sabots, which she had never worn, and the clergyman turned his head and looked at her as one looks at a person who has laughed in church. She laughed again. It was extremely good. It had caught the Marquess’s stoop to a hair. It had not caught the thumb; the artist had not known there was a thumb, and somebody had given her sabots instead; and she was standing in the middle of St James’s Street laughing at herself when the boy at the front, a lad of twelve with a tray of lavender, said clearly, “That’s her. That’s the one. Look at her hair.”

She stopped laughing. She did not stop all at once; it ran out of her, like the last of the water out of the pan, and what was left was a sensation which she identified, after a moment, as the difference between being a private joke and a public one, which was about three hundred persons. She took her glove from her left hand, and looked at the thumb, and put the glove back on. Then she walked on to the corner, with her chin up, and her hand at the rule in her hair, and a sort of burning behind the ears that she did not at all identify as pride.

At Hertford Street, that night, the house was quiet.

Lady Constance had gone to bed at ten, with the pug and a hot brick and a lecture to the housemaid on the drawing of curtains. The stuffed birds stood in the dark. In the attic, at the top of the last flight, which she climbed with her hand on the wall and her stockinged feet, a thin woman of forty-one let herself into the narrow room that had been hers for twelve years and shut the door.

Miss Agnes Fell had heard everything said in the morning-room that day. Being asked by nobody for her opinion of any of it, she had formed one, which she kept, as she kept a good many things, in a place where it could not be found. She was a person who, in a company of three, was apt to be taken for a piece of furniture, and in a company of twelve for two. She stood at the back of every room. She carried the shawl. She poured, and was sorry for the pot; and when she spoke, in her soft voice, with her mittened hands folded, the speaker nearest her would turn his head to see who had coughed. She had come to know to a nicety what nobody looked at, and she had a great deal of leisure in which to look at it.

She lit the night-candle from the stump on the washstand, and put it down on the table by the bed, where it would burn, as it always burned, until two. She took off the right mitten. The finger beneath it was stained blue-black to the second joint, and the ball of it, beside the nail, was hard with an old pale callus; she looked at it as one looks at an old acquaintance, without love and without surprise. From the drawer she took a penknife and a goose quill and a sheet of paper, and sat, and bent over the candle, and began to cut.

She had a way of sharpening a pen as though she were apologising to it.

chapters.title: A Marquess in the Composing Room
chapters.html:
“How do you do,” said the Marquess of Stanmere to the roof of a hackney coach. “How do you do. How do you do.”

“That was the nineteenth, my lord,” said Mr Minton, from the opposite seat.

“Has it improved?”

Minton looked at his watch, as though the answer might be kept in it. “It has become a different question each time. At the sixth it was a physician’s. At the twelfth, if I may say so, it was a magistrate’s. The last was the question of a man asking to be shown the door.”

“That was the one I was aiming at.”

They were toiling up Ludgate Hill in the rain, behind two horses of the sort that hackney proprietors buy at Smithfield for their opinions, and on the seat between the gentlemen, wrapped in a cloth and a spare sheet of the Corn Returns, lay a York ham of fourteen pounds. It was there because of a conclusion the Marquess had reached at one that morning, by candle, with the Articles of Agreement spread before him. Article the Third forbade him to lend, give, advance or promise money. It said money. It said nothing of swine. He had read it six times, as an honest man reads a contract in which he suspects himself of being outwitted, and had decided that a gentleman forbidden to be useful to a household might at least be permitted to feed it.

“Minton. Is a ham money?”

“It has a market price, my lord. Elevenpence the pound, at Leadenhall.”

“Money is what a price is paid in. A ham is what one gets for it. I have been over the ground.”

“Yes, my lord.” Minton looked at his watch again. “I only observe that Miss Pargeter set the Article.”

“I am aware who set the Article.”

This was his second call under the Second. The first, on Tuesday, had been paid in the manner of calls upon the dying: eleven minutes, a chair, the Drip, and Mr Pargeter’s foot discussed with great tenderness by everyone but its owner. “You will excuse me, my lord, I have a bishop,” Miss Pargeter had said, and gone on setting type, and he had stood in her composing room like a man who has brought the wrong gift to a christening. This time he proposed to be useful, in a manner not forbidden, and to begin by being received, which he understood to be the harder part. Minton’s inquiries had meanwhile established that the house was founded in 1781, kept two presses and a Methodist cook who sang, and had a roof that leaked. Of its debts Minton had learned nothing at all, which in his experience was where information usually stopped, and no sign that there were none.

The hackney would not enter the court. It put them down at the mouth of Paternoster Row, in a gutter that carried the opinions of every roof in the City, and went away with the air of a conveyance making a point. Over the arch hung the trade’s sign, a painted hand holding a painted pen, and the Marquess, who could not pass a signboard without examining its credentials, counted the fingers twice and was obliged to concede that the painter had gone on rather than stop. He said “How do you do” to the pump, once, for the sake of the practice.

The street door was opened before he touched it by a wide woman of sixty with a ladle, who looked past him, and past Minton, and at the ham. She looked at it as one looks at an idol carried in on a litter: with a deep and wary courtesy, and an unalterable intention of using it.

“How do you do,” said the Marquess. It was the twentieth, and the worst.

“’Cast thy bread upon the waters,’” said Mrs Hobday, weighing the ham in both arms. “It does not say it shall come back pork. But I never knew the Lord to be particular.” She received it as the pagan receives a sacrifice, gravely and without thanks, as a thing owing to the god for some time, and bore it down the cellar stair, whence presently arose Praise God from whom all blessings flow in the cheerful tone of a woman sharpening a knife.

Toby Mudge came out of the composing room with a pie in one hand and the pail in the other, saw the Marquess, and stopped as though shot. “Your Marquessship! Mr Fairweather says I’m to say my lord, and Miss says I’m not to say your honour on account of the bailiffs, so I’ve settled on Your Marquessship, which is both. Miss says gentlemen eat on alternate Thursdays. Is this one?”

“I shall have to consult an almanac.”

Winifred was at her frame under the best of the lamps, with her sleeves above the elbow and her mother’s stick in her left hand, and she did not turn round.

“You are early.”

“By the clock of St Paul’s I am ten minutes late.”

“By the clock of the press you are early. The press sleeps on a Thursday until nine and wakes at ten, and you have chosen a convenient hour, which I take for a compliment. I have a bishop and a circular and nobody to hold the cord. You have brought a ham.”

“I have read the Article six times.”

“Seven, I think. You have the look. It says money. It is silent on swine.”

“I had hoped you would find that.”

“I found it on Friday. I have been wondering what you would do with it.” She turned then, and looked him up and down, from the broken nose to the wet boots, as she might have looked at a sheet of poor paper she was nevertheless obliged to print upon. “Take off your coat. You will be in my light, my lord, and a man who stands in my light is a man I must find work for.”

The apron she took from its nail was her father’s, of leather, scarred and stiff and cut for a man of twice the Marquess’s girth; it went round him with a good deal to spare, and the pockets held a bodkin, a stub of pencil and the crust of a pie of great antiquity. She set him at the next frame and in six sentences explained the world.

“This is the case. The small letters live in the lower, under your hand; the capitals in the upper, because they are used less and may be farther off. The e has the biggest box because it is the commonest, and the j has a cupboard because nobody wants it. Every sort has a nick on its shank, and the nick faces out. If it does not, you will go wrong in a manner a pressman will describe to you at length.” She put the stick into his left hand. It was heavier than it looked, and warm from hers, and his thumb found the hollow worn in the brass and came out again at once, as a man steps out of another’s pew. “Mind it. It was my mother’s. Set your name.”

Julian, whose whole life had been an exercise in knowing which way a text ran, looked at the letters in the box, which faced the wrong way, and reasoned that to make a line come out forwards one must put it in backwards; and since the letters were backwards already, one must evidently begin at the far end. It was impeccable logic. He set his name from the last letter to the first, with the care of a watchmaker and an eye for the gaps, and Winifred pulled a proof on the little press in the corner and held it to the lamp, and one corner of her mouth went in.

“’Eremnats Nailuj,’” she read. “It sounds like a minor Egyptian god. Everyone does it, my lord. I set the Lord’s Prayer from the end at eleven years old and was sent to bed. You were being intelligent. It is the commonest mistake of the intelligent.”

“Is it?”

“It is the only one they make. The stupid make others.”

From the corner came a cough like a drawer being opened. Mr Orme had risen with his stick in his hand, and he crossed the floor at his own speed, which was a line a minute, and took the damp proof from her without a word and held it at arm’s length. He read it from the bottom right-hand corner to the top left.

“Julian Stanmere,” said Mr Orme. “Backwards, miss, it is perfectly plain. Even. Not a river in it. Who’s this?”

“Mr Orme, he is—”

“A new hand,” said Orme, with satisfaction, answering a question nobody had asked. “I thought so. You space like a man who was taught by somebody that hated rivers. That’s rare, young man. They’re all rivers nowadays. Where were you trained? Clerkenwell?”

“Harrow,” said the Marquess.

“Never heard of the house,” said Mr Orme. “But they’ve done you well.” He gave back the proof and went to his corner and sat.

Winifred opened her mouth to say what the Marquess was, in a voice that would have carried to Pomfret Yard, and shut it again. It was Orme’s first compliment to a living creature in three years, and she found, to her slight surprise, that she had no wish to take it back. The Marquess of Stanmere had been praised in his time for a great many things, none of them his own: for a griffin, for eleven farms, for a nose broken in a cause thought to do him credit. He folded the proof in four and put it in his waistcoat pocket, behind his watch, where he kept the things he did not intend to lose.

By noon he had set four lines of Lady Constance’s circular the right way round, been told three times to hold his thumb differently, and been made by Toby the Keeper of the Pan. “Your Marquessship, the quarter. I’m only a devil, and you’re in the apron.” He took the copper pan from the imposing stone in both hands, level, a little forward of the body, as Gantry carried a salver, and emptied it into the pail by the door. The Drip, he found, had a note and an interval and kept better time than the parish. At one, when the first sheet of the circular came off the Albion, Fairweather allowed him to lay a hand on the bar, an honour commonly reserved for visiting bishops and the owners of dogs, and said “Aye,” which meant that he might pull, and then “Aye,” which meant that he had pulled and might stop.
