SOCIETY FOR THE RELIEF OF DISTRESSED GENTLEWOMEN, said the sheet, and distressed was spelt correctly, and he was foolishly moved. He had steadied the paper with his right cuff. It came away grey-black from the wrist to the button, and in the doorway Minton closed his eyes.

They dined at half past one in the basement kitchen, on the ham, which Mrs Hobday carved with the air of a priestess in a good cause. Afterwards Winifred went up to her father, whose foot wanted its poultice at that hour as other men’s want a pipe, and Toby, through a mouthful, told the Marquess that if he wished to be of use he might fetch a bodkin from the long drawer under Miss Win’s frame.

The drawer held a whetstone, two pairs of tweezers, a paper of pins, the bodkin, and a round bonnet-box of faded green pasteboard, tied with tape, which had no business there and filled it from side to side. On the lid, in a small upright hand he would have known in the dark, someone had written K.F. 9.

The reader will have guessed what was in the hatbox. The Marquess had guessed it too, and opened it, which is the difference between a reader and a man.

Nine bundles, tied in red tape, one for each of the letters, and each made up of the proofs from the first pull to the last, folded in four and gone soft as linen with handling. He lifted the top sheet. He had written its first sentence in the library at Stanmere Court at four in the morning of last September, with a sleeping dog on his foot, and had never seen it in this condition, grey with other people’s thumbs. Down the margin ran her queries. You say “we” in this paragraph and “I” in the next. Which? W.P. He had said Which? to every vague question since he was nine years old. He found it in a stranger’s hand, and had to put the sheet down.

Pinned to the proof was a slip in Minton’s copperplate. The author is obliged. He means I. And at the foot of the sheet, after all her marks, the same pale hand: Thank you. Beneath that, in pencil, very small, in her own, was a thing nobody had been meant to see, because it had never been sent. Not at all.

Through the other bundles her pencil went like a hand through a hedge. Beside a passage on the poor-rate: True. Beside the labourer’s loaf, where the Farmer had set down what a family of six could buy on seven shillings: I have seen the loaf. He had the green pocket-book in his coat, with ninety of her questions pasted into it, and now he held the half of the correspondence he had not known existed, and it was kinder than his.

“You have found the bodkin.”

“I have found a hatbox.”

She did not hurry. She took it from him and put the lid straight, which is not the act of a person who is angry, and set it on the case between them like a thing that had been introduced. “They are the Farmer’s. You may look. Nobody ever has, and it is a dreadful waste of a hatbox. Nine letters. Ninety-one queries; I count them. Every one amended, and not once a word of dispute, and at the foot, Thank you. Do you know how many authors have thanked me in ten years? Two. One was a curate and the other was dead.”

“Dead?”

“His executors. He had left it in his will.” She lifted a proof out of the box without looking at it, as one reaches for a cup in one’s own kitchen. “Mr Ingram will say only that he is a gentleman in the Weald with a head for figures and no patience with ornament. I have made him a large man with a red face and a dog, who has been right about every hedge in Kent. I am quite prepared to find he is a clergyman with the gout.”

“And if he were something else?”

“I should be sorry. I have taken some trouble over the dog.” She did not smile, quite. “I read him, my lord. I do not read what I set; it would be like a butcher making friends with the animals. But the Farmer I read, right way up, with my hands in the stick, and some nights I cannot set the next line.” She held the sheet to the lamp. “’The price of corn is spoken of in this country as we speak of the weather, as a thing that happens to us, when it is a thing that is done by us.’ I wanted a semicolon after ‘weather’. He said no. He was right. It is the only time I have been glad to lose.”

It had cost him two hours, that comma. He had written it as a semicolon at four in the morning and taken it out at six and put it back at seven, and had walked about Stanmere Court ever since in the knowledge that nobody would ever notice. Somebody had noticed. She stood in the green light of the skylight with her blue thumb on his sentence, and she was speaking of him with the open, unguarded face of a person who talks of somebody she has never met and expects to like.

“Miss Pargeter,” he said. “The Farmer is—”

“Yes?”

The sentence in his mouth was five words long. He saw, with great clearness, all that would follow if he said it: she would be astonished, and then delighted, and then she would like the Farmer in him, with a loyalty already nine letters deep, and the Marquess would be introduced to her afterwards as the Farmer’s other self, and would stand at the back. He had been liked in his time for a griffin, for eleven farms, and for some months now by one woman in a hatbox for being right about the poor-rate. It had come to him that morning, with Mr Orme’s proof in his waistcoat, that nobody had yet liked him for a thing he had done badly and in good faith. It was an extremely small thing to want. He found that he wanted it very much, and that this was exactly the reason a man gives himself when he is afraid.

“—a very fortunate man,” he said. “To be so read.”

“He is not fortunate,” said Winifred. “He is read by a compositor. It is a different thing.” She put the lid on the box and the box in the drawer, and gave him the bodkin, and took up her stick.

Barnaby came down at three on Toby’s arm, backwards, a step at a time, with his foot in its flannel and the air of a man who has been told that a peer is using his Albion and means to see it done with respect. He was established at the end of the stone on one stool, with the foot on another. Winifred had set the Marquess to read the bishop’s proof, since he could not be trusted with the type. He found three errors, and she found two of them.

“My dear fellow, you have ink on your cuff.”

“I know.”

“It will not come out.”

“I did not suppose it would.”

“Good. That is how you tell a convert from a visitor. A visitor will wipe it, now, but I was going to say, about the toggle, that if it were set a trifle lower— no. Never mind.” He regarded the Marquess over the spectacles on his forehead, that is, at the ceiling. “You are looking at the stick.”

“I was looking at the thumb.”

“Everyone looks at the thumb. It is the stick’s, you know, not hers: the hollow. Two thumbs in the one place. Naomi’s first. Naomi Lamb; a compositor’s daughter. She set the Psalms at nineteen, in a back room in Warwick Lane over a chandler’s, in Long Primer, for a Bible-warehouse that never knew whom to thank. The whole Book of Psalms, by a candle in a saucer, in four months, and I went round to read the proofs. I read them for a fortnight. They were perfect on the first day. I am told it is called courtship.” The Albion sighed through the wall. “She died in the spring of 1807, of a consumption, and Win took up the stick the week after the funeral and has not put it down. She was seventeen. You will have noticed that she carries things.”

“I had noticed.”

“I let her,” said Barnaby, “which you will also have noticed. I am the one sitting down.” He lifted the flannel an inch, and let it fall. “It is a very fine excuse.” Then, quickly, as a man gets a tooth over: “I am bound to ask, my dear fellow. It is the form. A father who doesn’t ask is a father who can’t be blamed, and I would rather be blamed. What are your intentions?”

The Marquess had been asked in his time by eleven mothers and one bishop what his intentions were, and had answered them all with a number. He found that he had no number.

“Honourable,” he said.

“Quite right,” said Barnaby. “Nobody else’s are ever any use.” He looked immensely relieved, and as though he could not have said why, and took the spectacles from his forehead and put them on his nose and, as a result, saw nothing.

It was a quarter to four when the sound of the Albion stopped, which in that house was like the stopping of a clock, and everyone looked up.

A small gentleman stood in the door of the composing room with his hat in one hand and a furled umbrella in the other. He was perhaps forty-eight, and neat as a pin that has been polished. He wore a coat the colour of snuff, with no snuff on it, and a pair of spectacles pushed up on his forehead and a second pair above them, and a magnifying glass hung on a ribbon from his waistcoat; and his hands, folded on the handle of the umbrella, had been scrubbed to the pink of a new mouse.

The Chapel closed its ranks without anyone appearing to move. Orme’s stick stopped. Fairweather, in the press-room door, folded his arms. Sparrow, who had been whistling, broke off in the middle of a bar and found a great deal to do at the far end of the room, and in the passage below Mrs Hobday’s hymn gave out at “the Lord is.”

“Barnaby,” said the small gentleman, in a voice as soft as a clean cuff. “I would not have intruded on a day like this.”

“Hector!” said Barnaby. It rang a good deal too heartily. “My dear fellow, my dear Hector, come in, you are wet through—”

“Madam.” A bow to Winifred. “My lord.” A smaller bow, the exact bow due to a marquess and not an eighth of an inch beyond. “Hector Lovejoy, of the Phoenix Press, in Ave Maria Lane. Your lordship’s servant. I had the honour to be Mr Pargeter’s apprentice for seven years, and have been his neighbour for twenty-six. I have called to pay my compliments, as one does. I wish you joy, my lord. It is a very remarkable thing.”

“Mr Lovejoy,” said Julian. “You are very good.” It was not a lie, and he was aware of saying it carefully.

Mr Lovejoy looked up. The Drip let go of its slate and struck the pan. “You have a leak, Barnaby.”

“A trifle.”

“One in four seconds. It will have the beam in three winters.” He said it as another man would remark on a view. He was shown the Albion, which he asked to see as a man might ask to see a friend’s grave, and ran one pink finger down the toggle without touching the ink. “Ebenezer’s hand. Beautiful. I have always said, Barnaby, it was the handsomest folly in London.” Barnaby, who had heard it called the folly a hundred times in the Row and the handsomest never, laughed far too loud. In the corner Mr Lovejoy gave the Old Lady a small nod, as one nods to a lady met earlier in other circumstances, and she, being oak, did not return it.

Toby had stationed himself by the street door with a stack of folded Gazettes under his arm, relics of the Thursday of the sixth that he had found at the bottom of the loft stair and had been selling in the court since Monday to the curious, at a shilling a head. Mr Lovejoy stopped in front of him.

“You have a number of the sixth of June, I think, my boy.”

“It’s a shilling, sir. They’re relics.”

“The price is printed above the title,” said Mr Lovejoy. “Sevenpence, the stamp included. I should not like you to take a shilling off a gentleman when the Government has taken fourpence already.” He counted the money into the child’s palm. “One. Two. Three. Four. Five. Six. Seven.” Each coin was set down separately, in a voice of grave kindness, as pennies are laid on the eyes of the dead. He took the paper and folded it in three, with the care of a man who folds nothing carelessly, so that the end of the magnifying glass showed at the fold. Then he turned at the door to Winifred, who had not moved.

“A very fine W,” said Mr Lovejoy.

He bowed to the room, and went out under the arch, and the rain closed behind him.

Barnaby had gone the colour of tallow. Winifred stood quite still, with the stick in her hand and her thumb in the hollow, and her face showed nothing, which in a face so much used to showing the weather was a thing to be afraid of. Julian, who understood none of it, asked.

“What is a very fine W?”

“It is a remark on a letter.”

“I had gathered it was a letter. I am a reasonable man.”

“Quite,” said Winifred, which was his word, and she gave it to him in his own voice, and he heard it.

It was Barnaby who spoke at last, in the light high voice of a man making a joke so that the room will not have to. “He was the finest hand I ever trained, my dear fellow. Seven years. I never told him so. One doesn’t. They get above themselves.” He looked at his thumbs. “Hector holds my paper, you know. For the Albion and the damp. Seven hundred and forty pounds of it, at six per cent, falling due at Michaelmas, and a very civil gentleman about the interest.”

Michaelmas. The word went into the Marquess like a pin. He had asked her a week ago in this room why Michaelmas, and she had said that it was a Quarter Day, and it had been, as she said, perfectly true. In the time it took Barnaby to finish the sentence he had arranged four things in his head: a banker, a lawyer, a plumber, and a word in Mr Underhill’s ear. Three were money and the fourth was Mr Underhill. His hand had gone to his breast, where the Marquess of Stanmere kept, by long habit, the instrument for getting out of any difficulty in the world, which was a cheque-book on Child’s, and it had stopped there, half drawn.

“Article the Third,” said Winifred, without looking up.

The hand went back.

The Albion began again, and the room resumed itself piece by piece, as a room does after a bell. The lamps were lit at five, in June, in the rain-dusk of the Row. Minton went out to find a hackney, and the Marquess of Stanmere went out into the court by himself, in his coat and one ink-grey cuff, and stood by the pump.

He went through the verbs of the Third Article as a man tries the keys on a ring: lend, give, advance, promise. They were all the wrong key. He had signed it himself, with a tolerable laugh, in front of a witness who wept. It was an extremely well-made Article, and he had admired the placing of its second comma.

The rain ran into his collar. Behind him, through the window of the composing room, he could see the lamp over the first frame and under it a small square figure with a brass rule in her hair, who had picked up her mother’s stick again and was setting a line, quickly, without looking at the case. Nobody had asked him to stay, and nobody had asked him to go. There was a sum, and a woman, and a man with a magnifying glass, and the thing in his pocket that would have made it all go away had been forbidden him by a contract of his own devising. He stood in a printer’s court with his hands in his pockets and the ink of the Society for Distressed Gentlewomen drying on his cuff, obeying an agreement he had written himself, and found that it was the least comfortable thing he had ever done for anyone.

chapters.title: The Crooked W
chapters.html:
At seven in the morning on Friday the fourteenth of June, in a counting-room above the Phoenix Press in Ave Maria Lane, a very small man washed his hands. He washed them in yellow soap, in a basin that a boy had filled for the purpose and would empty and fill again, and it was the third time he had done so since rising; and when they were the pink of a boiled prawn and dry as paper he took up a magnifying glass on a ribbon, and went to the north window, and laid out the Gazette.

Mr Hector Lovejoy was forty-eight, and the neatest man in the Row, which he did not live in, being too exact to inhabit anything so crooked. He stood five feet two in his boots. He wore a coat the colour of snuff, with no snuff on it, and carried two pairs of spectacles on his forehead, one above the other, for no purpose anybody had discovered, since he read type with the glass. He believed nothing that he could not see, and nothing that he could see until it was enlarged.

There were three numbers of the Morning Gazette on the slope of the desk, set edge to edge: Tuesday the fourth, Thursday the sixth, Tuesday the eleventh. He had known since the sixth, at his breakfast, in the way a man knows who sees a face in a crowd and cannot yet say where; by Monday he had the where. He had gone to Hand and Pen Court yesterday to look at the faces. This morning he took the last step, which was to prove it, because Mr Lovejoy did not allow himself to know a thing that he could not lay out on a desk.

On the fourth, at the foot of the third column of the second page, stood three lines in a Long Primer that he had known for thirty years. FAIR COPYING in a plain hand, for authors, lawyers and composers of music; and beneath it, centred, Miss W. Pargeter, of Paternoster Row. On the eleventh, the same. On the sixth, between them, the advertisement stood with its name cut off, a gap of white at its foot exactly the depth of one line, the quads that had filled it shining faintly under the glass like the place where a tooth has been. And on the same page, at the head of the second column, under a lost spaniel, in a paragraph about a marquess, stood a line that had been somewhere else.

He put the glass to the W.

The Pargeter fount was a Long Primer that Barnaby had bought new in 1782, the year before a boy of fifteen named Hector Lovejoy had been bound to him. The capital W had been nicked in the left foot ever since, and it printed, as it had printed on every Pargeter handbill in the City, with a white hairline across the leg, as though the letter wore one boot thinner than the other. He saw it on the fourth. He saw it on the eleventh. And he saw it, black on grey, in the Marquess’s paragraph, in Miss W. Pargeter, of Paternoster Row, with the same hairline, and the line itself spaced out as a centred line is spaced, with quads at either end, to fill a measure it had never been cut for. A secretary writing for a marquess does not give the bride’s address as a trade imprint. A secretary does not give it at all. It was a printer’s line, from a printer’s own advertisement, and it lay in the wrong paragraph because it had been in a heap on the floor.

He did not need the Marquess’s words. He had set a hundred denials, and a denial has the shape of a door: one knows where the hinges go. Well founded wanted to be without foundation; engaged to the lady wanted to be engaged to no lady whatever. The Gazette had printed the joints of a denial, out of order, with a name in the middle that had no business to be there.

Standing at the window with the glass in his hand, Mr Lovejoy saw the whole of it as clearly as if he had been in the room. He saw the rain come in at the broken slate that every printer in the Row knew about, and the slip blotted. He saw the Gazette’s reader abed with a quinsy (the apothecary lived in Ave Maria Lane, and had told his barber). He saw the rule against proofs after midnight. He saw a page on the floor, because a page does not wander; a page is dropped, by a boy; and two lines of one measure lying side by side in the pie, and a woman of twenty-six at midnight with her sleeves above the elbow and the forme to be locked by one, setting what her hands knew. It was a beautiful error. It had the grace of a thing that nobody could have done on purpose. He would have given a year’s profit to have seen the page go down, and for the space of perhaps a minute Mr Lovejoy was almost sorry.

He had been Barnaby Pargeter’s apprentice for seven years, from 1783 to 1790, and in all that time Barnaby had never once told him to wash his hands, and never once noticed that he did. It is possible to build a good deal on seven years of that. Mr Lovejoy rang for his clerk.

Mr Fogg was long, damp and agreeable, like a candle left out overnight. He had been eleven years in the counting-room, in which time he had learned that his master wished to be told only what was so, by Mr Fogg’s own observation, and in the fewest words.

“We shall walk to Pomfret Yard, Mr Fogg. I have an advertisement to place.”

“Yes, sir. Is it a new advertisement?”

“It is a new fount of Pica, Mr Fogg. It is an advertisement in every sense that I can honestly give the word.”

Pomfret Yard lay six-tenths of a mile from the Row, down Ave Maria Lane and Ludgate Hill and into Fleet Street, and in the rain it cost Mr Lovejoy, Mr Fogg and one umbrella twenty minutes. In the course of them Mr Lovejoy said nothing whatever, and Mr Fogg, who understood that this was a good sign, said less.

The counting-room of the Gazette was long and low, with a stove at one end and high desks along both walls, and a smell of ink, tobacco and loyal sentiment; at the desks a dozen clerks sat entering sevenpences. Mr Lovejoy laid down four guineas for seven lines, to run a month, and counted them aloud into the clerk’s palm, “One. Two. Three. Four,” and the clerk, who had been robbed in his day by cleverer men, counted them again and found him exact. And from the inner room, with the sound of a vessel coming into dock, came Mr Ezekiel Underhill.

He was large and pink and fifty-five, with a speaking voice like the bass pipes of an organ, which he used on a clerk, a visitor and a coal-scuttle alike. He was blowing like a whale with pride. “Lovejoy! My dear sir! You find us in the full flood of success. You will have seen our number.”

“I have it by me, Mr Underhill.”

“Eleven hundred, sir, and six hundred more by Friday, and the Strand cleared by nine. I have been stopped in Fleet Street by two bishops. A marquess, a printer’s daughter, and the Gazette the first to announce it! I give you my word, sir, there is not a woman between here and Tunbridge who has not asked me whether it is true. I mean to raise the run again at Michaelmas. I mean to double it.”

“And is it true, Mr Underhill?”

“Is it—” Mr Underhill’s face, which was pink, became pinker. “The Marquess’s household authorised it, sir. The Gazette printed what it was authorised to print. I have always held that a newspaper cannot be answerable for the facts, only for the printing of them.”

“I have heard it said,” observed Mr Lovejoy gently, “that in nineteen years the Gazette has never found occasion to correct itself.”

“Nineteen years and a month, sir.” The pink deepened with pleasure. “The Gazette does not retract. It clarifies. Between ourselves, Lovejoy, Pargeter has two presses and a roof, and I have sometimes thought that a journal of our circulation might be better served by a house with, ah, a broader foundation. But he has this daughter, and now this marquess, and one cannot have everything. A very fine house, if the roof were mended.”

“A very fine house,” said Mr Lovejoy.

In the corner of the counting-room, on a hard chair beside the stove where no one sat and no one looked, an old woman in grey was reading the Gazette with a pencil. She wore a white cap. She had turned her better ear to the room, and she read as a farmer walks a field, line by line, from one hedge to the other, and now and then put a small mark in the margin and went on. Mr Lovejoy had known the proprietor of the Morning Gazette by sight for six years, and had never been introduced, because she was a person nobody introduced. He had once taken her for the stove.

“Does thee know the engagement is well founded, Ezekiel,” said Mrs Rudge, not looking up, “or only that it has been printed?”

Mr Underhill bristled. It was a remarkable thing to see, in so pink a man, like a ham in a rage. “The Marquess authorised it, madam.”

“A newspaper that cannot say it was wrong,” said Mrs Rudge, making a small mark in the margin of the Births, “cannot be trusted when it says it is right.”

“The Gazette has not been wrong, madam.”

“I did not say it had. I said it could not say.”

Mr Underhill discovered a pressing need to look at a ledger. The pencil moved down the column. And Mr Lovejoy, who had been watching the pencil with more attention than he had given the editor, understood in the space of one sentence what Mr Underhill had not understood in six years: that the sharpest instrument in that room was the one with the pencil. He had come that morning with the whole matter in his head, and a half-formed notion of laying it in Mr Underhill’s hands as a dog lays down a bird. He saw now what would happen. Underhill, in terror of a correction, would bury it. And the old woman, who read with a pencil, would not let him; she would order the Gazette to say it was wrong, and Pargeter’s would lose a paragraph’s pride and keep a contract, and Mr Lovejoy would have bought a bird for nothing.

He decided to wait. A fruit is picked when it falls into the hand; and it falls the harder for being left to ripen on a high branch.

In the yard a bent man in an oilskin was washing the wheels of a cart with a besom, in company with a horse of great age and no illusions. Mr Lovejoy stopped under the arch, with the rain running off the umbrella on to Mr Fogg.

“Who is that, Mr Fogg?”

“Sowerby, sir. The Gazette’s carter. Nineteen years on the box.”

“And he was in Hand and Pen Court at five o’clock on the morning of the sixth, with the cart, for the sheets?”

“He is there every Gazette morning, sir.”

Mr Lovejoy regarded the back of the oilskin for the space of a breath. It had a face on the other side, he supposed, like an old saddle, and it had been standing, he supposed, within a few yards of a woman with a sheet in her hand. “I should like to know what he saw. You will find him in the Goose and Gridiron, in St Paul’s Churchyard, when his round is done; he is a man of regular habits. You will buy him a quart. You will say that you are Mr Fogg, clerk to Hector Lovejoy, and that you have a thirst and a fellow-feeling for carters. If he asks who sent you, you will tell him. It is astonishing how rarely a man asks.”

“And what am I to ask him, sir?”

“Nothing. You will talk about horses.” He walked on, into Fleet Street. “A quart freely bought is the smallest debt in the world, Mr Fogg, and a man pays it in his own time. A fruit is better for being asked after before it falls.”

The Phoenix Press was the long building in Ave Maria Lane with the handsome front: a bow window of a hundred and twelve small panes, each of which its master had seen cleaned, and a brass plate on the door polished every morning at six by a boy who had been told what would happen if he did not. Behind the counting-room were six presses, forty hands and a silence of the kind only achieved by a man who has never raised his voice and never needed to. Mr Lovejoy did not print a lie. He held it to be the whole of his respectability. He printed true things in the places where they did the most harm, and since the Town Crier had been three times threatened with the law and never once cast, it may be said that the system answered.

At four in the afternoon a boy of ten, a very ordinary boy who looked as if he had been told nothing, put into the porter’s hand a packet sealed with a plain wafer, as he did every Friday, and went away. Mr Lovejoy took it upstairs himself.

It was the column called The Quizzing-Glass, by Peregrine Pry, and it came, as it always came, in a law-stationer’s round hand, as flat and characterless as drawn lead, so that nothing of the writer survived the copying but the opinions. The boy fetched it from a hole in a wall in Cursitor Street and could have told you nothing but the wall. Mr Lovejoy had never asked who Pry was. He held that a man should find out a thing in the order in which it was useful.

He read it standing, with the glass. Mr Pry presents his compliments to Mr Treacher, of St James’s Street, whose Misprint has sold four hundred and eleven impressions at a shilling plain and two coloured, which is three hundred and sixty-two more than the Marquess of Stanmere has sold of himself. Mr Pry has nothing to add to the title. It went on for a column. It was wicked and exact and unsigned, and it was extremely good. He found one fault, a comma after impressions that parted a verb from its object, and mended it with the pencil from behind his ear; it was his only liberty with Mr Pry, and he took it every week. Then in the margin, beside the last line, he wrote one word, and underlined it once.

More.

At four o’clock, in the basement kitchen of Hand and Pen Court, with an hour to spare before the copy, Winifred Pargeter sat at the end of the long table with the books of the house open before her. Her father sat opposite, with his foot on a stool and his spectacles on his forehead, and the Drip, which had followed them down in the form of a bucket, struck the bottom of it at her elbow with a small flat note.

There were the day-book, the ledger, the cash-box (eleven pounds four shillings and sevenpence) and three slips of stamped paper lying on top of the heap like a row of teeth. Each was in her father’s loose hand and another’s, neat as copperplate, in which the word Lovejoy had been written with a care that made it look like a monument.

“Three hundred pounds, the twenty-ninth of September, 1814,” read Winifred. “Two hundred and forty, Lady Day, 1815. Two hundred, Michaelmas, 1815. Seven hundred and forty pounds at six per cent, falling due this Michaelmas, renewed to it in March as it was renewed the September before. And the clause.” She read it with her finger under the line, as she would have read the proof of a man she distrusted. “’And in the event that the said Barnaby Pargeter shall cease, by whatever cause, to be the printer of the Morning Gazette, the whole sum shall become payable upon demand.’ By whatever cause. He wrote that, Father, in his own hand.”

“Yes, my dear. It is very clear. Hector was always clear.”

“And the bond to the Gazette is five hundred pounds, forfeit upon a correction. And the cash-box holds eleven pounds four and sevenpence.”

“Quite. Well, now, Win, about the bond—”

“The Lord is my shepherd,” sang Mrs Hobday, descending the cellar stair with a tureen held before her like the Ark of the Covenant, “I shall not want. Pease. It is a Friday, and the Lord provides on a Friday in pulses.” She ladled. “Cleft for me,” she told the bowl, and went up again.

“Go on, Father.”

“What? Oh. Yes. The bond.” Barnaby took a spoonful of pease, and put it down. “It is not the money, Win, is it? I see that. It is that W.”

“He said it to the room. He said it as another man would say good day.”

“Hector never in his life said a thing that was not so. It is a great fault in a creditor.” Barnaby shook his head. “He was the finest hand I ever trained. I never told him so. One doesn’t.”

“Father, in seven years, did you tell him anything?”

“I told him to mind the roof,” said Barnaby, and looked up at the ceiling, where the Drip came through, and they both began, helplessly, to laugh.

It stopped, as it does. She looked down at the three slips, and pulled the ledger towards her. “The Society’s circular is six pounds ten, when it is paid. There is the bishop. There is the Gazette. Father—”

“The thing is, Win, about the bond, that I have been meaning to—”

“Give us this day,” said Mrs Hobday, reappearing at the foot of the stair with a loaf under her arm, “our daily bread.” She set it down upon the ledger. “And forgive us our trespasses. It’s the Wednesday’s, but it has the virtue of age.” She went up singing.

Winifred moved the bread. “You were saying.”

“I was saying that— the bond, my dear, the bond is—” and the cellar door opened for the third time, and Mrs Hobday appeared with a second tureen, steaming, and wearing the expression of a woman who has been given a text.

“And the Lord said unto Peter, Rise, kill, and eat,” said Mrs Hobday, in a spirit of exegesis. “And Peter said, Not so, Lord. And the Lord said, What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common. Acts, ten. It is the bone of the Marquess’s ham, miss, with a turnip. I never was one to see a gift go to waste because of the donor’s rank.”

Winifred looked at the soup. She had ruled, on Thursday morning, that the Third Article said money; she could not in conscience now find that it spoke of soup. She took the spoon.

Barnaby ate. He was a man who had been given by Providence, three times in a quarter of an hour, a reason not to speak, and he took the hint. What he had been about to say, and had been about to say since the sixth of June, and indeed since the spring of 1812, was that the bond of five hundred pounds which Mr Underhill had required of him when the contract was signed had not been secured upon his word. It had been secured upon the house: upon the brick and the slates and the Drip, upon the table at which his daughter sat counting. He had signed it on a wet afternoon with a good pen and a light heart, because it had seemed to him a thing that would never be called. A correction had been unthinkable. The Gazette had not printed one in nineteen years.

At twenty minutes to five a boy came down the area steps in a coat with a phoenix on the button, and left a note, and would not wait. It was addressed in a hand so even it might have been engraved; Lovejoy wrote as he printed, and his letters had never in their lives been at odds. Barnaby took it. He read it twice, with the spectacles brought down to the place where they were meant to be, and passed it across the soup.

Mr Pargeter,—My compliments on your daughter’s engagement. I find I shall require the full sum at Michaelmas. H.L.

“Full,” said Barnaby. “He has renewed twice. I was going to ask him at the quarter-day for— ” He laid the paper on the table and set his hands flat on either side of it. “I did not know he was a man who could be cruel in so few words.”

“He is not cruel,” said Winifred. “He is exact. It is much worse.”

She read it a third time. My compliments on your daughter’s engagement. She had known since the sixth that someone would see it. It had never occurred to her that the someone would be so civil. A hundred and seven days: she had the figure before she had asked for it, as she always did. Ninety-one, with the Sundays out. Seven hundred and forty pounds was eight pounds two shillings of every working day of them, in a house that took, on a good day, three.

“Father,” she said. “Do you know, I have been looking at this the wrong way.”

“My dear?”

“I have been reading it as a thing done to us. It is not. It is a thing done in reply.” She laid her thumb, her blue one, upon the word engagement. “Mr Lovejoy does not send a compliment that he cannot sell. He has told us in sixteen words that he knows what we are worth and what we are not. Very well. I am engaged to a marquess. It is in the Gazette. Every duchess in Mayfair has a dinner-list that wants setting, and a visiting-card, and a funeral ticket, and a notice of an at-home, and the Society for the Relief of Distressed Gentlewomen is only the first of them. I am to be seen on six occasions. I shall be seen on sixty. I shall leave a card.” The colour had come back to her face, and with it something Barnaby had not seen in it since the sixth, and which he took, with misgiving, for appetite. “They want to look at a printer. Let them look at a printer. They shall pay for the privilege at ordinary rates.”

“My dear girl, you cannot print a Season.”

“Mr Orme has printed worse.”

St Paul’s struck five, through the rain, like a man with a cold. Upstairs the street door opened on the boy from Pomfret Yard with the copy, damp, in a clerk’s fair hand, and she wiped her hands on her apron and went up to be a printer. Barnaby remained below with the pease, the bread, the Marquess’s ham and the bond, and ate on; and it was to be a long time before he told her.

That night, a hundred yards apart, the two houses were engaged upon the same work, at the same hour, in the same fount, as like as two hands. In Hand and Pen Court Winifred Pargeter set the Fashionable Intelligence with the Drip at her elbow and no one to proof it. In Ave Maria Lane Mr Lovejoy set the Crier himself, as he did every Friday, because he trusted nobody else with the comma.

At one in the morning, with the forme locked and the presses begun and the Phoenix Press given over to the thump of the ink-rollers and forty men who did not speak, he went into the counting-room, and lit a candle, and drew up a stool to his own case. He took a W from the upper case of the Long Primer, from the same foundry as Barnaby’s, sound as a bell. He laid the glass to it. With the point of a penknife, by the candle, on a scrap of waste, he nicked the left foot of it a hair’s breadth, and pulled a trial, and nicked it again, three times, until it printed as the other did. It took eleven minutes, which was ten more than the matter was worth, and it cost him a W that had never done anyone any harm. In thirty years he had never put a flaw into a sort except by accident, and then he had thrown the sort away. He did this one perfectly.

He set a line. MISS W. PARGETER, in capitals, in the stick, with the spaces exact. He locked it into a little chase no bigger than a hymn-book, and inked it, and pulled a proof on the small press in the corner of the room, and held it to the candle. The glass found it at once: a thread of white across the foot of the W, the width of a hair, precisely where Barnaby’s had it.

Mr Lovejoy looked at it for some time. Then he folded the proof small, once, and again, to the size of a wafer, and opened the drawer in which he kept the three notes of hand and the other things he intended to be paid for, and laid it on top. He locked the drawer, and washed his hands, and put out the candle. In the dark, under the paper, the little square kept its secret: a W with one boot thinner than the other.

chapters.title: A Rout in the Rain
chapters.html:
“Say it again,” said Barnaby, “as though I were a duchess.”

“It is in the Gazette.”

“Too much Gazette. You sound as if you were selling it. A duchess will want to be told, my dear, not offered a subscription. Lower. Slower. Let the word come at the end like the imprint, where it belongs and where nobody looks.”

They were in a hackney on Piccadilly, in a line of carriages that had not moved in eleven minutes, and the rain was coming down upon the roof with the steady insistence of a creditor. Barnaby sat wedged into the corner with his gouty foot, in its flannel boot the size of a loaf, laid across the opposite seat, and his spectacles pushed up on his forehead, wearing the coat in which he had been married in 1788 and which had since been let out twice. He had refused to be left at home. He had also refused, with the dignity of a man who has been quoted the price of dress shoes, to go in; he was to see her as far as the carriage step, as a bishop sees a bride as far as the altar rail, and then be taken back to the Row.

Winifred sat very upright, because the silk allowed nothing else. It was blue-grey, four and sixpence the yard from a man in Cheapside, and in the three days since it had passed into the hands of Lady Constance’s dressmaker it had been cut, turned, taken in, let out and given what that lady called a line, which Winifred, who set lines for her bread, privately thought she had always possessed. At her throat was the seed-pearl brooch that had been her mother’s. Her hair was dressed higher than it had ever been dressed, and through the knot of it, because she had declined with a politeness that made the ear-trumpet tremble to be pinned with anything else, was the brass composing rule. “A pin,” Lady Constance had said at last, “is a pin,” and had let it pass. On her right hand she wore a white kid glove that fitted. On her left she wore another, two sizes too small, as a matter of policy: a glove that fits shows a thumb, and a glove that does not fit shows only a glove.

“It is in the Gazette,” said Winifred, lower and slower.

“Better. A little more disdain.”

“I have no disdain. I have a blister.”

“Then use the blister.” Barnaby considered her in the lamplight with his head on one side. “You are uncommonly like your mother, Win. I should mention that it makes me nervous. Her father asked me what I earned a week before he asked my name, and I said forty-two shillings and a good heart, and he said he could not eat the second.”

Somewhere beyond the roofs to the west a gun went off with a flat wet cough. Then, after an interval, another.

“What in the world—”

“The Park, Father. They are firing the salute. It is the anniversary.”

“It sounds like a sack of coals going down a stair.”

“The powder has been rained on since Sunday.” She counted the third. “Nine seconds apart. Fairweather pulls faster than that, and quieter.”

The hackney moved four lengths and stopped again. Ormsgill House stood back from the road behind a wall and a double row of flambeaux that the rain had reduced to sullen orange smears, and footmen in the Ormsgill claret were conveying ladies from carriage to awning under umbrellas the size of tents. The awning was striped, and leaked in stripes. When the hackney at last drew up at the step, the footman who opened the door took in at a glance the hackney, the flannel boot, the old man in the married coat and the lady in blue-grey, and produced the blank face of a man who had once served a Prince and did not intend to be surprised by anything again.

Barnaby leaned across the straw. “Go and be looked at, Win,” he said. “It is what a title-page is for.” And he caught her left hand, the small-gloved one, and held it a moment, and said to the thumb in a different voice, “Your mother would have given a month’s wages for a ticket.” Then he let go, and sat back, and said, “Mind the roof,” and the footman, who had heard him, looked at the sky.

There were forty-one steps in the great staircase of Ormsgill House, white marble with a gilt rail, and she counted them, as one does, to have something to do with her face. Lady Constance had met her in the hall, in black bombazine and the purple ribbon, with Miss Fell a pace behind carrying the shawl, and had said, “You are four minutes late. I allowed three. It is a question of arithmetic: four minutes is the interval at which a person is noticed arriving and has not yet been missed.” She had then taken the stair as a dray takes a cask, slowly, braced, and without conversation.

Winifred had read a great many people in her time, from the far side of a case. She had never before been proofed. It was done on the stairs, by eye alone, between the first landing and the second: a hundred faces leaned over the rail in postures of the most careless interest, and the whisper ran down ahead of her like a wet finger down a column.

“That is the printer.”

“She is a great deal smaller than the print.”

“I understood she carried a lance.”

“Is that a pin in her hair?”

“It is a rule, I believe. A printer’s rule. For measuring.”

“How very exact.”

“She has her own hair. One can tell.”

She had her own hair, and a rule through it, and a thumb in a glove that did not fit. She kept her eyes on a point at the head of the stairs, as she had been taught, and found that the point was a tall man in black, slightly stooped, who had been standing there for twenty minutes, which for a man who loathed routs was a form of courage and for a man who loathed waiting was a form of lunacy.

“Good evening,” said Julian. He looked at her for rather longer than the words required. There was a notch in his left eyebrow, white against the sandy brow, and it lifted. “You look as though you were about to be set in type.”

“Imposed, I think the word is.”

“I had the word justified ready and it seemed too hopeful.”

“Locked up in a chase,” said Winifred, “and wedged with a quantity of furniture.”

“And planed down.”

“Planed, certainly. It is how one gets the level.” She felt it begin in the ribs, where the stays were, and could do nothing about it; and he, with his hand on the gilt rail and the faintest of lines at the corner of that grave mouth, appeared to be doing nothing about it either. They laughed. It was the first time they had done so together, and rather more of the head of the stairs turned round than either of them had counted upon.

“Come,” said Julian, composing his face. “I am to present you to everybody. It will take a quarter of an hour, and you will not remember a name. It does not matter. They will remember yours.”

It will be known to the reader that there is no custom in English society so firm as the question, and none so easily answered by a person of nerve, who need only decline the question and reply to something else. Winifred did not know it. She had a formula, and a formula is a form of nerve.

The first to ask was a gentleman with a stick and a face like a disappointed ham, who put himself in front of her at the foot of the saloon and demanded without preamble whether it was true that she was to be Marchioness of Stanmere. “It is in the Gazette,” said Winifred. The gentleman stared at her, and she at him, and his colour altered by degrees from ham to something nearer salmon. “Ha,” he said. “Very proper. Very proper indeed.” And he went away to tell a friend that she was the soul of discretion.

The second was a Mrs Chalmers, a very broad lady in puce, who wore on her bosom, pinned like a brooch, the Waterloo medal of a Colonel Chalmers who had been in the battle for forty minutes and had not recovered, and who asked after the settlements. “It is in the Gazette,” said Winifred, and Mrs Chalmers said she was sure it was, and went on to tell her about a cook in Cheltenham for nine minutes without drawing breath.

The third was a pale girl of seventeen in white muslin, who said, with her hands clasped and her eyes enormous, “Oh, is it true?” and received her answer, and sighed, and said, “How romantic.” It was the first time in Winifred’s life that anyone had called her romantic, and it was for declining to say anything at all. She did not know whether to be flattered or to be afraid.

She heard Julian, ten feet off, asked by a bald earl whether the thing were settled. “I am assured that it is in the Gazette,” he said, in the voice of a man reading from a bill of lading, and the earl looked at him sharply, and then at her, and then, in a way that she found very instructive, almost with envy. By ten o’clock the saloon was saying that the Marquess and Miss Pargeter had a delicate reticence. By eleven it was a famous one.

“Ah,” said somebody at her elbow, in a voice like warm gravy. “So this is the young person.”

It was a lady of fifty, in raspberry silk, stout and rustling and tightly laced, with a fan she was using as a weapon and a pair of eyes that went over Winifred as a shopman’s go over a counterfeit shilling: front, back, edge. Lady Quarles. The lady swayed. She laid the back of her hand against her forehead, in the manner of a woman about to expire upon a sofa, and looked about for the sofa; but she had fainted at four routs already that Season and the footmen had become expert at not being near. After a moment she recovered with a great sigh, and went away, trailing raspberry, in the direction of the supper-room.

“That,” said a voice from behind the nearest pillar, “was Mama. She does it at the sight of any person who has not been introduced at the proper moment. You may come round here. It is quite safe. I have been standing here for forty minutes and nobody has noticed.”

Winifred went round the pillar. She found a tall young woman with a great many freckles, large capable hands and a brown dress that had plainly been to a great many routs before this one, and had a pair of spectacles on a chain round her neck, which she put on to look at Winifred and took off again.

“I’m the previous engagement,” said Miss Quarles. “Verity Quarles. I only wished to say thank you, because Mama has been trying to sell me to your Marquess since March and I should have had to refuse him, which is awkward when it is a Marquess, and I should have been shut in my room. And to say that if you are ever in want of a dull and honest friend, I am available. I keep books.”

“What sort of books?”

“Brewery.” She said it as another girl might have said Italian. “Papa’s. It is a perfectly good brewery and it wants a better man at the top, and I am not allowed to be one. But I can add up, and I can tell you that your Marquess’s waistcoat cost eleven guineas, and that everybody in this room is in debt but the two of us. It is very restful, standing behind a pillar with someone who is not.”

“I am in debt,” said Winifred, before she could think better of it.

“Are you? How much?”

“Seven hundred and forty pounds.”

“Heavens,” said Verity Quarles, with real respect, and took her hand and shook it. “Then you are better company than I thought. I shall call.”

Lord Rupert Tremayne came across the floor at a pace that suggested he had been heading elsewhere and had changed his mind at the sight of her. He was a lanky young man with russet-gold curls, a long amused mouth and a waistcoat the colour of a peach in a good year, and he carried a quizzing glass on a ribbon, which he did not need. He raised it. He looked at her through it. He lowered it.

“Miss Pargeter. Rupert Tremayne. Stanmere’s oldest friend, which is to say the man who has lent him least. I shall not ask you whether you are engaged to him, because I have just heard you answer that three times, and I think the answer excellent.”

“It is in the—”

“Gazette. Yes. Allow me, we might say it together. No? Then I shall tell you instead.” He bent a little, and spoke in a light quick murmur that carried exactly as far as her ear. “You are not engaged to him. He is not engaged to you. Somebody in Fleet Street has put a W where a Q ought to have been, and the pair of you have found it more amusing than a retraction. I should have done the same, with less to gain.”

Winifred looked at him. She had a great number of faces for such an occasion, none of which she had been taught, and she found that the most useful was the one she wore when a customer disputed a bill. “It is in the Gazette,” she said.

“Quite so.” He bowed to her, beautifully, from the waist. “My dear girl, I am enchanted. I have never been refused by anyone I liked, and I shall be very interested to find out how it is done. I intend to court you, you know. Honestly, as a rival, with all my cards on the table, so that when I become tiresome you may say you were warned.”

“Then you will leave your hat on the table,” said Winifred. “In the Row, a man who keeps his hat in his hand is a man who means to go.”

Rupert Tremayne’s mouth went up at one corner. “They took it at the door.”

“Then you have saved yourself an argument.”

“I think,” said Lord Rupert slowly, turning the quizzing glass over in his fingers, “that this will be the most diverting summer of my life.” And he went away, across the floor, tossing a guinea as he went, as though he were scattering it for the poor.

The Dowager Duchess of Ormsgill was enthroned at the farther end of the saloon on a sofa the size of a small boat, upon cushions arranged to raise her to a height consistent with her opinion of herself. She was seventy-nine. She was perhaps five feet tall, in a purple turban with a brooch the size of a pigeon’s egg, and she wore rings on every finger including both thumbs, and her eyes, which were black and very small, came to rest upon Winifred as two pins come to rest on a map.

“Come here. No, there, where I can see you. Sit. Constance, go away.”

Lady Constance did not go away. She stood a pace off with her trumpet at the port, like a ship refusing to be dismissed from a harbour. Miss Quarles had drifted to the arm of the sofa, and Lord Rupert was leaning against its other end in an attitude of the deepest unconcern; and at the back, a pace behind and a little to the left, in her grey gown and her mittens, holding Lady Constance’s shawl as she held it everywhere, and as little regarded as the shawl, was Miss Fell.

“You set type,” said the Duchess.

“Yes, Your Grace.”

“Do you read it backwards?”

“Forwards, backwards and upside down, at about the same rate.”

“A most disagreeable talent. Ormsgill had one like it; he could read a letter across a table, and he never forgave me for it.” She unhooked a gold pencil from her girdle, took a card from her reticule, and wrote upon the back of it, shielding it with a ringed hand. Then she laid it on her knee, written side up, and slid it with one finger across the satin until it lay precisely before Winifred, who sat at the end of the sofa, across the width of a pillow, and had it upside down. “Read that.”

Winifred read it. It took no time at all. A compositor does not read, as the narrator has said; she sees letters, as a baker sees flour, and she saw these with a clearness that was nearly rude.

“Aloud,” said the Duchess.

“Mrs Chalmers,” said Winifred, quietly, “is a bore.”

It went no further than the arm of the sofa. The sofa heard it: Lady Constance, whose trumpet flinched; Miss Quarles, who coughed; Lord Rupert, who made a noise like a man swallowing a hiccup; and the Duchess herself, who gave a laugh like a drawer of cutlery being dropped, and said, at the volume at which she said everything, as Mrs Chalmers went by with the Colonel’s medal on her bosom: “She has been a bore since Trafalgar, and tonight she is a bore with a medal.”

Mrs Chalmers went on past, unhearing, in her puce, towards the supper-room.

“Are you to marry that long young man?” said the Duchess.

“It is in the Gazette, Your Grace.”

“I have forgotten more engagements than you have attended. That is a very good answer. Do it again at supper.” The pins moved to Winifred’s hair, and rested on the rule. “Ormsgill would have hated her, so I like her, Constance. She will do. You will give a dinner. I wish to see her eat.”

“Ma’am,” said Lady Constance.

“Thursday fortnight. The fourth. I shall be dead by the eleventh.”

“It is the fourth of July, ma’am, and—”

“Then it is the fourth. I shall come at half past seven, and you may look at me as you like.” She waved the hand that had the thumb-ring. “Go and be looked at, child. Take Quarles with you, she is wasted on me.”

It was about this time that the roof of Ormsgill House, which had stood since 1752 and had been described by its architect as proof against anything but the Day of Judgement, declared an interest in the proceedings. The ballroom ceiling was painted with the gods of Olympus, among clouds, and from the largest of the clouds, at intervals of just under four seconds, there began to fall a single clear drop of water upon the parquet. A footman, with the air of a man who had performed the office before, came forward with a silver basin from the Ormsgill plate and set it down.

Plink.

Winifred stopped where she stood, in the middle of the floor, with Verity Quarles at one elbow and the Duchess’s blessing on her head. She counted. Three seconds and a bit. The Drip, in a gilded ballroom, being served with a silver basin by a man in claret.

“Four seconds,” she said, to nobody.

She began to laugh. She tried to stop, and a thing like that, once begun, is a printing-house matter: it spread from the ribs to the throat and out of the mouth in a series of small helpless breaths, until Miss Quarles was looking at her with a deep, delighted, perplexed expression, and the nearest dozen guests had paused with their glasses to see what it was that the printer had found so droll. It was not a ladylike laugh. It was a laugh that had been waiting twelve days for a place to be let out, and it carried.

Across the width of the room, past two hundred shoulders and a quantity of ostrich plumes, Julian heard it. He did not look round at once. He was talking to the bald earl, about the Corn Returns, and had been for some minutes, and he went on doing so with every appearance of attention. But the earl, who was not a perceptive man, remarked afterwards that the Marquess of Stanmere had been turning his signet ring on his finger the whole time, round and round, like a man winding a very small clock; and that he did not appear to know that he was doing it.

chapters.title: Queries in the Margin
chapters.html:
By the Saturday the letters addressed to The Hon. Miss Pargeter had filled the corner table in the composing room to a height at which they threatened to become a feature of the Court. There was no such title. Nobody had conferred it, and Winifred had not been consulted; but the Post Office, which sorts by what people hope rather than by what is the case, had decided overnight that the intended of a Marquess must be the daughter of at least a baron, and had written it on the covers in a hundred different hands.

Toby read them aloud. He sat on the stool beside the proofing press with a bun in one fist and the heap on his knee, in the voice he used for the Psalms on Sundays, which was the voice of a boy who has been told that this is how it is done.

“’Madam,’” read Toby. “’I take the liberty. The Reverend Josiah Pettifer, curate of nowhere in particular in the diocese of Lincoln, begs leave to offer his hand, his heart, and a living of ninety pounds in Rutland, the roof of which is entire.’”

“Dnaltur,” said Orme, from the far corner, without turning round. He was seventy-one and slightly deaf, and set the line in his stick like a metronome with a grievance. “A dreadful word backwards. Like a sneeze.”

“Here’s another curate. That’s three. This one’s got a cottage, a cow and a Hebrew grammar.” Toby turned it over. “He says the cow is amiable. Is that a good thing in a cow?”

“Go on,” said Winifred, not looking up from the stone.

“’The Emperor of Tartary, Hoxton, has the honour to inform Miss Pargeter that he will receive her at any hour between nine and noon, and has instructed his Chancellor, who is his sister, to prepare a throne in the back parlour.’ It’s got a seal. It’s a button.” He put it down reverently. “There’s a lady at Cheltenham, a Mrs Hepplethwaite, who wants to buy your wedding-gown in advance, miss, for eleven guineas, to wear to the Pump Room and give back clean. She asks what colour. There’s a widow with six children and a cough, and a poet who wants a subscriber for The Press, a Poem in Nine Books, and a gentleman of Clerkenwell with a pamphlet on the Second Coming, who thinks the Marquess would like to be told the date.”

“Put them in the box.”

The box lay under the imposing stone and was labelled in Toby’s hand Hon. Winifred answered none of them. She had worked out on the Wednesday that a person who replies to one begging letter will be obliged to reply to four hundred, and that a person who replies to none has only to be called hard-hearted by a small section of the Strand. There was, however, one letter that Toby read in his Psalm voice and did not finish, because Winifred crossed the room and took it out of his hand. It was from a milliner in Walworth, in a hand that fought every word, and it asked whether a girl of fourteen who could spell might be taken as a compositor’s apprentice, since the writer had been told that a lady of the Row would understand. Winifred read it twice and put it in her apron pocket, where it stayed.

“There’s the Crier, too,” said Toby, with his mouth full. “I bought it off the hawker at the arch, miss. Twopence. I put it down as research.”

“It is not research. It is a Crier.”

“It’s got a bit about the rout.”

She did not say give it to me. She said, “Read it, then,” in the voice of a person who would sooner have a tooth drawn, and went back to the stone; and the Chapel, which consisted that morning of Orme, who could not hear it, and Fairweather, who would not comment on it, and Brevier, who was asleep upon the cases, was spared nothing.

“’The Quizzing-Glass,’” read Toby. “’By Peregrine Pry. Mr Pry presents his compliments to the Waterloo Rout, which was held at Ormsgill House on Tuesday last in a manner worthy of the victory, that is to say, in a great noise and in the wet.’” He took a bite of bun. “’I beg your pardon, but is it quite usual for a lady about to become a Marchioness to wear in her hair a brass instrument for the measuring of lines? A gentleman of the press assures Mr Pry that it is called a rule. Mr Pry would like to know who is to be ruled.’”

“Very droll,” said Winifred.

“It goes on. ‘Her Grace of Ormsgill, who has been dispensing opinion from the same sofa since the Peace of Amiens, was observed to write upon a card and to show it to the young person in blue, whose accomplishments run to the reading of a thing the wrong way up. The card, Mr Pry is happy to report, concerned a Mrs C——, who was at that moment passing. “She has been a bore since Trafalgar,” observed the Duchess, “and tonight she is a bore with a medal.”’”

The stick in Winifred’s hand did not move. She had been in the act of setting a letter, and she finished the act, and laid the sort in its place, and stood.

“A bore with a medal!” said Toby, who liked it very much. “That’s good, that is. Who’s Mrs C——? Is it the lady in the puce?”

“Toby.”

“Only I should like to know, miss, because Mrs Hobday says—”

“Toby. Go and empty the pan.”

He went, with the bun. Winifred stood at the case with her hands on the edge of it and did what she always did when a figure did not come out right: she went back and counted. The card had been written on the Duchess’s knee, in a gold pencil, and shown to nobody. It had been read aloud once, in a murmur that went no further than the arm of the sofa; and the Duchess’s remark had followed it at the Duchess’s usual pitch, to which nobody in that saloon but the sofa had been attending, for the excellent reason that the sofa was where one attended. She ran down those who had been at that end. Lady Constance, with her trumpet. Miss Quarles, at the arm. Lord Rupert, at the other.

Three. She was seldom wrong in a count, and she was not wrong now, in her way: a person who holds a shawl is not, in anyone’s arithmetic, sitting down.

She did not like where her mind rested. It rested, with a lightness that seemed to her very unfair, on a peach-coloured waistcoat and a long amused mouth. She told herself that the whole saloon had had a hundred opportunities of seeing the Duchess’s pencil, that Lady Constance would sooner have swallowed her trumpet, that Miss Quarles kept books. The rest of the column was about Lady Quarles’s faint, and was, she was obliged to admit, extremely funny; which made it worse.

Mr Ingram of the Gazette came at noon, wrapped in a muffler in the second half of June. He was a long, yellow, kindly man with the damaged voice of one lately recovered from a quinsy, and the habit of correcting any signboard he passed, which he did now, upon entering the Court, with a small dry cough. He carried the Gazette’s bound file under one arm and a note from Mr Underhill under the other.

“The gentleman in the Weald,” he wheezed, “has asked that the nine letters be reprinted as a pamphlet. Three hundred copies, for private circulation, at his own charge, in Pica, upon a better paper than the Gazette ever sees. And he requests, as usual, Miss Pargeter’s queries in the margin.” He coughed. “He says he finds he has come to depend upon them.”

“Does he?” said Winifred. “He has never said so before.”

“He says a great many things to Mr Minton,” said Mr Ingram, and looked, with rather more attention than was needed, at the ceiling.

It was at this moment that the Marquess of Stanmere came in at the door, in a dark coat, with his umbrella under his arm like a rifle and an air of having been sent for. “Article the Second,” he said, to the room at large. “A Committee on the Poor Rate kept me on Thursday, and I am a call in arrears. I trust it is convenient.” Mr Ingram’s cough, which had been merely a cough, became in an instant an affair of the lungs, and lasted, remarkably, until Julian had crossed the room and taken up his station at the farther side of the imposing stone.

There he remained. It must be said for Winifred that she did not set him to any task; she supposed that a man who had worn an apron for the whole of an afternoon on the thirteenth had earned a rest. She opened the file at the first of the nine letters, which had been cut from the Gazette and pasted to leaves, and sat down at the stone with a pencil, and began to read as a reader does, with the end of the pencil lightly against her lip. Julian watched. He had a view of the whole sheet from the other side, upside down, and of the pencil as it moved, and of nothing else. He was a proofreader of the first water, but nobody had ever taught him to read a thing the wrong way up, and she, who had been taught it at six, wrote with her wrist curled round the page like a boy at an examination.

It is no light matter for an author to watch his prose being read by someone who has no idea whose it is. It went on for an hour and ten minutes. At each little scratch of the pencil he felt, with more precision than he would have thought possible, the exact place where a tooth had been put into a sentence he had been fond of; and at each long pause, when she drew the pencil from her lip and held it above the paper and put it back, he held his breath, and was ashamed of himself, and could not stop. At the seventh letter her pencil stopped altogether. She looked at the page. She wrote: You say that a labourer’s household eats a peck a week; your sum is for the quartern loaf. Which? Also, the commas. She did not read it aloud. She tore the slip from the margin, folded it into one of the plain covers that Mr Ingram had brought, and sealed it down with a wafer; and Mr Ingram, who watched this with an expression of studied blankness, laid the file under his arm and went away to have his lungs seen to.

“I should like to meet him,” said Winifred.

“Who?”

“The Farmer. Mr Ingram will say nothing. Nine months, my lord, and all he will tell me is a gentleman in the Weald with a head for figures, as if that narrowed it. I should like to meet him.”

“I am told he is a bore in person.” Julian turned the signet on his finger. “They generally are, the good ones. They spend it all on the paper.”

“I do not wish to be entertained. I wish to make him say that he was wrong. Once.” She put the cover on the stone, wafer uppermost. “I have queried him ninety-one times and he has conceded three. All of them commas. A man who has never been wrong in print is not a writer, my lord. He is a wall.”

“A wall is much admired,” said Julian, “by persons who want to lean on something.”

“I wish to put a window in it.”

“I think,” said Julian with care, “that a man who has never been wrong may write better than one who has. He has no excuses ready.”

“And no mercy.”

“Mercy is the other thing a writer wants less than people suppose.”

“It is the only thing I ever wanted from one.” She regarded him over the stone. “You argue very well for a person who has never met him.”

“I have a great respect for a wall,” said Julian, “having been educated beside several,” and the corner of Winifred’s mouth did something it had not been told to, and he looked down at the stone and found himself deeply interested in a quoin.

Rupert came at half past four. Toby announced him from the door in a whisper that carried to the end of the Court: “A lord with flowers, miss, and he says he isn’t a bailiff.” He wore a coat of bottle green, a hat with a rakish dent, and a waistcoat that on any other man would have been an offence against the Peace; and he carried in his arms a damp packet of Covent Garden pinks wrapped in a page of the Gazette, which he laid on the stone with a bow.

“A bad bargain at fourpence the bunch,” said Lord Rupert, “but I am told it is the thing. Miss Pargeter. Stanmere, how d’ye do. I have a pair of greys at the corner and a curricle, both belonging to a man who owes me two guineas, which makes them the only things in London that do. It is the fashionable hour and the Park is at your disposal. It will rain on us, of course. I thought you might care for a turn.”

Winifred looked at the pinks. She looked at the Marquess, who was standing at the end of the stone with his hands behind his back, and whose face had assumed the expression of a man reading a lease. It occurred to her that the Articles wanted her seen, and that Hyde Park at five o’clock, even in a drizzle, was where one was seen; and that she had not been seen at all since the Tuesday.

“I should like it very much,” she said.

“Quite,” said Julian.

She knew the word. She had heard it in the cold of a yard on the thirteenth, and used it, once, in his own voice, to his face. “Is that yes?” said Winifred.

“It is the other thing.”

“It is Article the Second, my lord. In company. I am to appear on not fewer than six occasions.”

“I had not thought of Lord Rupert as company.”

“He is a great many people,” said Winifred, getting her bonnet from the nail. “I shall be quite safe in the crowd.”

The curricle was an elegant, shabby affair with a hood that could be put up against the weather, and a tiger of nine years old in a striped waistcoat who clung behind with the stoicism of a limpet. The greys went at a decorous trot. Rotten Row in a drizzle at five o’clock that summer was a place of sparse and sodden grandeur, a dozen landaus and phaetons going round and round under dripping elms like exhibits in a small and expensive menagerie, and every head in every one of them turned.

“Now then,” said Lord Rupert, leaning back with the reins slack in one hand. “I know, and you will admit nothing, and I find it the most convincing admission I have ever heard.”

“I admit that it is raining.”

“Excellent. We shall build on that.” He tossed a guinea, caught it, and put it away. “My dear girl, I shall not trouble you with it again. I have said my say, and Stanmere is the best of men, and an ass, and I should not wish to be the person who explained to him that he is both. But I should like you to know what I am, because you will hear it elsewhere, and I had rather be the first with my own bad news. I am a debtor.”

“I had understood that.”

“I owe a great deal of money to a number of persons, and eight hundred pounds of it to a single man, who sends me a receipt for my own interest, spells Tremayne correctly, and has never once mentioned the matter. It is the only debt I have that frightens me, because he does not mind. He is a man who only ever does anything on purpose. I mean, of course, Lovejoy.”

The wheel of the curricle passed through a puddle; the tiger said Whoa to nothing; Winifred did not move her face. “Mr Lovejoy of the Phoenix Press.”

“The same. He prints the Crier, you know. I read it. I find it extremely well written. It gives me a pain.” He laughed, lightly, as another man might have remarked upon the weather. “I tell you only because I seem to be the sort of person you tell things to. It is a quality I have never been paid for.”

She looked at the side of his face, which was handsome and open and had a smear of rain along the cheekbone, and wondered whether she was being given a confession or a handkerchief to be dropped. He had been at the sofa. He owed the man who printed the paper. He had admitted both without being asked, and she had known him four days. She decided that she would not ask him anything. It is a great art, not asking, and she had been practising it all week upon the Marquess.

“Look,” said Lord Rupert. “The Duchess’s carriage. She will not bow, she never does, but she will see you have been seen. Wave your glove.”

She waved the small glove, with the thumb in it, and the Duchess’s yellow chariot rolled by without so much as a flicker of a purple turban, which was, in the language of the Park, a compliment of the first magnitude.

It was past seven when she returned to the Court, with the pinks damp in her arm. The pressroom door stood open on a smell of ink and warm iron and a thump she knew in her bones. The Society for the Relief of Distressed Gentlewomen having discovered that it had another fifteen hundred gentlewomen to distress, Lady Constance had ordered a second run, and in the back room, in a great grey light from the skylight, the Albion was at work. Fairweather stood at the bar. At the inking-table stood the Marquess of Stanmere, in his shirtsleeves, with his coat folded on a bench and ink to the elbow, wearing a leather apron that had been Barnaby’s and an expression of terrible concentration, applying a roller to a forme as though it might bite.

“Aye,” said Fairweather, which was the whole of his report.

Julian looked round. A smear of black lay across his forehead, and one of the white notches in his eyebrow showed through it like a star. “I came to see whether Fairweather needed a hand,” he said, “and found that I did.”

“Lord Rupert has been a very agreeable companion.”

“He is a rake.”

“He is a debtor.” Winifred put down the pinks. “He tells me it is not the same thing, and that he would much prefer to be called a rake.”

“I should think he would.”

“He says he owes eight hundred pounds to Mr Lovejoy. He said it as another man would say it was damp.”

“Did he?” Julian laid the roller down very carefully on the slab. For a moment he seemed to be considering the width of the forme, and the tympan, and the iron that held them both; and he said, “Quite,” in a voice so level that it might have been rolled. Then he picked up his coat. “I must go. Minton will have a dinner on the table and a grievance with it. I shall call on Tuesday.”

“It is Tuesday and Thursday, my lord.”

“So it is.”

He took the apron off, and hung it up, and nodded to Fairweather, who said Aye in a tone of the deepest approval; and at the door of the pressroom, as he went out, he glanced back at the imposing stone, where the plain cover she had sealed that morning lay waiting for Mr Ingram’s boy, with its wafer uppermost, and said, absently, as one speaks to a man who is not in the room, “The quartern, not the peck.”

He went out. The door swung. The Albion thumped.

Winifred stood where she was, with the damp pinks in her hand. She had not read the slip aloud to anybody. It was sealed; Mr Ingram had not opened it; the one other person who had been present was on the opposite side of a stone, and did not read upside down. It was a very small thing. Compositors, however, are trained to notice very small things.

chapters.title: The Old Lady Runs Away
chapters.html:
It is a peculiarity of Hand and Pen Court that nobody knocks. The street door of Pargeter’s stood on the latch from five in the morning until the pressmen went home, and callers, from bishops to baker’s boys, came in and shouted. So that when the Marquess of Stanmere walked under the arch at ten o’clock on the Thursday, with his umbrella furled like a sword and Minton behind him carrying the second one in the manner of a man carrying a spare soul, the first thing he heard was a knock, and the second thing he thought was that it was wrong.

It was three raps, evenly spaced, with the ferrule of a stick: the knock of a man who has stood at the doors of a great many houses and is in no hurry to be admitted to any of them.

In the middle of the Court beside the pump stood a dray with a skid laid to its tail and a large placid horse of the Suffolk sort between the shafts, which regarded the proceedings with the look of a horse asked to take a small part in a play it had not read. Two porters sat on the edge of the trough eating bread and bacon. On the step, with his stick still raised, stood a stout and civil man in a brown coat with brass buttons, who turned round at the sound of the Marquess’s boots and took off his hat.

“How do you do,” said Julian, who had rehearsed it in a hackney a fortnight before and found that it still came out.

“Gribble, sir,” said the man. “For Mr Lovejoy. A bailiff, in a manner of speaking, though I call it collecting.”

The door flew open. Toby looked out, in his shirtsleeves, with a pie in his hand; he took in the dray, the porters and the brown coat, and then, with deep and shining satisfaction, Julian. “It’s a bailiff!” he cried, over his shoulder, into the shop. “A proper one, miss! With a stick!” And to the Marquess, kindly, as to a colleague who had done his best: “You aren’t one, your Marquessship. Are you? Not today?”

“Not today,” said Julian.

Winifred came to the door. Her sleeves were above the elbow, the brass rule was through her hair, and she had ink to the wrist; and she took the paper from Mr Gribble’s hand with a politeness so extreme that Julian, who had known her three weeks, stepped back half a pace.

It was a bill of sale, dated the fourteenth of July, 1815, and it conveyed to Hector Lovejoy, printer, of Ave Maria Lane, as security for the sum of sixty pounds advanced to Barnaby Pargeter, one wooden common press, known as the Old Lady, of about the year 1770, with its bar, its tympan, its frisket, its ink-balls and its appurtenances, to be delivered upon demand after Midsummer Day. Midsummer Day had been Monday. It was signed by her father in the hand of a man who had been cheerful when he wrote it.

“There is a notice period,” said Winifred. “Fourteen days. I remember the clause. My father read it to me aloud, with some pride.”

“Notice was served by post upon Mr B. Pargeter on the tenth, miss. It was received. It was not, I understand, opened.”

“Father,” said Winifred, not turning her head.

From the speaking-tube in the composing room, which carried through the open door, a muffled and agonised voice said: “My dear, I took it for the coals.”

“It was under the cat,” said Toby.

“I shall have a great deal to say to the cat,” said Winifred, very quietly. She turned the paper over. She had already begun to count. “Mr Gribble, I have in the cash-box fifty-four pounds, eleven shillings. If you will wait until three o’clock, the Bishop’s chaplain is to pay nineteen pounds ten for five hundred sermons, and I shall have the sixty and the costs besides. If you will take the fifty-four now, I will give you my note for the rest.”

“I couldn’t, miss. A bill’s a bill. Sixty and costs, paid to Mr Lovejoy at the Phoenix Press between the hours of eleven and four, and Mr Lovejoy, I understand, is at Pomfret Yard until five.” He turned his hat in his hands, with real regret. “I am sent to take, not to receive. It’s the sort of distinction a man in my line has to be careful of.”

It was very neat. Julian, standing on the cobbles with the rain on his hat, saw all of it at once, as he sometimes saw the foot of a column before he had read the head. Friday’s Gazette was to be run from half past one in the morning. Without the second press, the Albion would do two hundred and fifty an hour, for an hour, for men who could bear it. Winifred was saying the figures aloud, in a steady voice, as one reads out the symptoms of a patient who will not recover. “Eleven hundred, at two hundred and fifty. Four hours and twenty minutes, for men who cannot be borne. Say six. The cart must leave at a quarter past five.” She stopped.

“Clause six,” said Julian.

“You have been reading the contract.”

“Minton has.” Minton, behind his shoulder, found something wrong with the second umbrella. “It was the cart in May, was it not? I thought, Miss Pargeter, that a second breach—”

“A second breach in any quarter voids it at the Proprietor’s option. Yes.” She smiled at Mr Gribble, with the smile of a person at a funeral. “Mr Lovejoy is a very considerate man.”

Julian’s hand had gone to his breast, to the pocket in which, under the pocket-book, a cheque-book on Child’s lay folded flat. It rested there as a hand rests on a pistol it has promised not to draw. “Article the Third,” said Winifred, without looking round.

“I know what it says. I was present at the composing of it. I am merely reciting it to myself.”

“You may recite it a little more quietly.”

So he stood in the yard. He had never in his life been so entirely without employment.
