He was a man to whom the arrangement of other people’s difficulties was a form of respiration; he had only to be told of a trouble to find that the means of removing it had already been put in his pocket. Sixty pounds. Sixty-three, with costs. It was less than a month’s wine. He stood on the cobbles with it unspent in his pocket, a Marquess without a purse, and the effect of the situation upon his temper was so remarkable that he drew himself up to his whole six feet and one, and said, in the voice that his steward in Kent called the old Lordship’s, “I am the Marquess of Stanmere.”

“Are you, sir?” said Mr Gribble, with the greatest civility. “I have had two earls and a man who said he was the Archbishop of Canterbury, and I find the effect is much the same. It doesn’t alter the writ.”

The title, thus employed, frightened Mr Gribble about as much as a hat.

The Old Lady came out of the back room the way a gallows comes out of a village green: unwillingly, in sections, and with a great many persons giving advice. She was eight hundredweight of oak and iron, with a bar like a ship’s tiller and a screw as thick as a man’s wrist, and she had been inked and beaten and sworn at for forty-six years in a dozen shops, and had printed in her time a quantity of sermons, a victory, three libels and the banns of the Row. The porters slid her up the skid with a tackle and lashed her to the dray with cords that Mr Orme, standing at the corner of the shop in his apron with his composing stick held like a lance, looked at for some time with an expression of increasing contempt.

“Chapel!” cried Orme, raising the stick.

“Aye,” said Fairweather, behind him, which was to say that the Chapel had been called and had answered; but Dick Sparrow, the second pressman, who might have been expected to be the second voice, stood by the pump with his hands in his pockets, whistling through the gap in his front teeth. He wore, Julian noticed, a very clean neckcloth. Fairweather looked at it, and then at Dick, in a manner which would have been a remark if Fairweather had been a man who made them.

“I’m going to guard her,” announced Toby. He had climbed up, pie and all, on to the tail of the dray, and was sitting with his boots against the Old Lady’s frame and his arms round her screw, looking pale and proud. “Somebody’s got to. She’s been in the Row since before I was born.”

“Get down, you little—” began Mr Gribble.

At which point Brevier, who had been watching from the window-sill with the attitude of a cat that has no opinions, rose, stretched, descended to the cobbles, and made one fluid leap on to the tarpaulin over the Old Lady’s bar, where she sat down and began to wash. The porters looked at the cat. Mr Gribble looked at the porters. And the dray, with the Old Lady, the boy and the cat, rolled out under the arch of Hand and Pen Court with an inch to spare on either side and a sound like a violin string being played by a drover, followed by a great fall of soot.

Winifred took off her apron. She did not say anything. She walked out of the arch behind the dray, with the rule in her hair and her pattens clacking on the stones, and the Marquess of Stanmere, who found that he was walking beside her and had no recollection of having decided to, said: “Where will he take it?”

“To the warehouse in Bridge Street, Blackfriars. Mr Lovejoy keeps his spare presses there.”

“Then we are on the Hill.”

“We are.”

Ave Maria Lane was a short steep pinch of a street, and the rain was coming down it in a sheet; and at the bottom, where the Lane meets Ludgate Hill, the dray turned west and began, quite quietly, to go down. It is a very steep hill. It is steep enough that a loaded dray wants its drag chain shipped and its horse held back; and the porters, who had not done up the lashings with the care of men who expected to be watched, had also not shipped the drag.

It happened in the following order. A street organ beside the church of St Martin struck up The Roast Beef of Old England with a wheeze like a dying lung. A boy with two dogs, bringing a drove of sheep up the Hill the wrong way to Smithfield, met the dray head on. The Suffolk horse, who had borne an enormous number of things with an enormous composure, looked at the organ, looked at the sheep, and decided that its engagement was over. It went forward. The dray went forward after it. Somewhere in the rattle there was the sharp twang of a cord parting, and the Old Lady lurched on her skid, and Toby screamed, in a shrill voice that carried the whole length of Ludgate Hill, “Your Marquessship!”

Julian ran.

He was thirty-one, and had never run in a street in his life. He ran like a heron that has been startled, all knees and neck, with his coat flying; and Winifred ran after him, and her pattens, which were of iron, caught between two stones and tripped her; she kicked them off, one, two, over the heads of the crowd, and ran in her stockings through the rain. The dray had a lead of thirty yards and was gaining. Julian had a long stride. By the corner of the Old Bailey he had got within ten feet, and by the Belle Sauvage yard, where a woman screamed and a pot-boy let fall a tray, he had a hand on the tail-board and a foot on the drag chain, which was trailing behind the wheel like a snake. He took it in both hands. He sat down in the road.

The chain ran out. He went along the cobbles on the seat of his breeches, with the iron round his forearms, for twenty yards, at what felt to him a speed exceeding anything attempted by man; and the dray, which had one hind wheel half locked by this unexpected anchor, slewed from the middle of the Hill, took a lamp-post by the shoulder, cut across the pavement, and fetched up with a crash in the bow window of Mr Mutlow’s pastrycook’s shop, which had been prepared that morning for the Thursday trade.

Pies went up like a covey of birds. Mutton pies, beefsteak pies, eel pies in their trays, a tall cold goose pie from the window, forty-one of them in a single hot brown tide that broke over the Old Lady, the horse, the pavement, a passing curate and the Marquess of Stanmere. He sat in the road with his hair on end and a pie on his collar and a bar of the chain round his arm, and looked at the Old Lady, who had come to rest with her frame against Mr Mutlow’s counter and her screw in the air, like a gallows that has just had a very good idea.

“Your Marquessship!” said Toby, from beneath a tarpaulin. “I held on! I held on to her, I did. Brevier’s in the goose.”

By the end of the quarter of an hour there were two hundred persons on the Hill, and a boy from Mr Treacher’s shop in St James’s, who had been in the Belle Sauvage yard by accident, was drawing in a book with the speed of an artist who sees fortune coming round the corner. News in the Row travels at the speed of an apprentice. They came down Ludgate Hill from every printing house in Paternoster Row, from Ave Maria Lane and Warwick Lane and Ivy Lane, boys and journeymen in paper caps and leather aprons, a hundred or more, hatless, in the rain; and they did not ask a question. They looked at the Old Lady, and at Mr Gribble, who stood in the ruin of Mutlow’s shop with his hat in his hand and a pie on his stick, and at the lady in her stockings; and a boy from Longman’s who had a voice like a bell said: “Chapel!”

They lifted her. It took forty of them, and they did it as a congregation lifts a coffin, under the bar, under the frame, with a hand under every beam, and set her on their shoulders. Somebody started to sing. It was a trade ditty, and had been sung in the Row at wakes and weddings and funerals since before anyone could say when, to a tune that bore no relation to any other tune in England:

Pull the bar, boys, pull it down, ink the ball and beat the town; wooden Lady, oaken Dame, take her home and take no blame!

They bore her back up the Hill in the rain, a hundred and twenty boys carrying eight hundredweight of oak, with Toby riding on the top, shrieking the chorus, and a cat on his shoulder, and a goose pie in the cat. Behind came Mr Orme, who had been brought down the Hill in the arms of two apprentices like a bishop on a litter, and who had risen in their arms to claim Chapel law. A stranger, he announced, who laid hands upon a press within the freedom of the Chapel without paying garnish to the Father, was liable to a solace of one gallon of porter. “Backwards, Mr Gribble,” said Orme, “it is perfectly plain.” And Mr Gribble, who had served writs upon four bishops and a harpist and been given tea by most of them, walked behind the procession with his hat in his hand, among forty apprentices, in the rain, like a man who has been taken prisoner by a very kind enemy.

Winifred walked with them, carrying her pattens. She had a pie on her shoulder. Her stockings were black to the knee. She had not said one word since the lamp-post. At the corner of Ave Maria Lane she turned her head, and saw, a little behind, the Marquess of Stanmere coming up the Hill with the chain still on his arm, and in his face, under the soot and the grease and the dripping hair, an expression she had never seen on it: of a man who has been in a fight and has no idea who won, and is very much inclined to go again.

Mr Gribble came back at six, as he had said he would, with the writ.

He came into the composing room with his hat held before him, in the manner of a man who calls upon a family after a bereavement and has not forgotten the cake. The Old Lady stood in her accustomed corner, gleaming with a certain smugness; she had been wiped by forty hands and oiled by Orme, and her bar was set in the position of one who has done her day’s work. The cash-box stood open on the imposing stone. The Bishop’s chaplain had come at three. Toby sat on a stool in the corner, consuming the surviving goose pie, and was in the happiest condition of his life.

“Mr Lovejoy’s compliments, miss,” said Mr Gribble, “and he regrets any inconvenience, and he begs me to say that the press must go to Bridge Street tonight or be redeemed.”

“Quite,” said Winifred. It was not her word, and Julian, standing against the far wall in a borrowed apron with soot in his hair and a pie on his collar, felt it go through him like a pin.

She began to count. She counted aloud, as she always did, in her quick dry voice, setting each coin on the stone in rows, so that every person in the room might see it done: fifty-four pounds eleven in the box in the morning; nineteen pounds ten from the Bishop’s chaplain at three; seventy-four pounds and a shilling in all. Out of the seventy-four, sixty to Mr Lovejoy upon the bill. Fifty-seven guineas and three shillings, which is sixty pounds to the penny; she counted the guineas twice, and pushed them across the stone in a bright heap.

“And costs, miss. Three pounds four. There is the dray, and the porters, and the damage to Mr Mutlow’s.”

“The dray is Mr Lovejoy’s own, and the damage to Mr Mutlow’s was your lashings, which are his affair and not mine,” said Winifred. She took the pencil from behind her ear and wrote the figures on the stone. “Your attendance, three days at a crown. The stamp on the writ, six shillings. The porters’ hire, twelve. That is one pound thirteen. Call it two pounds, and I will not ask for the pies.”

Mr Gribble looked at the figures for some time. He had the expression of a man who has been out-arithmeticked in a profession that sets great store by arithmetic. “Two pounds,” he agreed, at last, and signed the receipt on his knee; and Winifred, who had not smiled since half past ten that morning, put the writ in her pocket, as one puts away a handkerchief that has been of use. “You may tell Mr Lovejoy,” she said, “that the Old Lady is redeemed, and is grateful for the outing.”

Mr Gribble bowed to the press, to the lady, and to the Marquess, in that order. He went out through the Court with his hat on, whistling something that was not far from The Roast Beef of Old England.

The door closed. The Drip fell into its pan with a small flat note.

“I did not pay it,” said Julian.

She raised her eyes. They were dark and tired and rimmed with red from the rain, and she looked at him across the stone as one looks at a column of figures that has come out, at the last, to the penny.

“You did not,” said Winifred. “Thank you.”

It was, as it happened, the first time in thirty-one years that anyone had thanked the Marquess of Stanmere for doing nothing, and he found that he liked it a great deal more than he ought. He stood against the wall of a printing house with a pie upon his collar and a smear of ink from the Old Lady’s ball across his nose, watching a small woman put sixty pounds, in coin, into a cash-box that was not his, and not once, in the whole of the operation, did he reach for his purse.

chapters.title: A Red Sky Over Curzon Street
chapters.html:
At a quarter to nine on the evening of Sunday the thirtieth of June the sun, which had not been seen in London since the eleventh of May, was seen.

It stood on the rim of the world behind the chimneys of Hampstead in a smear of copper, the colour of a new penny held up to a candle, and the whole of the west took fire from it by degrees: first the slates, then the cloud-bank above the slates, then the long wet length of Curzon Street, which lay down under it like a ribbon dipped in rust. The rain, as though from a sense of occasion, had stopped. By ten minutes to the hour every step in Mayfair had its household on it. Footmen stood bareheaded, housemaids held up their aprons, an old gentleman in the Square had been brought out in his chair by two grandsons and sat with his mouth slightly open, like a man at a play he does not follow and has been told is very fine; and at the top of the steps of Stanmere House, in his black coat, with his hands behind his back, stood Gantry, who was sixty and had been in the family for forty-four years, and had seen a Prince drunk and a Prime Minister sober and was moved.

“It is an omen, my lord.”

“It is dust,” said Julian, from the doorway.

“Of what quantity, my lord?”

“Considerable.”

“Very good, my lord,” said Gantry, who went on believing in the omen.

Julian had been at the library window since eight, with a pencil in his hand and nothing to mark. He had been trying to see his house as she would see it. It was an exercise he did not recommend. Stanmere House was tall, cold and correct; it had been built by a man who disapproved of comfort and had the means to enforce his views, and its stair carpet was the exact grey of a clergyman’s opinion. Minton had put out the place-cards, and taken them in, and put them out again. Gantry had been asked for a plain dinner and, in the course of the afternoon, had translated plain into five removes. A fire was lit in the library grate, in the last day of June, because Gantry held that a fire was a form of welcome and that the library, without one, resembled a tomb in which somebody had been so careless as to leave the books. And the Marquess of Stanmere, who had given dinners to the Cabinet and the Corn Committee and the Dean of Westminster without feeling anything more than a mild wish to be elsewhere, found that his hands were damp, and wiped them on his coat, and was ashamed.

At ten minutes to nine a hired hackney came along Curzon Street at the walk, with its lamps unlit and its driver standing up on the box to see the sky, and stopped; and Mr Barnaby Pargeter was lifted out of it by a footman and the secretary, with his foot in its flannel and his spectacles on his forehead, like a monarch being conveyed to a coronation he had been dreading.

Of the dinner there is nothing to be said that a short paragraph will not cover, which is the case with most dinners and the whole of the reason that novelists make so little of them. There was Gantry’s soup. There was a boiled fowl, a tongue, a saddle of mutton and two removes of which nobody afterwards could say what they had been. There was a footman, whose name was William but who was called John, as were all the footmen at Stanmere House, the sixth Marquess having found names tiresome; and this footman held a tureen for twenty minutes at Mr Pargeter’s right hand, unable to put it down, while Mr Pargeter explained the toggle-and-lever action of the Albion to him with the assistance of two forks, a salt-cellar and a spoon. There was Minton, who ate three courses with his watch open beside his plate and said nothing whatever, and who removed himself with the dessert as a man withdraws from the scene of a pleasant crime. And there was, throughout, a sort of gap at the table, which all three of the guests of the house of Pargeter felt, between the courses, as a tongue feels the place where a tooth has been: the absence of a small flat note, falling every four seconds into a copper pan.

Article the Second, which required that Miss Pargeter dine at his table once, was satisfied at the fish. The Marquess did not notice it go by.

It was a little after ten when the cloth was drawn. By then the copper had gone out of the sky behind the house and something deeper was coming in. Barnaby, who had been walked by degrees into the library, passed through it like a man in a cathedral: slowly, with his hat in his hand though he had no hat, and his head tipped back, and his lips moving. “My dear fellow,” he said, at the foot of the gallery, “I have never seen so many books that were not for sale.” And he sank, with a sigh like a bellows, into the best chair, which was a great wing-backed leather affair by the fire, and laid his foot on the stool that Gantry had set for it, and said, “I shall close my eyes for a moment and consider the folio sizes,” and was asleep.

“He has been up since four,” said Winifred. “There was a leak.”

“There is always a leak.”

“In this house?”

“I should be surprised if there were not one in the roof of my own mind,” said Julian. “But I do not think there is one in the slates.”

She had taken off her gloves. It was the first time he had seen her do it in company, and she did it with an air of having decided on the stairs: the right, then the left, drawn finger by finger and laid on the arm of a chair, so that the left hand lay on the dark leather in the firelight with the thumb uppermost, blue-black to the ball, like a bruise that had been taught to read. He looked at it and then, with an effort, at the shelf.

The shelf stood in the east alcove at the height of a man’s elbow, and Winifred, who had not asked what was on it, had walked to it as a needle goes to the north.

He kept there what he called, when pressed, his ephemera. There were ballads, a pile of them, the Last Dying Speech of a quantity of gentlemen whose last speeches had been set up in type before the occasion; an eighty-year run of almanacs; a tavern bill for the year of Culloden; a playbill from Drury Lane with a hole burned in it; and in a frame of black wood, under glass, a single leaf from a great folio Bible.

“The Vinegar Bible,” said Winifred, bending, with her hands behind her back so as not to touch. “Oxford. Mr Baskett’s folio of 1717. The head of Luke the twentieth: the Parable of the Vinegar.”

“For Vineyard.”

“A basket-ful of printer’s errors, the Row called it, Baskett being his name. Which is just the sort of thing the Row says when it is jealous.” She straightened. She looked at the tavern bill and the burnt playbill and the ballads, and at the last, lying by itself on a velvet cloth, the Last Dying Speech of one Josiah Tapp, with its black border, and a line at the foot in a different fount. “’The above Person has since been Reprieved.’”

“I bought it for a shilling in the Mint. I think it the finest erratum in the language.”

“It is a masterpiece.” She laughed, a low startled sound. “Do you collect them?”

He took down from the shelf a japanned box, the size of a prayer-book, and opened it. It was full of slips of paper, long and narrow, yellowed, thick as a pack of cards: For Antioch read Antium. Page 86, line 11, for the read then. For Gothic read Gaulish. Two hundred and eleven of them, each cut from the back of a book or bought by the dozen from a stationer in Holywell Street who thought him mad, and each marked on the back, in his small even hand, with the date.

“As a boy,” said Julian, “I thought that a thing printed was true. I do not mean the opinions. I mean true in the way that a brick is hard. And then I found one of these pasted in at the back of my father’s Gibbon.” He had the slip in his fingers: For Gothic read Gaulish. He was not looking at her. “And understood that print could say it was sorry.”

“How old were you?”

“Nine.”

She said nothing. He noticed it, because it was the thing about her that he could least account for: a woman who answered every question by stating a fact, and who could, when the occasion wanted, leave a question lying on the floor between them like a dropped glove, without picking it up, as though a space were a thing she knew how to set. She was looking at the wall. She was looking, with the most perfect indifference, at the wall between the two windows, where the green silk, five feet by three, was a shade paler than the silk about it, as though a window had once been there and been boarded up; and a ghost of a nail stood in it, at the top, in the middle.

She did not ask; and Julian, who had never in his life been spared a question by anyone, discovered that he could not bear it.

“There was a picture,” he said.

“Yes.”

“My mother.” He put the slip in the box and shut the lid, and found that he had the signet in his fingers, turning. “She lives in Florence. She went there in the autumn of 1794, when I was nine, and my father had the portrait taken down the same week. It has been in a crate in the cellar for twenty-two years. I have not had the wall done over. It seemed an expense to no purpose.”

“Is she living?”

“She is, I am told, well.”

“Told by whom?”

“By my aunt. At intervals. In the manner of a weather report.”

“Does she write?”

He had been asked a great many questions in his life by a great many people, with every degree of delicacy, and had met them all with a Which? and a number. “No,” said Julian.

It fell between them. Over the fireplace, in a gilt frame of enormous size, the sixth Marquess of Stanmere regarded the room from beneath a plum-coloured coat and an expression of having just been contradicted at dinner and being resolved to win; and Julian, who had been under that eye for thirty-one years, observed to his surprise that it did not look at him but at the pale rectangle, steadily, as though the portrait and the place had been put there to quarrel.

“My parents’ marriage,” he said, “was a long quarrel conducted at dinner, in the best manners, in front of a child. I was the child. It is very instructive. One learns to pass the salt.” He heard his own voice, level as a rule. “I decided, at nine, that I would not marry unless it were impossible not to.”

“And is it impossible?”

“It is in the Gazette,” said Julian.

She laughed. It was not a success; it came out of her chest like something carried too far, and she put the back of her bare hand against her mouth, and over it her eyes were very bright. He found that he wished to say something. It was a very peculiar sensation, since he did not know what it was; he had the sentence ready, and none of the words.

She said it for him, or said something. She had taken the rule out of her hair. The hair fell down on one side, which she did not appear to notice, and she laid the brass strip in her hand, in the firelight, long and flat and warm, and turned it over to show him a worn place along the edge. “This was my mother’s. The stick is the other half of the set; it is at home. She was a compositor’s daughter and she set the Psalms in Long Primer at nineteen, in a back room over a chandler’s in Warwick Lane, in four months. It is bright where it is bright because she had a thumb like mine.” The thumb lay on the brass. “She died in March of 1807. It was a consumption. I was seventeen.”

“I am sorry.”

“The Row came to the funeral. That is the thing I remember. My father couldn’t do anything, he sat in the parlour and looked at the floor; and the night before, a compositor from every house in the Row came to our door, with his stick, and each of them set a verse of a hymn in his own house’s fount, and we pulled it at six in the morning, on a single sheet, on the Old Lady. It was in eleven different founts. It looked like a sampler.” She smiled, not at him. “It was the ugliest sheet ever printed in London and I have it still in my Bible. I took the stick the week after.”

“It is not ugly,” said Julian.

“No. It is the opposite of ugly. I haven’t a word.”

He had one, or the beginning of one, and let it go by. It would be a long time before he said it, and when he did, it would be in a church. He said instead, after a pause that he could not have measured, “Thank you.”

“For what?”

“For telling me which hymn.”

“I did not tell you which hymn.”

“No,” said Julian. “I find it was not necessary.”

They discussed Lord Rupert’s courtship for something under half a minute, with great restraint on both sides, as two persons might discuss a dog that has been left in the hall.

“He has called three times,” said Winifred.

“I am glad he is attentive.”

“He brought pinks.”

“I know. Your father told me, at length.” The corner of his mouth went. “I now know the Latin name, the price at Covent Garden in three seasons, and that a pink is a carnation which has not been given the chance. He meant it, I think, as a character reference.”

“It was a very good one,” said Winifred, and Julian said “Quite,” and Barnaby, in the best chair, with his chin on his chest, turned over, and said clearly in his sleep, “Not on the tympan, you fool,” and was quiet again. They looked at each other and, in the firelight, did not laugh, which was an achievement.

The window had gone from copper to red, and from red to something darker, a slow rich colour like the inside of a shell or the shadow in a glass of port. It lay over the roofs of Mayfair in a long smoulder. The street below was silent. Julian went to the glass, and she came with him, bareheaded, with her hair on her shoulder and the rule in her hand, and they stood side by side with a foot of clean air between them, looking at the end of the world. Out in the Square somebody’s footman was weeping, or laughing; one could not tell at that distance.

“It will be in the Farmer, I suppose,” said Winifred.

“I beg your pardon?”

“He ought to write about it. He has written on everything else.” She had put her forehead nearly to the glass. “Weather, rents, bread, the poor-rate. He cannot let this go by.”

His mouth was dry. “What would he say?”

“That nobody can explain it,” said Winifred, “and everybody is pretending to.”

He did not answer. It was precisely, to the syllable, what he had been going to write; he had composed it in his head at eight o’clock that evening, standing at this window with the pencil, and had not set it down. He stood very still. His right hand, with a will of its own, had begun to turn the ring.

“Is it a good thing to say?” said Winifred. “I thought it a rather good one.”

“It is exactly the thing.”

“He will think it his own, then. They generally do.” She laughed softly. “I never knew a writer who did not think everything good had been taken out of his head.”

At half past ten the Pargeters departed in the hackney, with Barnaby carried down the steps by two Johns and a secretary, awake and saying he had never in his life shut his eyes and that the folio sizes had been entirely satisfactory. Winifred went last, with her hair up again and the rule through it, done without a glass in four movements. She put on her gloves on the step, the left over the thumb, and looked up at the sky. “It is going,” she said; and it was. The red had ebbed into the black behind the roofs. A first thin rain, blowing along Curzon Street out of the north-west, had begun again, as though the sky had only stepped out for a moment and come back. “Thank you for the dinner. It was very pleasant. I never in my life had so many forks.”

“I will tell Gantry. He will put in for a medal.”

“Good night, my lord.”

“Good night, Miss Pargeter.”

The hackney went off at the walk, with its lamps lit now, and its wheels hissing on the wet. Julian remained where he was, on the top step, in his evening coat, with the rain coming at his face and a last long bar of crimson across the roofs behind him, so that he threw a shadow down the steps as long as the street. Gantry had gone in. The old gentleman in the Square had been taken home. He stood, a tall and slightly stooped man of one-and-thirty, with a pencil still in his hand, knowing that one person in London now knew what was in the crate in his cellar, and that he knew in return what had been set in eleven founts on the Old Lady in March of 1807; and that the exchange had been made without a receipt.

He remembered that he had signed Article 6.

He had signed it with a tolerable laugh. He tried the laugh now, on the step, in the rain, and found it had been used up.

chapters.title: A Dinner Afloat
chapters.html:
At four o’clock on the afternoon of Thursday the fourth of July the kitchen of Lady Constance Dyer’s house in Hertford Street stood eleven inches deep in water, and the water was still arriving.

A gutter above the area door, designed by a man who had never seen it rain, had overflowed into an area drain that had not been cleared since the death of General Dyer in 1811; and the area, having nowhere else to put what it was given, had sent it down the steps and under the door and into the kitchen, where it had risen among the legs of the table, the dresser and the coal-scuttle, and was now lapping at the bottom bar of the range. Sixteen persons were to sit down to dinner at eight. The Dowager Duchess of Ormsgill, who had not arrived anywhere before the appointed hour in thirty years, had sent word that she would be in Hertford Street at half past seven. And on the stairs, a little above the water-line, with her trumpet held out before her like a rod and the one-eyed Blücher under her arm, stood Lady Constance, regarding the flood as Moses regarded the sea, in the expectation that it would see reason.

It did not. At the foot of the area steps a French cook of enormous moustaches, lent for the evening from the Ormsgill kitchens, had just thrown a copper pan at the wall, and stood with his arms folded among the debris saying “C’est impossible” to the ceiling, which had not asked him. Mrs Bunting, who had cooked in the house for thirty years and never wept at a bill, was weeping into a roller towel over the turtle. It lay in a tub by the stove, a creature of thirty-eight pounds, the Duchess’s own gift, three guineas’ worth of Jamaica, with its chin in the water and its eyes shut. “He was lively at noon,” said Mrs Bunting, “he were lively as a lamb. And the Duchess coming. And the General’s own copper, and a flood—”

“I beg your pardon,” said a thin dry voice by the stove, addressed to no one in particular, “but I think the turtle is not dead.”

Winifred, passing at that moment down the plank of the scullery door with a bucket in either hand, looked round. It was Miss Fell, in her grey gown and her mittens, standing ankle-deep with her skirts held up in one hand and her eyes upon the tub, with the fixed polite attention she gave to everything, as though it might presently apologise. Nobody else had heard. Mrs Bunting was in her towel, Monsieur Gaspard in his apostrophe; Lady Constance, on the stair, was occupied with the flood. Winifred put down the buckets, rolled up a sleeve, and put one finger into the tub, and the turtle opened an eye, and shut it with the weary contempt of a magistrate.

“It is not dead,” said Winifred.

She was a good deal amused. She had come at four o’clock, summoned by a note to be coached in the matter of forks, with a band-box in her arms and a printer’s instinct for the exact moment of disaster; and she had stood at the top of the area steps and recognised it at once. It was a forme gone to pie. There were a great many things, none of them in the right place, and one of them was water, and the water was the Drip. One did not argue with the Drip. One worked round it.

“Mrs Bunting,” she said. “What is wanted first?”

“Miss?”

“What must be on the table first, and at what hour?”

“The soup, miss, at eight. But there’s no soup, there’s a turtle, and the range is—”

“Then the soup is a quarter to eight, and the rest can go on the housekeeper’s hearth.” She took the pencil from behind her ear and wrote on the back of a bill of fare which had been floating by the dresser. “Who has the key of the coal-hole? There will be planks in a house with a sedan chair. I want six, the length of the kitchen, and a chain of buckets to the area steps, and everyone who can lift one. Monsieur.”

“Mademoiselle,” said Monsieur Gaspard, with a bow of enormous irony, “it is impossible.”

“Il est possible,” said Winifred, in the French she had learned from forty menus, “mais il faut déplacer le feu.” She pointed up the stair. “The range is a fixture, like the stone. The saucepans go on the hearth in the housekeeper’s room, and the copper in the laundry will do for the turbot.” She paused, as he drew breath. “I do not know anything about cooking,” said Winifred, “but I know a great deal about being late.”

He looked at her for some seconds. Then, in the manner of a man who has found, in an unexpected quarter, a soldier, he unfolded his arms, and shouted, in English, for the knife-boy.

By six o’clock the thing was in the way of being done, on a system that Hertford Street had never seen and did not recognise as one. Planks ran across the water from the scullery door to the range like the bridge to a fortress. Buckets went up the area steps hand to hand in a chain of two footmen, the knife-boy, the scullery-maid and the butler in his shirtsleeves, with Verity Quarles, who had arrived at half past four in her brown dress as she had promised, at the head of the line, counting. “Eleven inches over three hundred and fifty square feet of open floor is two thousand gallons,” Miss Quarles had announced. “A bucket holds two, and a chain of six at twelve a minute will have us clear in an hour and a half.” They were clear in eighty-one minutes. She was a little sorry that it was not eighty.

The soup, such as it was, stood on the housekeeper’s hearth above stairs in a copper that Monsieur Gaspard regarded as a personal insult, and the pastry had gone to the first-floor pantry on a tray carried by the butler like a sacrament. The box of place-cards, which had been left on the pantry floor, had become a pudding; so Winifred, on the kitchen table, in ten minutes, with the butler’s ink and a hat-box lid cut into sixteen squares, lettered new ones in a plain Roman hand. She set the table by shape. A dinner of sixteen is nothing but a forme: the heavy matter must go to the edges, the quarrelsome must be locked apart, and the thin must be set between the stout so that the whole will carry. She put Sir Marmaduke Crake between two long ladies, and Lady Quarles, who was apt to faint, beside the colonel with one arm, who was apt to catch; she put Verity next to Lord Rupert, because the one had a head for figures and the other an urgent need of them.

At twenty past seven a voice at the top of the area steps said: “I understood there was a flood.”

The Marquess of Stanmere had come in his evening coat, sent by Constance, or by Minton, or by something in himself that he had not examined, to see whether anything remained of the house. He stood on the bottom step with his hat in his hand and the water at his boot-heels, and looked about him at the planks, the buckets, the Frenchman and the printer in the centre of them with a ladle for a baton; and Winifred, who had not heard him come, looked up, and her face did a thing that she afterwards put down to the heat.

“Good,” she said. “Hold this.”

She had stooped, as she spoke, to the tub by the stove, and lifted out of it the dripping and extremely indignant turtle, and put it into his arms. It was green, with a yellow belly like a Dutch cheese, and it looked at the Marquess with an expression of the profoundest disapproval.

“What is it?”

“A turtle. It is not dead.”

“I am relieved to hear it.”

“It is to go up to the dry pantry on the first floor, and be put on a chair with a cushion, and nobody is to say anything to it. Mind the third plank. It is not nailed.”

He minded the third plank. He carried the turtle across the kitchen with his head up and his back straight, in a black coat that had cost forty guineas, as another man might have carried a sleeping duchess, and mounted the area steps and went through the baize door and across the black and white of the hall at precisely twenty-nine minutes past seven, at which instant the footman, ignorant of everything, threw open the street door upon the Dowager Duchess of Ormsgill.

She stood on the threshold in purple satin, with her turban and her stick and her tiny glittering ruined face, and nobody behind her but a page. She looked at the Marquess, and at the turtle, and at the Marquess.

“Julian,” said the Duchess. “That is a turtle.”

“Yes, ma’am.”

“Is it dead?”

“I am assured not.”

“How very inconvenient for the soup.” She advanced into the hall, as an army advances into a conquered city. “Take it round by the back. I have not been greeted with a turtle since the Peace of Amiens, and then it was only the Prince.”

She dressed in four minutes, in the housekeeper’s room, with the housekeeper holding the candle and the knife-boy holding the shoes; and came to the drawing-room at eight with her hair damp under the rule, her cheeks very pink with the heat of the hearth, and her left glove drawn up over a thumb that no ordinary soap would have shifted in a week. Nobody in the room perceived that she had come by way of the coal-hole.

The dining-room was of the greatest austerity: fifty-two degrees by the thermometer on the wall, as it had been on every day of every month since the General died, the fire being lit only for the departure of the guests. His cases of stuffed birds had been moved into it for the occasion, to add to the company, and a heron the height of a boy stood on the sideboard with a fish in its bill and an air of having been invited. Barnaby had been asked, and had declined, on the ground that someone must stay with the Drip.

Lady Constance sat at the head, with her trumpet laid beside her fork. The Duchess had the place of honour, with Winifred on her left and Mr Underhill, the editor of the Morning Gazette, on Winifred’s other hand; Julian sat directly across, so that Lady Constance might give him the pleasure of watching. Beyond them were Sir Marmaduke Crake, M.P., and his lady; Sir Ephraim Quarles, who said “Plain terms” to the footman, and Lady Quarles, who looked about her for a sofa; Verity; Lord Rupert; Mrs Underhill, who spoke in a whisper and ate in a hurry; two bishops’ widows; a Colonel Fenn with one arm; and Miss Fell, at the foot, in her grey gown, whom Lady Constance had asked to make up the number as one sets a salt-cellar to level a table.

Mr Underhill was large and pink, with a voice so beautiful that it seemed a waste to have put it to the service of libel law. He had been invited to keep the Gazette sweet. He seized upon Winifred before the soup was down, and turned the whole organ of it upon her. “Pargeter’s! My printer! My dear young lady, I cannot express to you what a pleasure. The Gazette has been a matchmaker!”

“It was the Gazette that said so, Mr Underhill,” said Winifred.

“Exactly! Precisely so! It was in the paper and so it was. I do not call it chance, Lady Constance,” said Mr Underhill, to the head of the table. “The Gazette does not retract, madam. It clarifies. And in this case I venture to say that it has clarified a marriage.”

Winifred put her hand flat on the table, beside her plate. She did not say anything. It is no light matter to be congratulated on one’s greatest crime by the person whom it has most nearly ruined, and she found, on examination, that the best course was to look at the soup.

It was a very good soup. It was a calf’s head, with a quantity of green things, passed in the candlelight as turtle by a cook who had been told that it must be so passed; and it was received with a murmur. “A great deal better than I looked for,” said the Duchess, to the table at large. “I should not have thought a turtle capable of so much.”

Sir Marmaduke Crake, M.P., a broad man who had been waiting for the soup to be removed in order to deliver himself of an opinion, delivered it with the fish. Wheat, he said, stood at seventy-four shillings the quarter and was rising, and he called that prosperity. Where the farmer throve, the nation throve, and he would answer for it before any man.

“I beg your pardon, Sir Marmaduke,” said Winifred.

The table, which had been talking, ceased to talk.

“A quartern loaf was thirteenpence in the Row on Tuesday. A labourer in the Weald earns nine shillings in the week, and a household of five eats seven quartern loaves in seven days. That is seven shillings and sevenpence in bread alone, and leaves one and fivepence for his rent, his fuel, his shoes and his tea. Where the farmer thrives,” said Winifred, “the labourer has one and fivepence.”

There was a pause such as follows the dropping of a plate. Sir Marmaduke had turned the colour of the lobster sauce. “Madam,” he said, “who is your authority?”

“A Kentish farmer. I set his type.”

Across the table the Marquess of Stanmere, who had been engaged with a wing of pheasant, put his napkin to his mouth and made a noise like a man swallowing a coin. It was a larded pheasant, three months from lawful, sent up from the ice-house at Ormsgill Park with a note that said only Eat them, the Duchess regarding the Game Act as an opinion; and a small bone of it had entered his windpipe at the exact moment when the Farmer was named. He choked. Rupert thumped him on the back with the energy of a man who has been waiting years for the opportunity. Lady Quarles, finding the thing too much, laid the back of her hand to her forehead and slid slowly from her chair into the arms of the colonel with one arm, who caught her with the practised grace of a man who had done it before; and for a minute and a half the dinner at Hertford Street was, in the Duchess’s own words, as good as a play.

“You have been reading the Farmer,” said Verity Quarles, round the lady in the colonel’s arms, with her spectacles on, in the tone of one who has seen a ledger come right. “The figures are perfectly sound. I checked the seventh against the Corn Returns.”

“I did not doubt it,” said Winifred. Across the table, with the bone gone and his eyes streaming, the Marquess of Stanmere looked at her over his napkin and found that he could trust neither his windpipe nor his ears.

The menu cards stood by each plate in their silver holders. They had been ordered by Lady Constance from Mr Pratt of Bond Street, who was stationer to the nobility and, in her view, to nobody else, and they had been delivered at six that evening by a boy straight to the dining-room, dry. Winifred had not looked at hers. A person who sets type for her bread does not read a card in the ordinary way; it is borne in upon her, as a smell is, from across a room. She picked it up, looking for the date, and the card told her, in four places, in the voice of a small shrill relation at a wedding, everything that was wrong.

At Lady Constance Dyer’s, Hartford Street. Turtle Soup,. Turbot with Lobster Sauce. Saddle of Mutton. Pheasent, larded. Sallad.

There was the comma stranded after the soup like a hair on a plate. There was Pheasent. There was Sallad. And at the head, over the whole, in a copperplate of the greatest elegance, every one of sixteen cards had the street wrong: Hartford, with an a, and not Hertford with an e, the name of the street in which Lady Constance Dyer had lived since 1787.

Her thumb went out of its own accord. It was the old proof-reader’s gesture, and she had made it ten thousand times: the little loop that says dele, take out, strike. It passed across the a in Hartford, and the blue-black thumb, in its bareness, lay on the cream pasteboard beside the offending letter. And stayed. She looked at Lady Constance at the head of the table, upright in her bombazine, with a high colour under the powder, who had gone to a stationer in Bond Street rather than a printer in the Row because a Dyer did not take her cards from the people she was obliged to; and who had been so proud of them that she had not read them.

She lifted the thumb. She made no mark.

“You saw the street,” said the Duchess, at her elbow, in the voice in which she said everything, which carried to the saucepans.

“I saw it.”

“And?”

“It is her house,” said Winifred.

The pins in the Duchess’s face went out of focus, and then came back very bright. She looked at the girl beside her for some seconds with an expression that no one in Hertford Street, or Piccadilly, or the whole of the Peerage, had seen on it since 1786; and then, without turning her head, she addressed the length of the table. “Constance!”

“Ma’am?” said Lady Constance, behind the trumpet.

“You have overdone the turtle.”

There was a rush of laughter that might have been heard in the Mews. Lady Constance Dyer sat bolt upright for a moment, in a state of fury so complete that it was indistinguishable from joy; and then, with a movement of great dignity, raised her trumpet to her ear, as though she had not heard, and was heard by those nearest her to say, in a low firm voice, “The turtle was exact.”

It was the second time in her life that Winifred had seen an error in print and let it lie. It was the first time that she had done it out of kindness. The narrator mentions it only because the reader may be keeping count.

The moulded ice came with the dessert, in the shape of a pineapple, on a silver dish; and it stood in the middle of the cloth for eleven minutes, and did not melt. It was the first ice in the history of Hertford Street to complete a dinner in the shape in which it had begun, the dining-room being, as has been stated, fifty-two degrees; and the Duchess, who had eaten a quantity of it, put down her spoon and announced, to the cloth, that she would send her carriage to the Row in the morning to engage Pargeter’s for her cards. “All of them,” said the Duchess. “I have six hundred. And the funerals.”

Mr Underhill said, in his organ voice, that he was gratified beyond expression.

“I was not speaking to you,” said the Duchess.

When the last of the guests had gone, a little after eleven, and the street was a clatter of wheels in the wet, Winifred stood in the hall in her cloak, waiting for the Stanmere carriage to be brought round. Lady Constance had settled the matter in a sentence: the Marquess would see his betrothed to the Row, since the Gazette had declared them as good as married, and the distance was two and a half miles, which was thirty-five minutes in the rain, and a question of arithmetic. He was finding his hat. The drawing-room door stood ajar behind her. Through it, in the light of one candle, sat Lady Constance and the Duchess of Ormsgill at either side of the fire that had at last been lit, the pug between them on a footstool. Lady Constance had taken off her ear-trumpet. It was the first time that Winifred had seen her without it, and it made her look smaller, and her ears, which were perfectly sound, stood out.

“Well,” said Lady Constance.

“Well,” said the Duchess. She said it at the pitch at which she said everything. “Which of them knows?”

There was a silence in the drawing-room. The fire settled.

“Neither,” said Constance.

“Good. It is much the best way.”

Winifred stood with a hand on the newel. She had no notion what they meant. There was the engagement, which each of them knew to be a lie, or there was something else, and she could not tell which of the two she was afraid of. She put it away, in the place where one puts a proof that has come back with a mark one does not understand; and she would find it again before the night was out, at the instant when she least expected it, and had least armour.

The footman announced the carriage. She put on her gloves, the right and then the left, drawing the kid over the thumb that was still, in the lamplight, a faint blue, as it always would be, as it had been since she was seventeen; and she discovered, standing in the hall of a house in which she had been cold and wet and ridiculous and, for the first time in her life, wanted, that she did not mind in the least who saw.

chapters.title: Let It Stand
chapters.html:
The Stanmere carriage stood in Piccadilly with its lamps lit and its wheels hub-deep in an arm of the sea. It had come down from Hertford Street in good order as far as the dip below Devonshire House, where the road falls towards the Green Park and the drain beneath it, which had been asked since six o’clock to carry away the whole west end’s opinion of the weather, had given up the attempt. There it had stopped, with its four lamps shining on a sheet of black water that went off down the hill into the dark, and the rain coming down upon the roof with the exact sound of a great many people drumming their fingers.

Inside it were two persons, each in a corner, and neither saying anything.

After some minutes the coachman climbed down from the box. Pegg was fifty, with a face like a walnut and a gift, much prized by his employers, for hearing nothing. He took a horse by the head in either hand and went forward into the flood in his drab coat, up to the thigh, at the pace of a funeral, and he did not look back. This left the carriage, to any eye that cared to look, a lit yellow box with its blinds drawn, from which nothing could be seen and in which nothing could be heard but the rain; and it should be set down here that the arrangement was entirely Pegg’s. The Marquess had given no order. Pegg had driven the sixth Marquess through the whole of a quarrel and the seventh through the whole of a Season, and he would be remembered at Michaelmas for his tact; there are men who can find the lamps of the next carriage at the bottom of a hill without once turning the head.

“My lord,” said Winifred.

“Miss Pargeter.”

“I have something to tell you which is not covered by the Articles.”

“Is it a thing I should sit down for?”

“You are sitting down.”

“Then I am prepared,” said Julian; and was not, as it turned out, in the least.

She said it plainly, in short sentences, looking at the blind. She had practised it for twenty-eight days, in the dark, in the room on the second floor with the cat on the foot of the bed, and it came out in the order in which she had practised it, as a line comes out of a stick. “At twenty minutes to five on the morning of the sixth of June, Fairweather handed me one of the first sheets, which had been hanging to dry since two, and a heel of bread. I read the Fashionable Intelligence. I found my name in it. I did not need to be told what had happened, because I had set the page; I knew where each line had come from. I knew at once.”

He said nothing.

“I did the arithmetic. If I stopped the cart, I must reset the forme and print eleven hundred again, and the cart would go at nine, not a quarter past five, and that was Clause Six, and Clause Six was a second breach, and the contract was void. If I let it go, there was a chance that the paragraph would be corrected, and that was Clause Nine, and the contract was void in another way. But a chance is not a certainty. Stopping the cart was a loss I could count. Letting it go was a loss that might not come.” She drew a breath. “It is the sort of arithmetic a person does who has seven hundred and forty pounds to find. I took the uncertain one.”

“And the carter?”

“Sowerby. He asked if there was anything the matter with the load. I said nothing. I stood in the arch with the sheet in my hand until the cart had turned into the Row, and he looked back once, at the corner. My father’s bell rang. I went up and gave him his tea.” She turned her head at last. In the light that came through the blind she was very small and very upright, with the rule in her hair. “I have told my father that I made the error. That is true. I have not told him that I saw it. I have not told anyone. You and I are the only two people living who know it for certain, and Mr Lovejoy, I think, knows enough. I thought you should hear it from me.”

He was silent for so long that she began to count. She had reached forty-one.

“Say something,” said Winifred. “Please. Anything. You may say that it was wicked. It was.”

“I am considering the arithmetic,” said Julian.

It was, in point of fact, what he was doing; but it was not what he was feeling, and he was a little surprised to find the two so far apart. He had thought since the sixth of June a number of generous things about the error. He had pictured the rain through the slates, and a tired woman, and a mischance; he had been prepared to forgive it, handsomely, as one forgives a rose for its thorns. He had not pictured this. He found, examining himself in the lit dark of his own carriage, that he preferred it. A mischance is a thing that happens to a person. A choice is a thing a person does; and he had sat for twenty-eight days beside a woman who had done one, in the same hat, and been exactly as civil as before.

“Then we are the same sort of coward,” he said.

“I beg your pardon?”

“When I read the paragraph at breakfast, I laid a pencil on it. An H pencil, sharpened at five. I laid it flat across the words entirely well founded, and I did not make a mark. Minton stood at my elbow with the draft of a correction in his hand, and said My lord?, and I said In a moment. I said it twice. It is the second moment I should like to take back.” He turned the ring. “I had a pencil, Miss Pargeter. I was in the act of correcting the Gazette. I am the only man in England who reads it with a pencil. And I put it down.”

“You said on the seventh that you would let it stand.”

“I had decided on the sixth. I only did not know that I had.” He looked down at his hands. “It is the whole of my character. It would be a great relief to me to suppose there was another.”

She did not say that it was not true. It was the first time that he had known her not to say a kind thing that was untrue, and it moved him more than the kind thing would have done.

“I should like to show you something,” said Julian.

“Is it a thing I should sit down for?”

“You are sitting down.”

“Then I am prepared,” said Winifred; and there was a little breath of a laugh in it, the first since Hertford Street.

He took it out of his breast pocket. It was a small flat book of green morocco, much handled, with a ribbon marker, and he laid it in her gloved hand and said nothing at all. Inside the lid, on the first leaf, in a small even hand she did not know, was a date in November: and below it, pasted square on the leaf with a thin tide of paste at the edge, a slip of proof the size of a thumb-nail, cut with scissors from a margin. The slip said A semicolon is not a courtesy.

It was in her own hand.

She turned the leaf. There was another. Delete ‘deplorable’. You have used it three times in a column. And another, and another, a pasted slip on every leaf and under each a line in the same even writing, in pencil, dated: She is right. She is right. She is wrong, and I shall not say how. Quartern. She is right. There were pages of them. She went through them with her thumb, the blue one, past a hundred, a hundred and three, with the lamp of the carriage swinging a little on its bracket as the horses moved and the rain going on overhead; and she saw her own commas, and his figures, and the whole of a year laid out in two hands, one over the other, as a proof lies over a forme.

“You are the Farmer,” said Winifred.

“I am the Farmer.”

“The author is obliged. He means I.” She heard her own voice go up. “That was Minton’s slip. In the hatbox.”

“Minton wrote it. At my instruction. I thought it was amusing.”

“You thought it was—” She shut the book. She held it in both hands in her lap and looked at it with an expression that Julian could not read in the dark, and then could, quite suddenly, when the lamp swung: she was white round the mouth, and her eyes were very bright, and it was not at all certain which of two things was about to happen. “Nine months,” said Winifred. “I wrote to you for nine months in the margins of a sheet, and you were in a house in Curzon Street, with a pencil. I told Mr Ingram I should like to make you say you were wrong. I said it in front of you. You stood at my stone and let me say that a man who has never been wrong is a wall.”

“You did put it very well.”

“I said it to your face. On the twenty-second of June. And you told me that the Farmer was a bore in person.”

“I said I was told.”

“You have the conscience of the Articles,” said Winifred. “I will give you that. You did not lie aloud.” She struck the book with her hand, once, on the cover. “And at Lady Constance’s table, before sixteen persons, I informed Sir Marmaduke Crake that I was acquainted with the Kentish farmer, and you choked on a bone.”

“It was a pheasant.”

“It served you right.”

“It did,” said Julian. “It was extremely painful. I assure you, it was not a thing done for effect.”

“You came to the Row on the seventh of June,” said Winifred, and there was an odd shake in the voice, “to find out who had been correcting your commas.”

“And to ask who had set the type. The one reason was a pretext for the other.” He had the grace to look at the blind. “I have not yet decided which.”

She laughed. It broke out of her in a helpless rush, and she put the green book against her mouth, with her shoulders shaking, and he sat across from her and watched it happen with an expression of the most extraordinary gravity, as a man watches a thing he has been told he will not be shown. It was a long time before she could speak. “The quartern, not the peck,” said Winifred, into the morocco.

“I was waiting to be asked.”

“I should have asked.”

“I should have said.” He took the book from her gently. He did not take the hand. “You wished me wrong, once. I am prepared to oblige.”

“Then oblige.”

“I was wrong. I was wrong on the sixth of June, and every day after it; and wrong at the stone on the twenty-second, and in my own library on Sunday. I have been wrong in the Gazette a hundred and three times, and you have the receipts.” The carriage rocked. Somewhere ahead, in the rain, Pegg was speaking to a horse. “It is a very strange thing. I find that I don’t mind it at all.”

They came to the arch at a little after one in the morning, with the flood behind them and the rain easing. Pegg drew up in the Row, at the mouth of the Court, which was too narrow for the carriage; and Julian handed her down, and paid no attention whatever to the coachman’s absence of expression, and walked with her under the brick arch, eight feet wide, into the dark.

The Court was empty and shining. The pump stood in the middle with its handle laid like a drowned arm, and above them the sooty brick of Pargeter’s went up three storeys into the black, with one light in it, high up, where Brevier sat in a window. Under the keystone of the arch, a smaller cousin of the Drip was falling into a puddle with a note she could have sung. She stopped under it.

“Here,” said Winifred. “I stood here.”

“I know.”

“I had good boots. I did not use them.” She laughed, shakily, at nothing. “It is a stupid thing to say. It is the thing I have said to myself, in the dark, for twenty-eight nights.”

He did not say that it was not stupid. He did not say anything. He stood in front of her, a tall man a little stooped, with the lamp of the court’s one lantern in his eyes, and the white notch in the left eyebrow lifted, and he put out his hand and took the rule from her hair, which came down. He put the brass strip in her palm and shut her fingers over it. And then he kissed her, under the arch where the cart had gone out, with the rain falling beside them and a small clean drop between: once, with great care, as he would have set a word, and then rather less carefully, and for some time.

It was Winifred who stopped. She stopped with her hand against his waistcoat, flat, as one lays a hand on a forme to feel whether it is level, and she took a step back, and looked at him in the lantern light with her hair on her shoulders and her mouth not at all steady.

“We have broken an Article,” she said.

“Which?”

“Six.”

The corner of his mouth went. “I believe it said an Attachment of the Affections. I have been seeking a loophole for some time. I find that it cannot be done by attaching one oneself.”

“Do not be clever. You are not clever. You are exact, which is a different matter.” She put her hand to her hair, and discovered the rule in her fist, and looked at it. “I will say it once, and I shall say it properly. I will not say yes tonight.”

“I haven’t asked.”

“You are about to. I can see the clause forming.” She drew a breath. “While my father’s notes are Lovejoy’s, I will not be a woman who was bought by a dinner. Do you see? I should never know. I should be in your house, and I should think, he arranged it; and it would be a thing between us for forty years. I have seven hundred and forty pounds to find and eighty-seven days. Ask me at Michaelmas. When I do not need you.”

He was a long time silent. It came to her that she had never before seen the Marquess of Stanmere with nothing in his face at all. He had a trick of answering a vague question with Which?; he had been put, as it were, by a question into the state of a man in a chair with nobody on the other side of the table, and she watched him find it was possible to sit there.

“Stet,” said Julian.

“Yes?”

“Let it stand. The Articles, to Michaelmas. And I shall ask you then, and you will tell me.” He stopped. “I have, as you may have observed, a very bad habit of arranging things. I propose to be broken of it by an expert.”

“And the Farmer?”

“I would ask you not to tell anyone the name. Not yet. Not your father. It is not the shame of it. I find that I should like, once, to be answered by the man and not the peer. I should like to be argued with.” The signet turned. “I have not had that very often.”

“I shall not tell,” said Winifred. “It is not in the Gazette.”

It came back to her then. She had not been looking for it; it came as it always does when it is not looked for, as a letter drops out of a case of its own accord. It was the Duchess, in the dim drawing-room in Hertford Street, at the pitch at which she said everything: Which of them knows? And Constance, with the trumpet laid by: Neither. She stood under the arch, with a drop of cold water falling upon the toe of her shoe, and understood precisely what had been meant, and who it was that had not known, and how long; and that it had been settled at a dinner for sixteen, by two old women with a pug, a good while before she was told.

“Heavens,” said Winifred.

“What is it?”

“Nothing. A proof coming back.” She turned to the door.

It was on the latch, as it always was. She pushed it, and the passage was dark and smelt of ink and lye, and a draught went up the stairs; and out of the wall by the composing room door, from the brass mouth of the speaking-tube Barnaby had rigged to his bed, came a long sleepy rumble that carried a good deal further than he supposed, out through the open door and across the Court to the tall man standing in the lantern-light with his hat in his hand.

“Win? Is that you? Is that rain, or the Marquess?”

Winifred put her mouth to the tube.

“It is rain, Father,” she said.

The rain, which had been easing, came on again at that moment with a fine unanimity, in a long grey wash across the Court, upon the pump, upon the sooty bricks, upon the Marquess of Stanmere standing in his evening clothes with his face turned up to it; and it would be an exaggeration to say that Winifred Pargeter had told her father a lie. It was rain. The Marquess was merely also there.

At two in the morning, a hundred yards away, in Ave Maria Lane, there was one light burning in the long front of the Phoenix Press, in a first-floor window, behind a bow of a hundred and twelve small panes. It had been burning since eleven. It was a candle in a tin sconce, and under it, at a high desk, with a pair of spectacles pushed up on his forehead and another pair on his nose, a small neat man in a snuff-coloured coat was bent over a ledger. He was counting something. His lips moved. From time to time he made a mark with a very sharp pencil in the margin, and drew a line, and counted again; and he did not look up when the rain came on harder, since it was not his roof.

chapters.title: The Road to Yalding
chapters.html:
The Season, which had been wet from its first night, guttered out through July like a candle in a draught, and nobody was sorry but the milliners. Parliament had risen. The Duchess had gone to Brighton to disapprove of the sea. The Gazette, having nothing to say in August, said it at length in the second column, to the satisfaction of Mr Underhill, who held that a quiet month was a form of praise; and in Hand and Pen Court the Drip fell upon the stone with the regularity of a clear conscience, while two persons who had once broken an Article under an arch kept all the others with a rigour that would have shamed the Chapel. The Marquess of Stanmere called on Tuesdays and Fridays at hours convenient to the press. He stood at the far end of the composing room and discussed the price of paper. Once, handing her a proof, he touched her sleeve instead of her hand, and they both regarded the sleeve for some time as though it had said something improper.

That was how matters stood on the morning of Tuesday the thirtieth of July, when Lady Constance, on the principle that an engagement left in London through August turns like milk, removed the whole of it to Kent. The party, assembled in the Row at five o’clock in a rain that had not the grace to wait for daylight, looked less like a visit than the migration of a small and eccentric nation. There was the Marquess’s travelling-coach, Pegg on the box, which held Lady Constance, the pug, Miss Fell with her writing-case upon her knee, and the Marquess. There was a second coach, yellow, enormous and hired, which smelt faintly of the dogs of a former century, and into which Barnaby Pargeter had been handed with his gouty foot in a bucket of warm bran.

Mrs Hobday, who stayed to keep the house and Mr Orme, stood under the arch with her arms folded and commended the bucket to the Lord. “Thy foot shall not be dashed against a stone,” she said, “provided the ostlers do their part.”

And at the tail of everything, behind two horses the colour of old boots, came a waggon belonging to a carrier of Bermondsey named Heaver, who spoke seldom and then chiefly in oaths. It bore, under a tarpaulin and a great deal of rope, the Old Lady, whom eight men had needed the whole of the previous afternoon to get on to it; two cases of Pica and Great Primer; eleven reams of paper in oilcloth; and, on a hamper from which a single indignant ear protruded, Toby Mudge, who had been given three pies to see him to Kent and had eaten them by Lewisham. The hamper spoke at intervals, in a voice not unlike Mr Underhill’s.

The Quarleses were to follow at their own pace, and Lord Rupert upon a borrowed hack; and in a gig of her own went Miss Verity Quarles, who had declared that she would sooner drive thirty-eight miles in the rain than sit eleven hours beside her mother’s smelling-salts, and who set off first, at a speed that suggested she meant to arrive before the weather.

The reader will forgive the narrator for not taking him over every mile of the Maidstone road, which was that summer a river persuaded to carry vehicles. The hay stood rotting in its cocks the whole length of the Kent Road, and the wheat beyond Farningham, which ought by the thirtieth of July to have been gold, stood the colour of a wet mouse.

Winifred had counted the days to Michaelmas that morning, from habit, as other women count stitches. There were sixty-one. She did not mention it, and the coach, which was large, held her father, Mr Minton and a quantity of silence of the kind that has been politely agreed upon. Mr Minton sat opposite with his watch in his palm, consulting it every four minutes with the expression of a man waiting for it to confess. Barnaby, who could bear a silence about as long as the Albion could bear a loose quoin, said somewhere past Foots Cray:

“My dear Win, did I ever tell you of the Bible of ‘thirty-one?”

“Yes, Father. Four times.”

“The King’s printers, Barker and Lucas, who left the not out of the seventh commandment, so that the whole kingdom was instructed in the plainest English to commit adultery. Three hundred pounds fine, and every copy burned that could be found. I have never been able to read the Decalogue since without feeling for the compositor.” He gazed with great benignity at the rain. “A man may be hanged for a thing he did on purpose, my dear, and it is no great matter, he knows where he is. It is very much harder to be fined for a thing he didn’t.”

Mr Minton looked at his watch. Winifred looked out at a hop garden gone black on its poles. Barnaby, who had not the least notion what he had done, took a pinch of snuff with the air of a man who has contributed to the conversation.

At the Bull in Wrotham, a little after two, they took up Dr Orlando Pym. He was waiting under the archway with a hat that held a puddle and a portmanteau that clanked: a long mild gentleman of fifty-odd, in a clergyman’s green-black coat, who had a living on the Medway and had gone up to London the previous Friday to petition the Dean and Chapter of St Paul’s to take the lightning-rods off their dome. He had been received by a verger. Lady Constance, appealed to from the step of the first coach, said that her carriage was full and held up her trumpet to prove it; and so it was Barnaby who put out a hand and said, “My dear fellow, you will be wet,” and brought the Doctor in.

“It is the rods, madam,” said Dr Pym to Winifred, arranging the portmanteau upon his knee, whence it continued to clank. “They went up in ‘sixty-nine, and since then the electrical fluid that ought to discharge itself in an honest clap has been drawn quietly out of the heavens, and what is left has nowhere to go but down. I have figures.”

“For what period, sir?”

“For Kent, madam, since the first of May.”

“That is ninety-one days.”

“It has rained on eighty-six of them,” said Dr Pym, with the deep content of a man whose theory has been borne out by the weather.

The hill at Wrotham comes down off the Downs into the Weald in one long slope of chalk and clay, which in a dry year is a pleasure to the eye and in the wet of 1816 had the surface and the temper of a cheese. The postilion put the skid under the near wheel at the top, as he ought, and the skid did what a skid will do on grease, which is to become a sledge; and half-way down, in the middle of a sentence of Dr Pym’s concerning the discharge of the clouds, the whole ponderous yellow coach turned slowly to the left, as a stout lady turns to look at a hat, and lay down in the ditch.

Nobody was hurt. The ditch was deep rather than wide, and held to the depth of a man’s thigh a liquid the colour of tea. The coach lay at a cant of thirty degrees with its off-side wheels turning in the air, and the bucket of bran had travelled the length of the interior and, by way of Dr Pym’s hat, arrived at Dr Pym. Barnaby, wedged in a corner with his foot above his head, observed peaceably that he had been wishing to put it up since Lewisham. Winifred got the door open over her head and climbed out upon the side of the coach, which was now the roof, and from there to the bank. Mr Minton, who had gone out first through the window in the interest of lightening the load, had arrived in the ditch up to his chest.

She took him by the tails of his coat, in both hands, and hauled. He came up out of the clay like a cork out of a bottle and stood on the verge streaming, and looked at his watch, which was full of ditch.

“Five minutes to three,” said Mr Minton, with the calm of the thoroughly ruined. “It has stopped. Miss Pargeter, I think I ought to tell you something before we arrive. It may come up.”

“Come up, Mr Minton?”

“Peregrine Pry.” He wiped his face with a wet glove and made it worse. “After the Crier of the sixth of July, with the flood in Lady Constance’s kitchen, which only the household could have known, his lordship suspected me. It was perfectly reasonable. I have ink upon my finger; I am anxious; and I had, as it happened, a motive of shame. He put the question on the Tuesday, in the library, quite baldly: Minton, are you the author of the Quizzing-Glass? It had been three days. It had felt a week.”

“And were you?”

“No!” said Mr Minton. “I had one proof of it in the world, Miss Pargeter, and it was in my pocket, and it was worse.” He lowered his voice, although the nearest person was a postilion. “A sketchbook. Forty drawings. Of his lordship. His lordship as a heron. His lordship as Atlas, with a ham. His lordship correcting the Archbishop’s signboard with a pencil. They are not unkind. I think they are, rather, the contrary. But one does not wish to be found out.”

Meanwhile, at the ditch, the rescue had begun. The first coach had gone on a quarter of a mile before it was found that the second was not behind it, and the first to return was Lord Rupert, on his hack, who looked at the yellow coach in its ditch and said “Good God” with real feeling and “Is anyone hurt?” with rather less. The second was the Marquess, bareheaded, on foot, at a run, whom Winifred observed coming down the hill with an interest she attributed entirely to the coach. Rupert, in a waistcoat that had cost more than the coach, remarked that Stanmere had asked him to a great many things in twenty years but never before to a ditch; and Julian said “Lift,” with his shoulder under the axle and his hat in the mud; and they lifted, with the postilions at the horses and Sir Ephraim, who had come up behind in his own carriage, calling “Plain terms, gentlemen, together,” and the coach came up out of the clay with a sound like a cork leaving a bottle, and stood on the road, steaming.

“He turned over all forty,” said Mr Minton, at her elbow, in a low and unsteady voice. “It took ten minutes. He said, You have my nose right. And then he said, and I have it by heart, I accused you on no evidence but your fingers, which are inky because you work for me. I am sorry for it, and I should like the one with the ham, if you can spare it.” He swallowed. “Two sentences. I have them written in my pocket-book.”

“And Mrs Bunting?”

“Her ladyship decided that the leak must come from the kitchen, and dismissed her. It lasted a day. She was reinstated when her ladyship recollected that Mrs Bunting could not spell turtle.” Julian, passing with the mud to his knees, put a hand for a moment on Mr Minton’s wet shoulder and took it away again, and Mr Minton went the colour of a ham. It occurred to Winifred that if Mr Minton was not Pry then somebody else was; and she put the thought away, as she put away a good many that summer, in the drawer where she kept the proofs she had not yet found time to correct.

The waggon arrived at the foot of the hill at four, at a walk, with the tarpaulin streaming and Toby asleep upon the Old Lady with his mouth open. It crossed the brook that had left its bed at the bottom of the road; and the near hind wheel dropped into a hole the brook had made, and the axle-tree parted with a noise like a pistol.

Heaver stood in the road and said what a carrier says, at length and in a regular metre. Winifred waited for it to end, as she had waited for many things to end, with her hands folded before her.

“How far to a wheelwright, Mr Heaver?”

“Wrotham, miss. Four mile up the hill.”

“And a sound axle?”

“Maidstone.”

She looked at the waggon. It stood on three wheels and the stump of a fourth with its tail in the brook, and on it, lashed under the tarpaulin, eight hundredweight of English oak, the only press in Kent. “Hop-poles,” said Winifred.

There was a stack of them in a gateway, ranked like a palisade: a thousand ash poles, fourteen feet long, which had stood there since March waiting to have bines put on them. She had two taken down. From her bag she took a coil of page-cord, the string with which a compositor ties up a page of type; and out of her hair, after a hesitation in which Rupert, who was watching, said nothing at all, her mother’s brass rule, which she laid flat along the break like a splint along a bone. The poles went alongside the axle, one on either hand. The cord went round them, wet from the brook, to shrink as it dried; and into the angle of the cord she drove four wedges, in the order in which one drives the quoins of a forme, from the middle outward, a little at a time. The difficulty was to lift eight hundredweight in order to do it, and for that she needed six men, who were found in the next field, idle for want of work, and persuaded by a stone jar of Black Bull Entire, a full gallon, which Sir Ephraim produced from the boot of his carriage without being asked. “I never travel without the product,” said Sir Ephraim, “any more than a physician travels without his lancet.” It was a principle of her father’s that no machine was ever lifted by an argument.

They let it down. The splint creaked. It held.

“My dear girl,” said Rupert, “I have seen a duke take less trouble over a divorce.”

“Mr Heaver will drive at a walk,” said Winifred, putting the rule back into her hair with a care she did not give to her own head, “and if he hears it speak, he will stop.”

They came to Yalding at the last of the light, which was not much. There was the long old bridge, and the church of St Peter and St Paul at its foot, and the Medway running full and brown beneath the arches, a good deal fuller than a river should be that is not yet in flood. The road ran out of the village between hedges that dripped, and turned at a lodge into an avenue of limes; and at the end of the avenue the Court stood on its slight rise, Elizabethan red brick with a Georgian front put on like a clean collar, with the meadows going down below it to the river, silver and drowned, and the oast-houses of the home farm with their white cowls all turned to the wind like a congregation. No smoke rose from any chimney.

At the lodge gate a cluster of women had gathered under sacks, to look at the carriages. They had stood an hour in the wet to do it, with a number of children distributed among them like the effects of a sale; and when the first coach had gone through, the women closed in upon the second, which was slower, and a voice at the window said, “Be you the lady in the paper?”

Winifred let down the glass. The voice belonged to an old woman as small and brown as a nut, in a man’s coat and a sack for a hood, leaning on a stick; she was, Winifred afterwards learned, eighty, and she looked in at the coach with the unsparing interest of a person who has not many entertainments left.

“I am Miss Pargeter.”
