“That’s what it said. Miss W. Pargeter, of Paternoster Row. Jem’s mother had it read out to us at the Plough, off a bit of a newspaper somebody’s cousin left. Is it right?”

“It is in the Gazette,” said Winifred.

It came out as it always did, evenly, with the small pause before the second word that Lady Constance had taught her in Hertford Street. It had served her at Ormsgill House and at the Duchess’s table and before an Archdeacon. It had never before been said to anyone with a stick.

Mrs Fryer considered it. “Then it’s a lie, my dear,” she said, not unkindly, “for I can’t read it.”

Somebody behind her laughed, and was hushed. Winifred sat with her hand on the window-strap. For six weeks the formula had been a shield and a joke and, by degrees, something very like a principle; it was true, every word of it; and it had not till this moment struck her that it was only true for those who could read it. It was a thing one said to people who believed in print rather than in faces. Mrs Fryer believed in faces. She had stood in the rain for an hour to look at one.

He had got down from the first coach and come back along the line on foot. He stopped at the window, and took off his hat to a woman of eighty in a sack.

“Mrs Fryer. How is the leg?”

“Wet, my lord.”

“And Jem? Is the fever down?”

“Down, thank the Lord and the Doctor’s physic.”

“And Mrs Pankhurst’s youngest? The croup.”

“Mended. Though Pankhurst’s cow’s gone dry.”

“Duchess?”

“Duchess,” agreed Mrs Fryer, “for want of grass, my lord, there being none.”

He listened. That was what Winifred observed, from the window, with the rain running down the glass between them. In London he had a manner for every room, and all of them were dry; in Kent his sentences grew short and his silences long, and the silences were not empty, but were used, as a compositor uses a quad, to give the words about them room. He knew the wives by their Christian names and the children by their ailments, and, with a gravity that made Winifred look hard at the window-strap, the cows by their grievances. A thin boy hung at his mother’s skirt with a sleeve over his mouth, and Julian’s eye went to him and rested a moment and went away, as the eye of a man goes to an account he has not been able to balance.

“Is it true, my lord?” said Mrs Fryer. “Her in the coach.”

Winifred waited for it. He had said it for six weeks to dukes and archdeacons with a face of stone, and it would have served him now.

“I’ll tell you what is true, since you cannot read it,” said the Marquess of Stanmere. “Miss Pargeter is a very good printer, and I am more fortunate than I deserve to be seen in her company.”

It was an answer Article 4 would have passed without a mark. It had the advantage of being perfectly accurate, and of containing no engagement whatever. “Ah,” said Mrs Fryer. She considered him a while longer, and then Winifred, with her sack-hooded head on one side. “Well. That’s better than a newspaper.”

Mr Wragg was on the step with a lantern: a grey man of fifty-eight, with a face as unrevised as a milestone, who regarded London as an infection that sometimes arrived by carriage. “This is the printer woman, my lord?” he said. “This is Miss Pargeter, Wragg.” “Ah,” said Mr Wragg. “The printer woman.” Beside him stood Mrs Pickett, who had kept the keys of Stanmere Court for forty years and carried them like the Last Trump, and who announced to the assembled company that there was no fire lit in the house but the kitchen, the wood being wet and the coal not come, and delivered it as one announcing a death in the family.

The waggon came up the avenue at ten o’clock, at a walk, with Heaver at the horses’ heads listening to the axle as one listens to an invalid; Toby asleep upon the Old Lady; and Brevier, released at last from the hamper, sitting on the tarpaulin with the air of a cat who has been to Kent before and thought little of it. The steward’s office was the old brewhouse of the Court, from the days when the Court had brewed: a long stone room with a copper the size of a bath in one corner, a high desk, eleven bundles of leases in red tape, one for each of the farms, and a smell of cold hops. Mr Wragg unlocked it with the air of a man opening the family vault to a stranger who has expressed an interest in the bones.

“The press, miss. Nobody told me.”

“I am telling you now, Mr Wragg.”

“Ah,” said Mr Wragg.

It took her, Toby and two footmen, both of them called John, until a quarter to midnight to put the Old Lady where she wished her, on the flags under the great beam, from which Wragg’s man hung the block and fall by which she had been swung down from the cart; and when it was done, and the footmen gone, and Toby rolled up in a sack on the settle with the cat on his feet, Winifred lit a single lantern, set it on the stone, and stood a long while with her hand on the cold bar, doing nothing whatever. She could not sleep in a house that had no press in it. It was a failing of the same family as the Drip.

It was after midnight when a second light came into the yard. She saw it through the window, smeared with rain: a lantern, carried from the direction of the house by a tall man who wore no hat. It crossed the cobbles to within ten yards of the brewhouse door and stopped. He did not knock. She did not go to the door. He stood in the wet with his light on the stones about his boots, and she stood in the dry with her hand on the bar, sixty days now from Michaelmas, it being past midnight, and rather more than that number of feet from him; and the rain came down between them in the two cones of lantern-light with a good deal of patience. Two lanterns burned in Kent that night, one in a brewhouse window and one in the yard outside it, and for a good part of an hour neither of them moved.

chapters.title: The Weald Relief Subscription
chapters.html:
At six o’clock on the morning of Wednesday the thirty-first of July the great tithe barn at Stanmere Court held sixty persons in wet clothes, steaming gently, and a Marquess standing on a hay-cart reading aloud from a table of figures.

It was a barn of the kind built by men who expect to be paid in kind: oak and stone, a hundred and twenty feet long, roofed like the nave of a church and a good deal better kept, with the grey light coming in at the gable and lying along the threshing floor in a cold bar. The farmers sat in front on bales, their hats upon their knees. Behind them stood the labourers, and behind the labourers the women; and at the back, on a bale that had been covered with a shawl in her honour, sat Lady Constance Dyer with her trumpet raised, Miss Fell beside her with the umbrella, and Winifred Pargeter at the end of the row, with her hands in her lap and her left thumb in plain view, since nobody in Kent had yet thought to look at it.

Julian read the table in his dry flat voice, which was not an orator’s, and had never in thirty-one years been raised, and which carried to the back of the barn for that reason. He had written a speech at five that morning and burned it at a quarter past, because it contained a metaphor.

“Wheat, at Maidstone on Saturday, seventy-eight shillings the quarter. The quartern loaf, thirteen pence.” He turned the paper. “The wage of a labourer in the three parishes, nine shillings the week. A family of five eats seven quartern loaves in a week, which is seven shillings and sevenpence. That leaves one shilling and fivepence for rent, fuel, shoes and a shirt.” He looked up. “I have done the sum six times. It does not come out.”

Somebody in the third row laughed, not unkindly, as a man laughs at a joke that is not one, and the laugh went round the barn and died. Of the eleven farms, Julian went on, nine had no hops worth the picking; the bine had mouldered on the pole in July; and the duty on a crop that did not exist was a matter he proposed to write to the Chancellor about, and expect no answer. At his elbow Mr Gideon Wragg, in a grey coat the colour of his hair, supplied in a voice like a gate the figures for the barns. “Eleven farms, my lord. Not a third full.”

Julian was aware, without turning his head, of a small square person at the end of the back row who had read every one of these figures nine times in a clerk’s fair hand and queried the commas. It was an odd sensation, to be heard by the single person present who knew whose they were. He found that he was reading rather more slowly.

“What’s to be done, my lord?”

It was a man in the third row, with his hat upon his knee and hands like roots: Amos Pankhurst, of Hope Farm, who had asked Julian’s father the same question in the year ‘ninety-eight about a different failure, and been told. Julian had been asked it in one form or another all his life, and his habit was to answer it by arranging something before the question was finished.

“I do not know yet,” said the Marquess of Stanmere.

It is a thing a man may say once or twice in a lifetime, and he said it to sixty people and a dairymaid. “I can tell you what I shall not do. I shall not tell you it will be well. I wished you to have the figures from me, and not from the overseer, who has them wrong. You shall have the rest when I have it.”

Nobody cheered. This was Kent. Pankhurst nodded slowly, twice, as at a price that was fair if disagreeable, and put on his hat; and at the back Winifred, who had expected an orator and been given a man reading out his own account, found that she was looking very hard at the toe of her shoe.

It was Lady Constance who found the use for him. She did it over cold ham, rapping on the table with her trumpet like an auctioneer.

“A subscription.”

“Aunt?”

“It is a question of arithmetic. Kent has twelve hundred landowners and no reason to give. It will give if it is asked in print, with a table, by a man with a title. Every reader of the Gazette in the county, and every name in the Directory.” She turned the lorgnette upon the far end of the table, where Winifred was dividing a roll with the economy of one who knew to a farthing what it cost. “You have a press.”

“We have a press,” said Julian, and looked at Winifred.

“We have a common press, my lord, one case of Great Primer and no damp paper,” said Winifred. “I can give you five hundred broadsides in a week and a thousand in ten days, if the Medway permits.”

“The Medway,” said Mr Wragg from the doorway, where he had come with a ledger and the face of one who regards breakfast as a luxury of the idle, “will do as it pleases.”

She designed it that afternoon at the steward’s high desk, with a pencil, Julian’s table at her left hand and her father in a chair at her right with his foot on a bucket, offering views. A broadside is a small thing and the hardest of all to set, since it has to be read by someone walking past; it must say everything in the time it takes to cross a yard. She cut the appeal to four sentences and the Farmer’s adjectives to none, and set the heading in Great Primer, and ruled the table with brass, and on the Friday evening, with the first proof damp upon the stone, she showed it to the Marquess.

THE WEALD OF KENT. A SUBSCRIPTION for the Relief of the Labouring Poor of Yalding, Nettlestead and Hunton, where the hops have failed and the wheat is dear.

The quartern loaf, thirteen pence. A labourer’s wage, nine shillings the week. Seven loaves for a family of five, seven shillings and sevenpence. Remaining for rent, fuel and clothing, one shilling and fivepence.

“The price of bread is the one arithmetic from which the poor are never excused.” A KENTISH FARMER.

Subscriptions are received by Mr Wragg, Steward, Stanmere Court, Yalding, and by the Overseers of the three parishes. Printed at Stanmere Court by B. Pargeter, Hand and Pen Court, Paternoster Row.

He read it standing at the high desk with the proof flat beneath his long hands. “The last line but one,” he said. “I did not give you that.”

“Letter the Fifth. Second paragraph. I queried excused; I thought spared was cleaner. You said no.”

“I was right.”

“You were. It is a better sentence than I could write, and it ought to be on every barn door in Kent.” She wiped her hands on her apron. Her father slept in his chair with his spectacles on his forehead, and Toby was at the pump, and she spoke low. “It ought to have your name under it.”

“Quite.”

“That is your word for no.”

“It is.” He took off the pencil from behind his ear, which he had not known was there. “A peer on corn is a landlord pleading for his rents. A farmer on corn is an honest man in a bad hat. The Farmer has been listened to for a year because he is nobody.”

“He has been listened to because he is right.”

“He has been listened to because he is nobody who is right. It is an uncommon combination, and I should not like to spoil it.” But he was smiling, a little, at the proof. “You told me once you wished to hear him say he was wrong.”

“I wished to hear him say it in his own name. Mr Underhill would print a Marquess before he would print a kitchen. The Weald would pay for it.”

“The Weald will pay for the table.”

“My lord, you are the most obstinate person I ever set type for.”

“It is a family trait,” said Julian, and was sorry at once, for the last time he had used the phrase it had been about something else; and she did not smile, and he put down the pencil. “No. Not yet. I will think of it.” It was not yes. She did not tell. She had promised, and she had a habit of keeping what she had promised, and it was a better habit than most.

The notice on the tithe-barn door had been wrong for eleven years. She had seen it the first morning, and had not said so, which was a thing she was learning to do. It was a printed sheet in Great Primer, nailed up in the year ‘five by a Maidstone printer, and it read: TITHES AND RENTS DUE AT THIS BARN AT LADY DAY AND MICHAELMAS. NO ABATEMENT. BY ORDER, G. RAGG, STEWARD. The W of Wragg was gone. For eleven years the steward of Stanmere Court had gone about his master’s farms as Mr Ragg, and not a man in Kent had had the courage to tell him, or, which was more likely, the wish.

At Hertford Street, three weeks earlier, she had learned to let an error stand. It was among the most useful things she had ever learned, and she had been rather proud of it. But the error at Hertford Street had been a friend’s, and had cost no one anything; this one was costing a man his name, in public, every Lady Day. There is a difference, which a compositor knows in the thumb, between an error that is a friend’s and an error that is a wound; and on the Thursday morning she set the notice afresh in the corner of the forme, with a W at the head of Wragg as clean as a new pin, and nailed it up herself, over the old one, from a ladder, in the rain, while the steward watched from the barn with his arms folded.

He read it for some time. He read it as a man reads his own epitaph, to see whether they have got it right.

“That is my name,” said Mr Wragg.

“Yes, Mr Wragg.”

“It’s been Ragg these eleven years. I never—” He stopped. “A man doesn’t like to ask.”

“No,” said Winifred, with feeling.

“Ah,” said Mr Wragg, and went away; and sulked, in the manner of a person who has been done a kindness without his leave, until dusk, when he met her crossing the yard and touched his hat to her without a word. In the morning it was Miss Pargeter.

The post came that afternoon, by a boy on a pony, with a letter in a hand like type: each letter standing by itself, and none touching. It was from Mr Orme.

Miss,—Mr Trigg’s young man called Monday with a paper. Mr Trigg has made over his account against this house, being four hundred pounds for paper, to Mr H. Lovejoy, who will take it at Michaelmas with the rest. The paper is stamped. Mr Lovejoy’s boy waited for a receipt and was given a glass of water. Sparrow is punctual and clean, which I do not like. The Gazette went to the cart at a quarter before five on Tuesday with a Bishop on the second page. The Drip is steady. I have read your last letter backwards as well as forwards and find no difference. Your obedient, A. Orme.

She read it twice, which for her was a form of weeping. “Seven hundred and forty,” said Winifred aloud. “Four hundred. One thousand one hundred and forty pounds.”

“Trigg has been very kind to us these eleven years, Win,” said her father, brightly.

“He has now been very kind to Mr Lovejoy.”

“A paper merchant, my dear girl, is a man who sells what is shortly to be worth less. He is accustomed to disappointment.” He took his spectacles from his forehead, found them in his hand, and put them upon his nose, from which he regarded her face. “Don’t tell Stanmere.”

“Article the Third.”

“Quite right. Nobody ought to be the poorer for being fond of us.”

On the Saturday, Mrs Pickett having at last dried enough wood in the bakehouse oven to light a fire in the dining-room, the whole party dined for the first time in a warm room, which made them garrulous. Dr Pym had held the table since the soup. He had reached the electrical fluid at the fish and the dome of St Paul’s at the saddle of mutton, and he was explaining, with a pear in his hand for the cathedral, that the rods drew off the discharge of the clouds and left the rain with nowhere to go but the Weald, when Miss Quarles took off her spectacles, which hung on a chain, and put the question that had been forming behind them for some days.

“How many rods were there on St Paul’s in 1810, Dr Pym? And how much did it rain?”

“One, madam. And the rain was—” The Doctor paused. “I believe the usual.”

“One rod and the usual rain. And in this year one rod, and the unusual.” She put the spectacles on again and looked at him through them with her flat kind eye. “I should say the rod was a constant.”

“It is the accumulation of the effect, madam.”

“Ah,” said Verity.

“Plain terms, Doctor,” said Sir Ephraim from the other end of the table. “She thinks you’ve chosen the wrong sum.”

“I think he is an honest man,” said Verity, “and has taken a great deal of trouble over it.” Rupert, who throughout the Doctor’s discourse had looked at her as at an interesting piece of pastry, asked her afterwards to dance in the hall, where the carpets were up on account of the damp. She said that she did not. He said that neither did he; he merely walked about in time. They went off to do so, with Miss Fell at the pianoforte, who played what she was asked and said in the whole of the evening eleven words.

At midnight, in the old brewhouse, Julian stood on one side of the stone and discovered that he had not known a hand-press could be so quiet.

He was there as a customer, which is to say on sufferance. Barnaby sat on a stool with his foot on a bucket; Toby, in a paper hat, stood by the ink slab with the leather balls; Verity, who had come to see a thing done properly, sat upon the copper’s edge with her hands on her knees. The forme had been locked at half past eleven, and Winifred did not leave a locked forme overnight. She stood at the Old Lady in her apron, her sleeves above the elbow, and she did not look at him; and that, he was beginning to learn, was her way of looking.

Earlier in the evening, while Toby ran for the ink and Barnaby was admiring the lock-up, she had gone to the table at the wall, where her mother’s brass stick-case lay open, and taken out of its lid the folded foolscap that lay there, and carried it to the lantern. He had seen her at it from the corner of his eye: a short square woman looking, under a light, at the foot of the sixth paragraph, where a thumb had left a smudge of ink. She had looked at it for about the time a person takes to read a clause. Then Barnaby had cried, “Win! The quoin!” and she had laid the sheet down by the case and gone back to the stone. He did not know what it was she had looked at. He found that he could very easily guess.

“Ink,” said Winifred. Toby beat the forme, left and right, with a sound like a man patting a horse. The damp sheet went down on the tympan; the tympan folded; the bed ran in. She took the bar in both hands.

The Old Lady is not the Albion. The Albion sighs; the Old Lady groans. The screw goes down, and the great oak platen comes to rest upon the sheet, and the whole frame takes the strain with a creak like a ship at anchor; and there is a pause, such as there is at the top of a swing; and then the bar is released and the thing lets go its breath, slowly, and the bed runs out. It is a sound with a rhythm in it, but the rhythm is slow, slower than a man’s. It is the sound of a very large and very patient heart. She pulled once, and ran the bed out, and lifted the tympan, and drew the sheet off the type, and held it to the lantern; and there was a hush, such as there is in a church when the last hymn is done and the sexton has not yet begun to cough.

“Plain,” said Verity, from the copper. “And correct.”

“One comma,” said Julian.

“Where?”

He looked. He read it through twice, the loaf, the wage, the seven shillings and sevenpence, the line from the Fifth Letter. “I appear to have been mistaken,” he said.

“Then I must look again,” said Winifred, and did not look at him.

Barnaby was taken off to bed on the arm of a John, with the air of a man who has seen a launch. Verity went after them with her hands in her pockets, having said “Plain terms, good night.” Toby lay down on the settle among the sacks, and Brevier climbed upon his feet, and he was asleep before the cat had settled. And then there were two people either side of a stone, in a stone room, with a damp proof lying between them like a treaty, and about three feet of oak; and they did not touch. It was not, the narrator is bound to say, that either of them did not wish to. It was that neither of them could think how it was done.

“It makes a sound like a heart,” said Julian.

“It is the only sound in the world I would trust to count by.” She took up her lantern. “Good night, my lord.”

“Good night.”

He took his own, and went out into the rain. Winifred, with her mind on other things, left the brewhouse a little after, and pulled the door to behind her on the settle and the sleeper, and the lamp on the high desk burning low.

The door opened four inches, and a candle came in at it, in a hand wearing a mitten. Miss Agnes Fell, in her grey wrapper and her shawl, who could not sleep and had a habit of walking the house with a night-candle till two, stood on the threshold and did what she did with every room she entered, which was to count it. Toby, on the settle, did not stir. She was very good at counting, and the narrator will leave it at that. She counted the proofs upon the stone, which were nine; she counted the lines on the top one; and then, for no reason she could have given, she counted the lines on the paper that lay beside it, under the lantern, out of its case.

chapters.title: Rupert in the Hop Garden
chapters.html:
“I wished to say it in the most improbable setting I could find,” said Lord Rupert Tremayne, “so that if it is received badly I may put it down to the scenery.”

A hop garden in August ought to be a green cathedral: twelve feet of bine climbing every pole, the cones hanging like small pale lanterns, and the whole acre smelling of beer before there is any beer to smell of. The garden at Hope Farm, on the morning of Monday the fifth, was a field of poles from which a black wet rag was falling. The bine had rotted at the root and slid to the ground; the cones were brown and soft as old gloves; and down the alleys between the poles, bent double, in a line, moved a dozen Sussex women picking the mould from what survived with their fingers, for sixpence a day, and singing nothing.

Winifred had come up from the brewhouse in pattens, holding her skirt in her hand, having left her father in charge of the Old Lady, which had pulled two hundred Subscriptions since seven and was owed an hour’s rest. Rupert stood at the end of an alley with his hands in the pockets of a coat that had been made to be seen in at Newmarket, and surveyed the hop garden as one surveys an account. He took a guinea from his waistcoat, tossed it, caught it, and put it away again without looking at it; and she understood from this that he was in earnest, since it was the first time she had known him to put the guinea away.

“I owe two thousand three hundred pounds,” said Rupert. “I have it by heart; I say it in my sleep, like a collect. Eight hundred of it is to Mr Lovejoy, whom I dislike a great deal more than my tailor, and I dislike my tailor with a warmth that does me credit. My father the Earl has said he will pay no more. He said it at Christmas, and at Lady Day, and I took no notice, but this time he wrote it, which is how I know he means it. And there is Miss Quarles, whom I like a great deal too well to marry for her brewery. She would not have me for it in any case. I have no brewery.”

“Lord Rupert—”

“I come to the point, you see, by the longest road I know. Marry me.” He said it quite gently. “It is a perfectly sensible match. Lady Rupert Tremayne, with her press behind an earl’s second son: not much, but a name, and a name is a very useful thing to put across a door. Stanmere need bear no blame, because you could not jilt him if you were engaged to somebody else; you would merely have been flighty, which is thought of a Season. I should leave you to your type and you would leave me to my debts, and we should be extremely civil at breakfast. I say it with the most perfect seriousness. I have said nothing lightly since Thursday and I find it exhausting.”

Winifred looked at him. He was a long amused young man with russet-gold curls beaded with rain, and his mouth, which was made for laughing, was for once only straight. “Do you wish to marry me?”

“Not in the least,” said Rupert. “I wish to be of use to somebody once before I am thirty, and you are the only person of my acquaintance who would put me to a good one.”

“No,” said Winifred.

She said it as gently as he had asked. “I am grateful. I will tell you why, since you have told me so much. I have been a convenient thing once. I was a paragraph, and I am being a decent one until Michaelmas. I will not be one twice.”

“Because of Stanmere.”

“Because of me.” She did not look away. “You are a good sort of rascal.”

“I am told it is the best sort,” said Rupert, and he laughed outright, and she saw that he was delighted. “My dear girl, I have never been refused by anyone I liked. I find it extremely interesting. It is a great deal more interesting than being accepted by anyone else.” He pulled a hop-bine from a pole, looked at it, and let it fall. “Now I have a thing to say that is less amusing, and I should be obliged if you did not make the face you made at the Duchess.”

“Which face is that?”

“The one that says you have counted the sofa.” He turned the guinea out again, and did not toss it, and held it. “Lovejoy called on me. At my lodgings in Albany, a week ago Friday, in a snuff-coloured coat, with his hat in his hand. He was entirely civil. He said that he had held my paper for some time without once troubling me for it, and that he was sure I should wish to be of use. He then asked, in the same voice, whether I had ever happened to see a paper. I said, which? He said, a paper, signed by two parties, in a printer’s type. I said I could not think what he meant. He said he was sure I could not.”

Winifred’s skin went cold along the arms. She said, in a perfectly level voice, “And what did you tell him?”

“That I would think of it. It seemed the safest answer to a man who counts aloud.” He gave her the full benefit of his long mouth. “I have thought. The answer is no, and I am telling you instead, which I imagine is the opposite of what he hoped for. I find that I am not a man who can be bought; it is extremely inconvenient. I had always meant to be.”

“Why tell me?” It was the question a compositor puts to a proof that is too clean.

“Because he asked me to find it, and it did not appear to me that a man could find a thing in a woman’s keeping and be of use to her at the same time. One has to choose.” He shrugged, and the Newmarket coat shrugged with him. “I had meant never to choose anything. It has been the whole plan of my life, and it has worked extremely well until this week.”

She had counted the sofa. She had counted it on the twenty-second of June, in the composing room, with Toby reading aloud; Constance, Verity, Rupert; and she had put Rupert at the bottom of the list, and the bottom of the list had moved. She stood in the hop garden with the rain on her face and found that she had stopped counting.

“You should burn it,” said Rupert. “Whatever it is. I do not ask.”

“A printer does not destroy a record.” It came out sounding like an article of faith, and she heard it. “It is very nearly the only one we have.”

“Then lock it up.” He put the guinea in his pocket. “Lock it very well.”

“Rupert.”

The voice came from the far end of the alley, and was not raised, and Winifred knew whose it was before she turned. The Marquess of Stanmere had come up from the barn with a bundle of Wragg’s accounts under his arm, in boots to the knee in mud, and he had been standing at the end of the alley, it was clear, for a little longer than was strictly polite. There was no misunderstanding. A good many persons in this book will misapprehend each other before Michaelmas, but the Marquess had seen what he had seen, a man in a good coat saying something serious to a woman in the rain, and he did not pretend to have seen anything else.

“Rupert, are you asking Miss Pargeter to marry you?”

“I was.”

“Did she accept?”

“She said I was a good sort of rascal.”

“Quite,” said Julian.

They had known each other for twenty years, since the day a boy with a broken nose had given a boy with russet curls the use of a Greek lexicon for a pillow, and their quarrel took the form of two men conducting a debate of great courtesy in a hop garden, up to the ankle, while twelve Sussex women pretended to be deaf. Julian said that he might at least have been told. Rupert said that to tell him would have been to have it arranged. Julian said that he would not have arranged it. Rupert said that he would have had a dinner for sixteen and a settlement drawn by Thursday, and Julian, who could not honestly deny it, said that was not the point.

“What is the point?”

“The point,” said the Marquess, “is that I would be obliged if you would go and drown yourself in the river.”

“It is already in the river,” said Rupert, with a bow. “It is the whole county. I have no doubt that I shall find it presently.” He lifted his hat to Winifred, with the rain running off the brim, and walked away down the alley with his long loose step, and did not, she noticed, take out his guinea.

They were left standing among the poles. For a time neither of them said anything at all. He shifted the accounts from one arm to the other.

“You were not jealous,” said Winifred.

“I was extremely jealous. I find it very ordinary, like toothache.” He looked at the mud on his boots. “I should have liked to hit him, and I should have missed. He has been proposing to people since Harrow and nobody has taken him seriously, which has been his misfortune and also his protection. I think he meant it. I think it was the most honest thing I ever saw him do.”

“He said he wished to be of use.”

“He wishes to be of use to everybody. It is the only occupation he has ever followed.” He did not look up. “Did you want to say yes?”

“No.”

“Good,” said Julian. And then, in the tone in which he would have read out a column of figures: “Fifty-five days.”

“Fifty-five?”

“To Michaelmas. I counted.”

She had counted it herself that morning, between the Old Lady’s first pull and her second, and she did not say so. She did not answer at all. She did not need to.

She might have told him then what Rupert had said about the paper. She had the sentence ready, in order, like a line set and justified; and she saw quite clearly what would follow, which was that he would have it arranged by dinner. He stood in the rain with Wragg’s accounts under his arm so plainly arranging nothing that she let the sentence go back into the case, to be thought of afterwards at some length. He nodded, as Pankhurst had nodded in the barn, twice, as at a price that was fair if disagreeable, and went away up the alley with the accounts, and she found that she was holding a hop-bine she did not remember picking up. It was the black rotten kind. She put it down.

Far across the garden, past the last of the poles, two figures could be seen at the top of the slope: one in a brown dress, with a ledger under her arm and her spectacles flashing on their chain, and one in a coat made for Newmarket. The brown dress was telling the coat something, with her free hand, in a series of short flat movements like a person laying out a hand of cards. It appeared to be the price of something. The coat was bending to listen with its head on one side, and the distance did not conceal that it was delighted. Whatever they said, they were quarrelling, and happily; and Winifred, who had been refused no one and asked a good deal, stood among the dead hops and watched them with a feeling for which she had no name in any type.

That night, when the house was asleep, she sat on the edge of the bed in the room they had given her, with the green baize lid of her mother’s stick-case open on her knee and a candle on the washstand.

Her mother’s brass composing stick lay in its slot, worn bright at the thumb-rest. The lid had a lining of green baize, and the baize had a flap, and under the flap, flat against the wood, lay the second counterpart of the Articles of Agreement: foolscap, one fold, seven paragraphs in Pica, an imprint at the foot, and beside the sixth a smudge in the shape of a man’s left thumb. She had taken it out, on Saturday, to look at that smudge. She had put it back on Sunday morning, from the table where she had found it, a little to one side of where she had left it, and had thought nothing about the side.

A printer does not destroy a record. She had said it to Rupert as a principle, and it had been one; but by bedtime it had turned into something else, which she would not have cared to look at in a good light. It was that she could not have burned this sheet if the house were afire. She was in the habit of the dele. She had cut her way out of every difficulty of her life with a stroke of the pen, and put the mark in the margin, and gone on, and been called quick. It had not before occurred to her that there might be a piece of paper she did not wish to be quick about.

She smoothed the foolscap flat. She laid the baize flap down over it, and pressed it, and turned the little brass key in the lock that her mother had had put on the case for the Psalms; and she hung the key on its ribbon about her neck, under her night-gown, where it lay cold for a moment against her breastbone, and then warm.

It was, as the narrator is bound to admit, two nights too late.

chapters.title: A Wet Day for Forfeits
chapters.html:
On the morning of Wednesday the fourteenth of August, Dr Orlando Pym stood at the library chimney-piece at Stanmere Court, where a fire burned, in August, and added with a pencil one stroke to a column of strokes that he had been keeping on the oak since the fourteenth of July, to the quiet horror of Mrs Pickett. There were thirty-one. He regarded them with the sorrow of an honest man who has been proved right and would have preferred not to be. Behind him the library windows ran like the sides of a fish-tank; and beyond them, where in a decent year there would have been a lawn and a ha-ha and the Ham meadows going down to the Medway, lay a grey and enormous wetness in which a few trees stood about like people who had come to the wrong party.

In the breakfast-room, at the end of the table nearest the urn, Miss Agnes Fell opened her letters. There was one. It was directed to Miss Fell, Stanmere Court, Yalding, Kent, in a small upright extremely clean hand, each letter standing like a recruit; and she knew the hand, though she had never had a letter in it, for she had seen it in a margin, when a boy from a hole in a wall in Cursitor Street brought her column back with a single word written beside the last line. The word was More.

She read it under cover of the toast-rack.

Madam,—I have lately had the honour to acquire from Mr Pountney, hosier, of the Borough, an obligation of Lieutenant Matthias Fell, half-pay, for three hundred and twelve pounds with interest. I mention it only that you may know in whose hands it lies. I should be sorry to see it called in before Michaelmas, and I do not think I shall have to. The fee of the Marshal of the King’s Bench on a commitment is eleven pounds; it falls due when the writ issues; and the writ need not issue before Monday the nineteenth. I am, madam, your obedient servant, H. Lovejoy. P.S. The last Quizzing-Glass was thin in the second paragraph. I do not think it was the fault of the prose.

She folded it in four and put it into the pocket of her gown, with the care of a woman putting away a snake in a handkerchief. For two years she had supposed herself a name in a column. It had not occurred to her that a man who could tell a letter by its foot could tell a writer by her commas; and she sat for a minute with her hands in her lap and her mittens on, at a table where nobody was looking, and the thing she had supposed for two years was taken out of her, quietly, like a tooth.

She did not decide anything. She buttered a piece of toast and ate it, and poured Lady Constance’s chocolate, and said “I beg your pardon” to the milk-jug. The narrator, who would like to be fair to Miss Fell, and has been offered the choice of being merciful or accurate, has chosen to be both by declining to say what went on in her head that morning, except that it went through the house from attic to cellar, touching things. There was a sum in it, which was three hundred and twelve and eleven. There was a cough, in a room in the Rules. There was Lady Constance’s shawl, which she had held for twelve years, and a pair of mittens, and a candle that burned till two; and there was a thing in the bottom of her trunk upstairs, under three flannel petticoats, folded in four, which she did not call by any name at all. It had not been sent. That was the whole of the case in her favour, and she knew exactly how much it weighed.

Lady Constance, to whom boredom was a personal insult, struck the drawing-room table with her trumpet at half past two and called for Forfeits.

“The house has been indoors since the thirtieth of July,” she said. “This is the thirty-first day of the rain; Dr Pym has it on the chimney. I will not play at Consequences, I am too old to be rude on paper, and I will not play at Charades, I have seen General Dyer attempt a camel. Forfeits. Everyone will give up a trifle.”

They gave them up. Verity Quarles, who was the one person in the room who could be trusted to keep an account, took them into Sir Ephraim’s hat: a lorgnette, a snuff-box, a watch-seal, a glove, a pencil, a spectacle-case, Lord Rupert’s signet, and from Toby Mudge, who had been summoned as an extra and sat on a hassock chewing, a button. Mr Minton, applied to for a trifle, was found to have nothing in his pockets but a stopped watch full of the ditch at Wrotham, which Verity accepted on the ground that it was the one thing in the room that had stopped on principle. It was a long room, with a fire at each end, and the faces of six Marquesses looking down from the panels on a company of persons in various stages of boredom; and the windows streamed. Winifred, appealed to for something to do with her hands, produced from her mother’s case two sticks and a handful of Pica, and taught the company in four minutes the first and greatest difficulty of her trade, which is that type is set upside down and backwards and read, as it were, in a looking-glass. The line was to be The quick brown fox.

“Quick, madam?” said Dr Pym. “This year no fox in Kent has been quick. They are up to their hocks in the Beult.”

“Then set it slowly, Doctor,” said Barnaby, with his foot on the stool and a stick in his fist, “but set it.”

He did it in forty seconds, talking all the while, of a Psalter he had known in ‘seventy-nine, and laid the stick upon the card-table with the air of a man laying a wreath. Dr Pym took two minutes and a quarter, and then, in carrying the line to the table, tipped the stick, so that it went on the Turkey carpet in a fall, which Winifred noted was the first time that summer a page had gone into pie in the presence of a clergyman and nobody had been to blame. Lady Constance, who had backed the Doctor on the ground that a clergyman ought to be able to do something with his hands, forfeited her lorgnette.

Verity set it in fifty-one seconds, counting under her breath, with her large capable hands moving among the case like a person sorting coin. Her mother, who had been sitting very upright in a raspberry shawl, swooned lightly at the sight of those hands among the type, and was brought round by Sir Ephraim with a glass of the product. Rupert took three minutes and ten, set the x upside down, and said that it was an improvement; and he staked his signet against her to make the thing interesting, and lost it. She weighed it in her palm. She said it was about four guineas of gold. And she put it upon her thumb, where it rode like a curtain-ring, and he looked at it with an expression that his friends would not have known.

The last pair was Julian and Toby. Toby set the line in thirty-eight seconds, with a pie in his other hand that he had somehow acquired in the interval, and the sorts went into the stick as if called. Julian took two minutes and ten, devoting most of them to the spacing; and he laid down his stick beside the boy’s, looked at the two lines side by side, and said, in tones of the deepest satisfaction, “He has beaten me.” It was a thing no one in that room had seen the Marquess say before, and several would not have thought possible. “Your Marquessship,” said Toby, “the space after quick is wide.” “I know,” said Julian. “I was trying to make it fit.”

“What will you have for the prize, Toby?” said Constance, through the trumpet, as one asks a bishop.

“A pie, my lady.”

“I have not one about me,” said Julian.

“I’ll wait,” said Toby, and went on chewing the one he had.

“Heavy, heavy hangs over thy head,” said Verity, drawing from the hat the lorgnette, and holding it up. “Fine or superfine?”

“What is the penalty?” said Lady Constance, who was a woman of her word.

“Let her say aloud a thing she regrets,” said Rupert from the hearth-rug, with the cheerfulness of a man who has lost a signet and cannot bear that anyone else should be exempt. The room laughed. Lady Constance sat up. She lowered the trumpet to her lap, which in itself was an event. Behind her chair, a pace back, with the shawl over her arm, Agnes saw that the hand that held the mouthpiece was shaking, very slightly, like a leaf in a house where a door has been shut.

“My hat,” said Lady Constance.

The room laughed. There was a moment in which she seemed about to say more. Her mouth opened on “And—“; and then she said, “The one with the cherries,” and they laughed again, harder, and she took back her lorgnette and sat as straight as a poker and put the trumpet to her ear; and the moment went by on the other side of a hedge, like a coach with its lamps lit.

Verity went in again. “A seal and a glove.”

They were Julian’s watch-seal and Winifred’s left glove. She had taken it off for the type, and her thumb lay in her lap in full view of the room, a little blue. “Heavy, heavy,” said Verity, rather quickly. “They are to tell the company how they met,” said Rupert, who had no mercy, and she did not look at him.

“It was in the Gazette,” said Winifred.

The company laughed. It had come to be a joke, and a good one; it was the thing she said, and had been said so often at so many tables that it was thought the cleverest in London. And under cover of the laughter, with her face turned a quarter toward him, she said in a voice not meant for the room: “He came to the shop to find out who had been correcting his commas.”

The room laughed. Julian did not. He sat with his long hand on his knee, and the laughter went round him like water round a post; and Rupert, who missed nothing, looked at the ceiling.

At five they broke up to dress, and Agnes went up the stair a pace behind Lady Constance with the shawl. The long gallery at Stanmere Court is lined with the portraits of Marquesses who were each, in his day, certain of having got matters right. At the end of it she said, “Lady Constance.”

The trumpet did not come up. Lady Constance stopped, with her back to her, and stood.

“I beg your pardon,” said Agnes. “It is only that there is something I ought to say. I have been meaning to. I have been—” Her hands, in their mittens, had found one another. “I think you ought to know that I—”

She was never to know afterward what her face did. Lady Constance turned and looked at her: a tall rigid woman in black bombazine, with a purple ribbon, and under it a face that had held a house together for forty years by declining to be moved. She looked at a thin woman of forty-one with a streak of white at her temple. What she saw is not recorded.

“You are the only person in this house,” said Lady Constance, “who never asks me for anything.”

It was said as one states a fact in arithmetic. She went on down the gallery, and her door shut. Agnes stood with the shawl over her arm, in the cold, understanding that she had been handed something, and that she had not the least idea where to put it.

She went up to the attic, which was at the top of the last flight, and took the packet out of the trunk from under three flannel petticoats, and unfolded it on her knee. It was a single sheet of foolscap, in a round law-stationer’s hand that was not her own, which she had learned in a year of copying; it had taken her four hours on the night of the third, by a night-candle, in the brewhouse, to get it down to the smudge at the foot of the sixth paragraph, and she had made the smudge too. She sat with it on her knee until the dressing-bell, and then until the dinner-bell; and then, for she was a punctual woman, she put it back in the trunk, and went down.

They dined at eight. There was a leg of mutton, and the Doctor upon the dome; and afterwards in the drawing-room they played Blind Man’s Buff, as a game suited to the rain, and the Marquess had been blinded with Verity’s handkerchief and was groping toward the sound of Toby’s cough when the door opened and Mr Wragg came in, hatless, with the water running off him, and stood on the Turkey carpet.

“My lord. The river’s up. Two foot since dinner. It’s over the Ham, and it’s coming up the Beult at the back.”

The game fell over. Julian took off the handkerchief. Nobody spoke, and in the silence the fire spat, and on all the windows the rain went on, which no one had listened to since the thirtieth of July. Dr Pym, who had come in from the library with the pencil still in his hand, said:

“That will be the rods.”

And nobody laughed.

chapters.title: High Water
chapters.html:
At a quarter past ten that night the Medway came up the lawn at Stanmere Court in the light of forty lanterns, black and wide and in no hurry at all. It had taken the Ham meadows at dusk, and the lower orchard and the ha-ha before nine; and it advanced now across the grass toward the terrace with the leisurely thoroughness of a bailiff taking an inventory, noting the garden seat, the sundial, the gardener’s barrow, and the first of the stone steps.

The Marquess of Stanmere had asked, as his first act, how many head of cattle were on the Ham; and as his second, how many persons lived below the hundred-foot line; and Mr Wragg, who knew everything about the estate except until lately the spelling of his own name, had answered both to within a dozen. From these two numbers everything followed. Grooms went down to the Ham with lanterns and halters and brought the cattle off in the dark, lowing and unwilling, up the cart-track to the home paddock. A rider went to Yalding to have the church bell rung. The tithe barn was thrown open, and Mrs Pickett’s girls set to baking.

Lady Constance commanded the kitchen like an admiral from the head of the scullery stairs, with the pug under one arm and the trumpet under the other, issuing orders in a voice that carried to the bakehouse without the assistance of the trumpet; and Verity Quarles took her station at the barn door with her ledger and her spectacles on their chain, and counted heads as they came in, and by midnight had forty-three and a dog.

Dr Pym, to his own surprise, was useful. There was a tide-gauge in the portmanteau, which was what had clanked from Wrotham to Yalding: a brass staff, graduated in inches, with a float and a bell. He planted it at the foot of the terrace steps and read it aloud every ten minutes in a voice of mounting joy, which was a mistake in a man whom the weather was vindicating, but a comfort to everyone else; a river that is being measured seems less likely to do something unprecedented.

Winifred had watched the water from the brewhouse window for as long as it took to understand it, and then had done what she did with every emergency, which was to ask what wanted setting. She found Julian on the terrace in his shirtsleeves with a lantern.

“Which of the cottages have a clock?”

“None.”

“Can they read?”

“A third.”

“And can they hear the bell?”

“Not through this.”

“A bell says come,” said Winifred. “It does not say why. Give me a quarter of an hour.”

It took her six minutes to set, in Great Primer, three lines of four words, a thing she had been practising for thirteen years without knowing it. She set it twice on the stone, two-up, so that every pull gave two bills, and a hundred pulls would give two hundred; and Barnaby was carried in, chair and all, by two Johns, and put at the ink with his foot on the bucket, and Toby beat the balls, and Winifred took the bar. Miss Fell sat at the table by the lantern with a pair of scissors and cut the sheets across, one after another, without being asked, and without looking up.

THE WATER IS UP. ALL TO HIGHER GROUND. THE CHURCH BELL WILL RING.

She pulled two hundred in forty minutes. Print was not a thing that did anything quickly at Yalding. It came on Thursdays in somebody’s cousin’s pocket and was eleven weeks old. Now a page of it reached a cottage while the water was still on the lane. Toby took the bills to every door on the low ground, in a washtub found in the scullery, paddling with a coal shovel, since the lane had already ceased to be a lane; and Brevier sat in the bow with an expression of complete resignation. And at the last cottage but one, a boy of ten named Jem Fryer, who had been taught his letters by the curate on Sundays, read the bill aloud to his grandmother in the kitchen with his finger under the words; and Mrs Fryer, who was eighty and could not read, put down her knitting and said, “Well, if it says so,” and put on her coat.

They went out into the dark. The lane was already a stream to the knee, and the only thing left to do was to climb the highest thing within a quarter of a mile, which was Fryer’s kiln.

It stood a hundred yards from the terrace, across what had been the ford of the Beult: a round brick oast with a conical roof and a white cowl, and on the roof, in the light of forty lanterns, an old woman and two children. Rupert and Wragg launched the hay-boat to reach them. The current took it at the hedge, turned it twice like a leaf, and drove it down the lane; and it fetched up against a pollard willow, with Rupert in the water to his chest and his coat gone, and Wragg, grey and silent, hauling him out by the belt. They had got a line to the kiln, but it was the one thing they had accomplished, and Wragg had left a boot.

Barnaby had it drawn on his knee with a wet finger. He sat in his chair on the terrace with his foot up and an oilskin over his head, designing, in the light of a lantern held by a groom; and his daughter, coming from the press with ink to her elbows, found him in a state she had seen only at the birth of the Albion.

“My dear girl, it is the simplest thing in the world. A line from the oak at the end of the ha-ha to the kiln, which they have, and hauled taut with the Old Lady’s block and fall. A traveller on the line. A sling made of her own girth-strap. The people come across above the water like Sunday linen on a line.” He looked up. “The only difficulty is that somebody must go out.”

“I’ll go,” said Julian.

He had come up behind them. He was bareheaded and wet to the skin, in his shirt and breeches, with his boots off, and a bowline had already been put about his chest by a groom who knew the knot. There was a short silence on the terrace, in which the river said what it had to say, and Winifred opened her mouth, and found that she had nothing to put in it. She had given him no leave, and he had not asked it; it was the first thing he had ever done in her presence that he had not arranged. “Mind the traveller,” she said, which was not what she meant.

“Quite,” said Julian.

He went out along the line, hand over hand, with the traveller hauled after him; and for twenty yards he was a tall man crossing a river in lantern-light, and for the rest of it, where the current had the line, he was a pale shape, going down by inches and coming up. The men on the fall paid out the rope. At the kiln he got the children into the sling, one after the other, the girl Patience first, and the fall brought them in, and Wragg handed them out on the bank to a dozen hands. He came back for Mrs Fryer.

“I’ll not be put in a basket like a cheese,” said Mrs Fryer, from the roof, at the top of her voice.

“Then you shall be put in my arms,” said the Marquess.

He took her down in the sling with himself. Barnaby’s rig was beautiful, and had one fault, which is the fault of all beautiful things: it assumed that the rope would not stretch. A wet rope stretches. With two persons on the traveller the line sagged in the middle until the sling trailed in the current; and the current, which had been waiting for something to do, took the Marquess of Stanmere by the legs.

They saw the sling come in. It came up the line, jerking, with the men hauling on the fall like a team at a tug-of-war, and in it, held by the shoulders in a thing like a bag, was an old woman in a man’s coat with her mouth shut tight. There was nobody else in it.

“Julian!” cried Winifred.

She had not said it before. It is a short name, and it carried a great way. She was in the water before the sentence was done, up to the waist and then past it, with the line in both hands, which she had taken for the traveller’s rope, and she was aware of Wragg beside her, who had called her the printer woman for a week and now took hold of the rope behind her without being asked. The slack was coming in, wet and heavy. It had a weight at the end of it. She hauled, hand over hand, with the cold going up her like a ruler, and something came up out of the water on the end of the rope that was a man’s shoulders and the collar of a shirt; and she took him by the collar in both fists and Wragg took him by the belt, and between them, with the river pulling, they dragged him in on the stones.

He was on his hands and knees. He coughed up, so far as an observer could judge, the greater part of the Weald. When he could speak he looked up at her, with the water running out of his sandy hair and the white notch in his eyebrow filled with river, and said:

“Quite.”

At three in the morning, in the tithe barn, the Fryers slept on straw under horse-blankets: Jem and Patience, and Mrs Fryer in the midst with her stick across her knees and a limp wet handbill clenched in her fist, which she would not give up. “I can’t read it,” she had told Winifred, who had sat by her with tea, “but Jem read it me. It said the water was up. It was.” It is a notice that a printer might have framed.

In the far corner, by a bale, under a blanket that smelled of horse, the Marquess sat with his back to the wall and his hair drying in spikes, and Winifred sat beside him with her hands in her lap. They did not talk. After a time one of her hands was in his, under the blanket, in the dark, as if it had been left there, and he held it as one holds a thing one has been told not to drop. Nothing was said about Michaelmas. Forty-five days, she thought, with her head against a bale; and then she was asleep.

Barnaby came across the barn at half past three with two bowls of Mrs Pickett’s broth, limping, with the gouty foot in a flannel boot and a lantern in his teeth. He put one bowl in the Marquess’s hands and sat down upon the next bale with a grunt, and looked at his daughter, asleep, with her mouth a little open and her mother’s brass rule coming out of her hair.

“My dear fellow,” said Barnaby, low. “You will have observed that I have a daughter.”

“I have observed.”

“She carries things. She has carried me eleven years, and the house, and a quantity of Psalms. I have sat in a chair with my foot up and let her, and called it the gout.” He stirred his broth. “I have been thinking it over this evening with my leg in the air, and I find that I would very much sooner ask the Marquess than let my girl carry it alone. The notes, I mean. It is a matter of some eleven hundred pounds. I do not say it is a fine thing to ask. I say that I would rather.”

Julian did not move. The signet turned once on his finger, in the dark, and stopped.

“I am bound, sir,” he said, “by Article the Third.”

“Quite right.” Barnaby nodded slowly. “Quite right. I printed them, I recall. No, she printed them; I merely wept.” He drank his broth. “They are wiser than they look, my dear fellow, those Articles. They will keep a proud girl from being obliged to you until she can afford the obligation. It is the only way, I find, to give her anything. I should know. I gave her a printing house.”

Toward dawn, Julian went out to the barn door with the blanket about his shoulders to see what the water had done. It had stopped. It had drawn back in the night as far as the ha-ha, and stood there brown and shining, with Fryer’s kiln in the middle of it like a rook on a ploughed field; and above the oasts in the east the sky had turned the colour of an old penny. It was the first hour of that sort of light in a month. It lay in a thin copper line between the cloud and the drowned meadows, no more than a pencil-stroke, and every pool on the lawn took it up and held it.

Behind him, at the other door, Miss Agnes Fell stood in her shawl. She had not slept. At the gate to the avenue, on a pony the colour of wet bread, in a sack for a coat, sat the Yalding post-boy, fourteen years old and blue with cold, who had come up by the high road to say that the post-office was under three feet of the Medway and that the mail would go from Wateringbury at seven if anybody had anything for it.

Miss Fell had something. She had it in the pocket of her wrapper: a single sheet of foolscap, folded into a cover and sealed with a wafer, and directed in a round law-stationer’s hand to H. Lovejoy, Esq., Ave Maria Lane, London. She had written the direction in the night, between the second hour and the third, at the kitchen table, while the household baled the scullery about her. Nobody had looked at her. Nobody ever did. In the course of that night she had boiled the kettle eleven times, and cut four hundred slices of bread and butter, and held a child with a cut hand while Mrs Pickett sewed it, and by her own computation she had done more good between ten o’clock and six than in the whole of the previous twelve years put together. She crossed the wet gravel and put the packet into the cold hand of the post-boy, and a shilling after it; and it seemed to her that a little more sin would hardly show.

chapters.title: The Town Crier Cries
chapters.html:
“Marquess’s Misprint!” cried the hawkers in St Paul’s Churchyard at seven o’clock on the morning of Saturday the thirty-first of August, in the rain, with armfuls of a damp sheet held against their chests like firewood. “The Articles of Agreement in full! Twopence! Read the Marquess’s Misprint, sir, the Articles in full and the carter’s tale!”

It had been, until that hour, a remarkably sweet time, or as near as made no difference. The last week in Kent had gone to the Subscription, which by the twenty-second had raised six hundred and eleven pounds from landlords who had read it over their breakfasts and, to their own astonishment, paid; the water had gone down in five days, leaving a mark on the tithe barn at the height of Dr Pym’s chin; and on the Thursday the Pargeters had come home to London by the Maidstone road without once going into a ditch. Since then Julian had called at Hand and Pen Court on the two days Article 2 required, and not a minute over. He stood at the far end of the composing room and handed her proofs by the corner. Mr Orme had remarked that it was the most correct courtship he had seen in fifty-two years. Winifred had counted the days to Michaelmas aloud, to the Drip, and found that the figure had begun to frighten her for a new reason, which was that it was getting small.

On the Saturday morning at half past one, Dick Sparrow did not come in.

The Gazette’s forme was locked up, the Albion was inked, and the second pressman’s place at the bar stood empty. Fairweather, asked where he was, said “Aye,” with unusual weight, and went on inking. So Winifred and Fairweather pulled the inner forme between them, two hands short, with Toby on the balls, and the sheets went to the cart at a quarter past five with eleven minutes to spare; and it was twenty past six, and she was sitting down for the first time with a heel of bread, when she heard the cry in the Row.

Toby came in at a quarter past seven with his paper hat over one eye and a sheet inside his jacket, which is where a boy keeps what he has been told not to read.

“Don’t,” said Winifred.

He read it aloud. It was a long column, and he began in a loud voice, and grew smaller as he went. It was headed The Quizzing-Glass, and was by Peregrine Pry, and it began:

I may be quite wrong, but I have long thought that the most dangerous thing a printer can set is her own name. Readers of this paper will recall that on the sixth of June the Gazette, which had never been known to be mistaken, informed a delighted town that the Marquess of Stanmere was engaged to Miss W. Pargeter, of Paternoster Row. We are enabled this morning to lay before them the Articles by which that engagement was made, and kept, and, as it is hoped, ended: a document which for neatness of drafting has not been equalled since the Fall.

Then came the Articles, all seven, from the heading to the imprint, in a clear Long Primer; and the imprint at the foot, which Winifred read three times, had been altered. Printed by H. Lovejoy, Phoenix Press, Ave Maria Lane. They were word for word as she had set them. They were the same to the comma. Whoever had set the thing had had it before him, flat, in a good light, and had kept even the space before the sixth.

“Toby.”

“There’s a bit more, miss.” He swallowed. “There’s a carter.”

We have this further from the carter who for nineteen years has taken the inner forme from Hand and Pen Court to Pomfret Yard, and who has the plain honesty of his trade. He states that on the morning of the sixth of June, at a quarter past five, the young lady stood in the arch of the Court with a wet sheet in her hand and said nothing, and let the cart go. We make no remark. A compositor, it is said, does not read; she sees letters. The reader will decide for himself how many it takes to make a Marquess.

Toby stopped there. Winifred put out her hand and he gave her the sheet, and she folded it very small, and went to the table, where her mother’s stick-case lay, and turned the key at her throat, and lifted the baize. The foolscap was where she had left it, flat, with the smudge at the foot of the sixth paragraph. She laid it open beside the Crier. They were alike in every line, and it was this, rather than anything the column said, that she looked at for some time. Her paper had not been taken. It had been looked at.

Mr Underhill came at nine, in a hackney, which he never did, pink and trembling, in a coat buttoned wrong, with the Crier crushed in his fist like something he had caught.

He stood in the door of the composing room with the water running off his hat. He had a beautiful voice, the best in Fleet Street, and it shook. “Mr Pargeter. Miss Pargeter. I have come to say what a gentleman must say in person. The Gazette has been made a laughing-stock. In the Strand this morning, madam, a boy sold me my own paper with the Crier folded round it. In nineteen years the Gazette has not once been shown to have printed what was not so.”

“The paragraph was a misprint, Mr Underhill,” said Winifred. “It is a thing that happens.”

“It is a thing that has never happened to the Gazette.”

“It happened to the Gazette on the sixth of June.”

“Clause Nine.” He drew himself up. “An error of the press requiring a correction. The Crier has shown that the paragraph of the sixth of June was an error of the press. It requires a correction.”

“Then print it. It is a single paragraph. I will set it myself.”

“The Gazette does not retract, madam.”

“You might clarify.”

“At this length,” said Mr Underhill, “it is not clarity. It is confession.” He swallowed. “The clause, madam, says requiring. It does not say printing. Mr Ingram, who read the contract at my request, is of the opinion that it is satisfied by the requirement. The contract is void. The bond is forfeit. Five hundred pounds, secured, I believe, upon this house.”

“Secured upon—” said Winifred, and turned.

Her father had come down on his gouty foot, with his spectacles on his forehead, and was standing at the foot of the stair with a hand on the newel. He looked at his daughter with the face of a man who has been caught in a moment of his own.

“Win,” said Barnaby. “I meant to tell you on the fourteenth of June. Mrs Hobday came in with the soup.”

“Mr Underhill,” said Winifred, after a time, in a voice that had gone extremely polite, “Mrs Rudge would wish to be told.”

“Mrs Rudge is at Bath for her chest, madam, and I will not distress her. I take no pleasure in this. Nineteen years.” He turned his ruined hat in his fingers and looked at no one. “I wish you good morning.”

He went out. In the corner, at the case by the window, Mr Orme, who had set type every working day since the year ‘sixty-four, put his stick down upon the ledge of the frame, and laid his hand flat on top of it, and did not pick it up again. It made no sound. It was the loudest thing in the room.

Mr Lovejoy came at ten. He was in his snuff-coloured coat, with his hands scrubbed pink and his hat in front of him, and the two pairs of spectacles pushed up on his forehead; and he bowed to her as a gentleman does who has come to a house in which there has been a death.

“Madam. I shall not detain you. I do not come to gloat; it is a vice of the untidy.” He glanced at the Crier in her hand. “The press of this morning is mine, madam. The prose is another person’s. I never print a lie. I print a true thing in a place where it will do the most harm, and I do not think that anything in it is untrue.”

“No,” said Winifred.

“That is what I thought.” He turned his hat once. “I am obliged, in the circumstances, to mention the notes. Under the third clause the whole is payable on demand upon the loss of the Gazette. The sum, with Mr Trigg’s account, is one thousand one hundred and forty pounds. I do not make the demand. I mention it, as one mentions a window that has been left open. In consideration of the long acquaintance between our houses I shall wait until Michaelmas.”

“Hector,” said Barnaby from the stair, in the voice of a man speaking across a long time.

“Mr Pargeter.” Lovejoy inclined his head. He went, with great tact, to the far end of the room, to the stone, where the forme of Tuesday’s Gazette was standing, and bent over it with his glass, as a man looks at a house he used to live in.

Julian came into the Court at a quarter past ten. He had walked from Curzon Street, two and a half miles in fifty minutes, without a hat. Gantry had brought him the Crier on the salver where in June there had been cards; he had read it standing; and he came into the composing room with the water running out of his hair, white, a tall man a little stooped, and saw Lovejoy at the far end of the room with his glass, and bowed to him, and turned to her.

“Miss Pargeter.”

“My lord.”

“I have read it.” He was turning the signet. “I have come to say this. I can have a special licence from Doctors’ Commons by noon on Monday. St George’s, or St Vedast, or your own parlour if you prefer it. The Crier cannot touch a Marchioness. It will not dare. A wife is not a party to any Articles; she is a wife.”

“A special licence.”

“Yes.”

“It is what a lord uses to make a mess disappear.” She had not raised her voice; she had gone, as she did when angry, extremely polite. “I will not be disappeared, my lord.”

“I did not—”

“You would correct the Misprint by making it true. It is a very handsome erratum. I am not an erratum to be corrected by matrimony.”

He took it as one takes a blow in the dark: without a sound, and with the whole of the frame. At the end of the room the glass was lowered. Mr Lovejoy straightened, and put the glass away on its ribbon, and came forward with his hat in both hands, and bowed.

“I beg your pardon, madam. In so small a room I could not help hearing the end. I came only to thank his lordship for his call on Tuesday. It was handsomely meant.”

Winifred did not move. “His call.”

“At Ave Maria Lane, at eleven, in person. His lordship offered me twice the sum for Mr Pargeter’s paper: two thousand two hundred and eighty pounds. I confess I admired the arithmetic. I declined.” He bowed again. “I mention it, madam, since it is true, and since it may be useful. It is why the Crier appears today, and not at Michaelmas. A man who sees a marquess coming up the Lane with a cheque-book prints early. Good morning.”

He went out through the arch. The rain shut behind him.

“Is it true?” said Winifred.

“Yes.”

“You signed Article the Third.”

“I signed it before I—”

“Before you what?”

He stood in the composing room of Pargeter’s with the water running down his neck and his mouth open upon the word. It was a short one. He had never in his life said it aloud in front of a witness. It would not come. He had signed it, he might have said, before a barn, and a rope, and a sleeping girl’s hand in the dark; before a great many things, none of which was in the Articles; and he stood there with it in his throat, like a sort in the wrong box, and she, who could not abide a gap in a line, looked at him, and let it stand.

“Of seven Articles I asked for one,” said Winifred, “that was not for the Gazette’s sake. It was the third.”

“I know.”

“Then you will understand that I shall keep them all, to Michaelmas, because I keep my word. And that I do not wish to see you before. You are released from the second.” She picked up the stick from the ledge, and found that it was Orme’s, and put it down. “Good morning, my lord.”

He bowed. He turned his ring once on his finger and went out into the rain.

He walked the whole length of Cheapside. He did not choose it. He turned east out of the Churchyard because it was the way his feet were pointed, and he walked past the Poultry and the Mansion House and the shop windows, with the water running down his collar, among hawkers who cried the Marquess’s Misprint in his face, and a man in a doorway who looked up, and recognised him, and looked down again with the tact of the English poor. He did not hear them. In his head a single sentence was going round, in the voice of a boy of nine: I decided that I would not marry unless it were impossible not to. He had said it to her on the thirtieth of June, in the library, with the sunset in the window. He had not said, because he had not known it, that the same boy would grow up to be a man who could not ask a question without first having arranged the answer.

At the end of Cheapside he found that he was not in Curzon Street, and had not been, for some time.

By four in the afternoon the composing room was empty but for the cat, the Drip, and Barnaby, who had been put to sleep in his chair by the fire with the Crier over his face, like a handkerchief, and his spectacles pushed up over it. Orme had gone home to his lodging in Warwick Lane. Fairweather had gone to the pump and stood there. The rain fell steadily on the skylight, and the Drip fell on the stone, every four seconds, into the copper pan, which nobody had emptied since the morning.

Winifred stood at her frame with her mother’s brass stick in her hand. She had not set a line. She was holding it as she had held it at seventeen, the week after the funeral, when she had not known what it was for; and the thumb-rest, worn bright by a woman who set the Psalms, was cool against her thumb. She was conscious of the pan. She ought to empty it. She did not move.

A shuffle behind her. It was Toby, who had been sent to bed three times and had come back, and who now stood at her elbow in his paper hat, with his ears sticking out and his freckles very bright, chewing; and in his hand, held out with the care of a man handing a document across a table, was a pie. It was Mutlow’s. It had been, a few hours ago, a whole one. There was a bite out of it, and a neat clean edge where he had broken it in two. He had never in his life been known to offer anyone food.

Toby held it out. It was, she saw, the larger half.

chapters.title: What Lady Constance Burned
chapters.html:
At seven o’clock on the first of September the Marquess of Stanmere sat in a closed carriage in Hertford Street, with the blinds down, and did not get out of it.

The bells had begun. They begin early in Mayfair on a Sunday, for the convenience of persons who like to be reproached in good time: St George’s had led off, and St James’s, which would not be outdone, had come in a little flat. On the box Pegg turned up his collar and fixed his walnut face upon the horses’ ears, as a man does who has driven his master to a number of doors at a number of hours and has formed no opinion of any of them. The rain was the fine, tired rain of the fifth month of a summer that had never begun.

Julian had not been to bed. He had come in from Cheapside at ten the night before, wet to the thighs, and Gantry had taken his coat without remark, which was Gantry’s way of weeping; and he had sat in the library until the windows went grey, in the chair that faced the wall between them, where a pale oblong showed the shape of something that had hung there until he was nine. Somewhere about four he had understood that he was going to Hertford Street. He told himself it was to confess Tuesday to his aunt before the town did. This was half a lie. He was going to be told what to do. It was what Hertford Street was for. He was thirty-one, the master of eleven farms and the author of nine letters on the Corn Laws, and he sat with his hand on the carriage door like a boy who has been sent for, and was ashamed to find that it was a comfort.

At a quarter to eight he got out.

The butler, who had opened that door to him since he wore frocks, said that her ladyship was in the morning-room and that Miss Fell had gone to the early service, as she did every Sunday; and he said it to the middle distance, in the manner of a man letting a gentleman know that the house is empty of everyone but the person he has come to see.

The morning-room was as cold as it had been in June. The hundred and forty birds of the late General Sir Hugh Dyer looked down from their shelves with the glassy surprise of creatures that had been shot and not told why. Lady Constance sat by a fire the size of a hat, in a grey wrapper with the purple ribbon at the throat, which she wore with everything. On her knee lay the Town Crier. At her feet Blücher opened his one eye, found that it was only the Marquess, and shut it again.

“Sit down,” said Lady Constance. “Not that chair. There is a nuthatch in it.”

He sat in the other, under the heron.

“I have read it,” she said. “Five times with the trumpet and a sixth without. You will not be able to tell me anything in it that is not so.”

“There is one thing it does not say.” He turned the signet on his finger. “On Tuesday I went to Ave Maria Lane.”

He told her the whole of it, in figures, because figures were what he had. The hour: eleven. The sum: two thousand two hundred and eighty pounds, being twice the paper. The reasoning: that Article the Third forbade him to lend, give, advance or promise, and said not one word about buying, which he had found out at three in the morning and hated by four. The refusal. The Saturday, and Mr Lovejoy bowing to him in a composing room with a glass in his hand and the whole affair in his mouth like a sweet.

“Perfectly sound,” said Lady Constance.

“It was not sound.”

“It was exactly what I should have done.” She took up the ear-trumpet, looked down the wrong end of it, and laid it in her lap. “I should have sent Gantry with the money in a purse and a story about a cousin’s mortgage. You went yourself, which is more honest and a great deal more stupid. What did she say?”

“That a special licence is what a lord uses to make a mess disappear. That she would not be disappeared.”

“Did you ask her?”

“I told her what I could arrange.”

“Ah.”

It was the smallest syllable he had ever had from her, and it went through the room like a door. Julian looked at the pug, who was asleep; at the vulture on the top shelf; at his own hands.

“You arrange people, Aunt,” he said. He had meant it for a charge. It came out flat, as a fact does that has been kept two days from the post.

“Yes,” said Lady Constance.

He had prepared a speech. He had made it at four that morning, with a good deal of syntax in it, and he found that nobody had ever agreed with him so promptly. It left a marquess with an armful of syntax and no one to throw it at.

“I have arranged you for twenty-two years,” she said. “It is the one subject on which I have never hesitated.” She took up the trumpet again and put it down, which in her was the equivalent of another person’s sitting. “Blücher is blind in one eye and discreet in the other. I am going to tell you a sum.”

“Which?”

“Twenty-one.”

He waited. When she said nothing more he did what he always did with a number, which was to look for what it was the number of.

“Twenty-one what?”

“Letters. One a year, on the twelfth of March, from ‘ninety-five to ‘fifteen. They came from Florence in your mother’s hand, with my name on the cover, because she knew that your father would not open a letter directed to his sister, and she trusted his sister to do what a sister does.” She looked at the fire. “I did what a sister does. I put them in it.”

The pug breathed. The clock on the chimney-piece, a gilt affair with a stuffed wren on top, struck the quarter, and neither of them looked at it.

“The first came in the spring of ‘ninety-five,” said Lady Constance. “Your father took it out of my hand in the dining-room. He read the direction.
