He said, ‘The boy is a Stanmere, Constance,’ and he put it on the fire himself, with the tongs. I was forty-three. I had been told since I was in frocks that this is how a family is kept.”

“And the second?”

“He did not ask for the second. He said, ‘You will know what to do.’ I knew.”

“And after he died.”

“That is what I cannot explain to you.” She said it exactly as she said everything, like a woman reading out a bill. “In ‘nine there was nobody left to obey. You were twenty-four. You were the Marquess, and might have been in Florence by the next packet if you had a mind. I thought, if the boy goes I shall have no one. I thought, if he reads it he will not forgive me the rest. I thought a number of other things, which came to the same sum, and it was the twelfth of March, and I burned it. One does not decide such a thing, Julian. One does it once, and the second time is habit, and the eleventh time is Tuesday. It is not done with a great fire. It is done with a great many small reasons.”

“Did you read them?”

“No. It was the one decent thing. I knew what I was burning and not what it said.” She stood, with the pug sliding off her feet in protest, and went to the escritoire in the window. The purple ribbon at her throat, which he had always taken for an ornament, turned out to have a key on it. “Until this March. I read the last. I do not know why. I stood at the grate with the poker in my other hand, and it had an address in it, and I found that I burn sentiments, Julian, but I do not burn addresses. An address is a fact.”

She unlocked the third drawer and took out a single sheet, folded in three, and held it out. Her hand was perfectly steady. It was the steadiness of a person who has resolved not to be seen shaking.

“Miss Pargeter read the direction of that across this room in June,” said Lady Constance. “From nine yards. I turned it face down. She said nothing to anyone. I watched her say nothing for three months, and thought better of her every week, and did not know why until I had your Crier in my lap and nothing to do but think.”

The paper was soft at the folds, as paper is that has been taken out and put back. The hand ran uphill. He knew it at once, which was absurd: he had last seen it in a nursery at Stanmere Court, on the flyleaf of an Aesop, For Julian, who is to be good, and had forgotten that he knew it, and his eyes remembered first.

My dear Julian, you are thirty-one today, and I have not forgotten one of them. I do not know whether Constance gives you these; I have decided that she does. I am at fourteen Via dei Bardi. The door is open. C.

It was four lines long.

He read it twice. He read it as he read everything, with a pencil’s attention and no pencil; and at the second sentence he stopped, and looked for some time at I have decided that she does, as a man looks at a sum that has come out right against all the odds and is therefore, on the whole, more frightening than one that has come out wrong.

He did not shout. The reader who has waited this long for a marquess to shout will be disappointed: Julian had never in his life raised his voice to an aunt, and did not know in which part of the house the voice was kept. What came was slower, and worse. For twenty-two years he had been a man whose mother did not write. He had built upon it as a house is built upon a fact: the shelf of errata, and the oblong on the library wall that he did not mention, and the boy of nine who resolved that he would not marry unless it were impossible not to. All of it rested on the plain sentence she did not write, and the sentence was a misprint. The copy had said something else. Somebody had read the copy, and seen, and let it go.

And there was another thing, which he could look at only sideways. He had gone to Ave Maria Lane with a cheque-book for the reason his aunt had stood at a grate with a poker. He had known what was best for a person, and had not asked her. It was the same fire. His had a better coat on, and a cheque-book where hers had tongs.

“I shall not ask you to forgive me,” said Lady Constance. “I do not ask.”

“No.” He folded the letter along its three folds, which fitted. “I should like to be alone, Aunt.”

“Go and be alone somewhere useful.”

At the door he turned. “You kept the last.”

“I kept the last,” said Lady Constance. “I should like it noted. I am told it counts for something.”

“Quite,” said Julian, which was his word for No and, on this single occasion, for the other.

When he had gone she sat for some time without moving, as one sits after a tooth has been drawn, to find out whether it is true. Then she took up the Crier from the floor, where it had slid, and turned to the second page, to the column headed THE QUIZZING-GLASS, and read the first line of it for the seventh time.

I may be quite wrong, but.

She had heard that sentence at her own breakfast table, at the foot of it, over the toast, in a voice that apologised to the butter, every morning since 1804. She had not mentioned it to her nephew. A woman who has just emptied one drawer does not reach for another within the hour; and it was a habit of hers not to say a thing she knew until it would be useful. She had known this since Saturday, and had said nothing for the same reason she had said nothing for twenty-one years, and it had occurred to her, somewhere between the burning and the giving, that it had not been a reason then either.

She took a sheet and wrote, in the upright and uncompromising hand of a fence: Agnes. You will come to the morning-room when you have read this. C.D.

She did not send it. Miss Fell came in from church at nine, wet to the mittens, and took off her bonnet in the hall and said good morning to the pug; and Lady Constance, who in twelve years had not once looked at her companion’s face across the toast, found that she could not look at it now. The note stayed in the pocket of the wrapper all day. It went up at ten that night, on the chocolate-tray, face upward, to lie on a washstand in an attic where a candle was burning.

The General Post Office stood in Lombard Street, in a house that had been built for a banker and had never entirely got over the descent. On a Sunday the foreign department kept a hatch open from ten until seven, for the convenience of persons who had spent the week finding a sentence.

Julian found a sloping desk with a chained pen and an inkwell the colour of the Thames. He took a sheet. He wrote Madam, and looked at it as he looked at a wrong signboard, and crossed it out. He wrote Mother, which he had not said aloud since he was nine, and found that it stood on the paper like a man in a doorway; and he put Dear before it, to give it something to lean on. Then he wrote There has been a misprint.

He sat twenty minutes with the pen above the next line. A blot formed on the nib, grew, and fell, and he watched it go. At the next desk a sailor in a pea-jacket, with his tongue between his teeth, wrote to somebody in six lines, kissed the sheet, and was gone; and Julian envied him with a ferocity that would have astonished the sailor. At last he folded the half page into his pocket-book, between two leaves of W.P.’s queries, and went out into Lombard Street without having got any further.

It turned out, as the afternoon wore on, that what he could do was correct himself in type. It was the one form of apology in which he had had any practice, having begun it at nine years old over his father’s Gibbon.

At three he sat down in the library, in the chair that faced the oblong, with a sheet of foolscap, and wrote without stopping the tenth letter of A Kentish Farmer. The first nine had cost him a month apiece, with a dictionary and a quantity of reflection. This took two hours, and he did not blot it.

To the Editor of the Morning Gazette. Sir,—In the nine letters which have appeared in your columns over the description A Kentish Farmer, for A Kentish Farmer read Julian, Marquess of Stanmere, who owns eleven farms in the Weald of Kent at rents he has not lowered. The figures, I am advised by an able reader, stand.

The rest was the arithmetic of bread, which he knew, and the arithmetic of a landlord, which he had never in his life set down; and the second was a good deal shorter than the first. At the foot he wrote his name and style in full, in the same hand as the figures, and sat looking at it. It was the first thing he had signed in twenty years that he had not read over.

Minton came in at four with the cold beef on a tray, like a man bringing a sandwich to a bomb.

“My lord, it is signed.”

“Yes.”

“With your name.”

“That is generally what a signature is.” Julian held out the sheet. “A fair copy, if you please, in a plain cover, to Mrs Rudge at Bath. Mr Ingram has the direction and will pretend that he has not.”

“Not to Mr Underhill, my lord?”

“Mr Underhill would print it and call it a clarification.”

“And the Row?” Minton did not look at him. “It is Miss Pargeter’s type.”

“No.” He turned the signet once. “Sent from Curzon Street to Hand and Pen Court, it would look like a present, and she has refused presents since June. It will go to the one person in London who can print it or not as she pleases. What Miss Pargeter does with the consequences is Miss Pargeter’s affair. I find that I am not to be consulted.”

Minton took the sheet. He had read it already over the tray, as a secretary reads, without moving his head. He consulted his watch from long habit, and found it saying five minutes to three, as it had said since a ditch on Wrotham Hill, and put it away with the face of a man who has been caught agreeing with a clock.

“It is the best thing you have written, my lord.”

“It is the only one in which I was wrong,” said Julian. “I expect that is the same thing.”

At six he went back to Lombard Street.

He did not take the carriage. He walked, east along Piccadilly and down Cheapside, and he noticed that nobody looked at him, which was the first mercy of the day. The hatch was still open. The sailor had been replaced by a clergyman, who wrote with his eyes shut.

The letter took eleven minutes. The tenth Farmer had taught him the form: one states what was printed, one states what should have been, and one signs. He wrote that he had been told for twenty-two years that she did not write, and that it appeared she had. He wrote that he had the last, of March, and should like the others, if any survived, and the rest of her, if the door were still open. He wrote that he would not come unasked, and that this was why he was asking. Then he wrote his name, and read it over, which he had said he would not do, and found nothing in it to correct.

The clerk at the hatch was a young man with a cold. He weighed the packet, turned it over, read the direction, The Marchioness of Stanmere, 14 Via dei Bardi, Firenze, and then looked at the griffin in the wax, and at the person on the other side of the brass.

“Florence, my lord?” said the clerk. “That will be two and sixpence. It is a long way.”

“Yes,” said the Marquess. “I know.”

chapters.title: Miss Fell Takes Off Her Hat
chapters.html:
At half past five on the morning of the third of September Miss Agnes Fell sat on the edge of her bed in the attic of Hertford Street with a pen in one hand and a sealed letter in the other, and looked at the window, in which, because the candle stood behind her, a thin woman with a white streak in her hair looked back.

The streak began at the left temple and ran back into the grey like a path through a field. She had spent twelve years persuading caps to cover it. It had not occurred to her until lately that it was the one memorable thing about her, and that she had been hiding it as other people hide a scar, when it was the only distinction she possessed.

The letter was directed To Lady Constance Dyer, on leaving. She had written it across three nights, in the voice she kept for her best work, and it was the best thing she had ever done, a fact she would have paid a good deal not to know. It said everything. It said it twice, in different tenses. On the washstand beside the ewer lay a second paper, folded in three, which had come up on Sunday night with the chocolate and which said, in a hand like a fence: Agnes. You will come to the morning-room when you have read this. C.D. It had lain there two days. She had read it, without once lifting it from the marble, some four hundred times.

It is time the reader was told how Peregrine Pry was born, since the reader has known for some weeks who he was.

In the autumn of 1814 Lady Constance, in a season of economy, had arranged to pay her companion forty pounds a year, a quarter in arrear, on principle. In the same month Agnes’s brother Matthias, a lieutenant on half-pay, who had by some process she had never been able to follow run up three hundred pounds in hosiery, wrote from the Borough to say that the hosier was growing weary. Agnes had by then sat a pace behind her employer’s shawl at a great many routs. People speak before a woman holding a shawl as they speak before a clock. One night, for no reason she could afterwards give, she wrote an account of the patronesses of Almack’s in the voice of a person whom everybody looks at, and sent it unsigned to the Phoenix Press by a law-stationer’s boy; and on the Friday there came back three guineas and a note of one word, which was More.

She had found out that she was good as one finds a shilling in an old coat: first with suspicion, then with joy, and then with the reflection that one has been wearing the coat all along. She was proud of it. That was what she could not get into the letter on the washstand, though she had tried it in three tenses. She was proud of the turtle. She was proud of a sentence about the Dowager Lady C——, whose ear-trumpet was the only instrument on which she permitted herself to be played; and she was proud, Heaven forgive her, of the little quizzing-glass that Mr Lovejoy set at the head of the column in a Long Primer italic of great beauty, and that she had looked at every Friday night for two years as one looks at one’s own name on a door.

At eight she went down, with the letter, and without her courage, which she had left on the washstand with the note.

The morning-room was cold, and Lady Constance was not. She sat bolt upright at the escritoire in the window, in black bombazine and the purple ribbon, with no trumpet in her hand and no Blücher at her feet; the pug, who knew a ceremony when he saw one, had retired under the table. She did not turn round. She said, to the glass:

“You have read my note.”

“I beg your pardon,” said Agnes. “I have read it a great many times, and—”

“Do not beg my pardon. It is a habit, and it spoils the sentence. Say whatever it is flat.”

So Agnes said it flat. She said it in four sentences, which she had made on the stairs, and which came out in the order of a column, with the best at the end. “I am Peregrine Pry. I copied Miss Pargeter’s Articles in the estate office at Stanmere Court on the night of the third of August, and I sent the copy to Mr Lovejoy on the fifteenth. He holds my brother’s debt, which is three hundred and twelve pounds, and I give that as a fact and not as an excuse. I beg your pardon.”

The last had slipped in after all, against orders.

Lady Constance turned from the window. Her face did not alter, which was how one knew. “You have been under my roof.”

“Yes.”

“For twelve years.”

“Yes, my lady.”

“I have given you a room with a window, and the use of a dog.” Her voice was cold, exact and perfectly level, and each word was laid down like a card. “In that room you sharpened a pen to say that I am played upon by my own trumpet.”

“Yes.”

“I thought it the best thing you ever did.” Lady Constance regarded the ceiling. “It has lain on my conscience since June that I admired it. Sit down, Agnes. Not there. There is a plover.”

Agnes sat. She had expected a good many things in the night, and had prepared against all of them but this.

“I have burned twenty-one letters,” said Lady Constance. “In twenty-one years. They were not mine, and I told my nephew so on Sunday. You posted one paper, which was not yours. We shall see which of us is the more ashamed. I have twenty years’ start of you, and I mean to keep it.”

“Letters?” said Agnes. “Whose?”

“You shall have the rest another day. I find that the habit of telling grows on one, and that it is very tiring.”

“Am I to go?”

“You are to stay. I have not decided what for, but the dog is accustomed to your biscuits and I am accustomed to the dog.” She looked at the letter in Agnes’s hand. “What is that?”

“My notice.”

Lady Constance took it, turned it over, read the superscription, and opened the third drawer of the escritoire, in which there was a space the exact size of a folded sheet. She laid the letter in it, unopened, and turned the key. “I shall keep it,” she said. “I am told it is better than burning. Where are you going?”

“To Hand and Pen Court. I should rather say it to her face than write it. I have done enough of the other.”

“Then go.” And as Agnes reached the door: “Agnes. You will say it flat.”

She walked, because a hackney is a closed box with a man in it who looks at one in the glass, and she had been looked at in glass enough that morning. Two miles and a half in the rain, under the black straw bonnet that she had worn for twelve years pulled down to the eyebrows, with a brim like a pent-house; and she saw nobody’s face, which had been the intention.

Toby opened the door of Pargeter’s, with half a pie in his mouth. He looked at her. “It’s the lady with the mittens!” he said, and ran off down the passage shouting for Miss Win in the voice of a boy who has seen a ghost, or a bailiff, or in either case something that might want pies.

On the step Agnes did what she had not done in a public place since 1804. She took off her bonnet. It was a small thing. It was like undressing.

The composing room was quiet. The Gazette’s inner forme had gone back to Pomfret Yard’s own press-room, where, Mr Orme said, it was being done with the enthusiasm of a man pulling his own tooth, and Fairweather stood idle by the Albion with a cloth in his hand, like a verger at an empty church. Orme had taken up his stick again on Monday, on the ground that a man must do something with his hands. The Drip fell. Winifred stood at her frame with her back to the door, setting a card for the Dowager Duchess of Ormsgill, who desired the pleasure of two hundred persons’ company on the nineteenth of October, and who had shown no sign of having read the Crier except by doubling the order.

“I am setting,” said Winifred, not turning. “If it is Lady Constance’s business, you may say it to my back.”

“It is not Lady Constance’s. It is my own.”

“Then you may say it to my stick.” Winifred held out a composing stick, over her shoulder, without looking; with her other hand she slid a pair of cases of Great Primer across the frame. “Set what you have come to say, Miss Fell. I shall read it when I reach the end of this line, and I shall not read it before.”

Agnes took the stick. It was an iron one, Toby’s, with a screw, and it was heavier than a pen by a good deal. She knew the lay of the case. She had counted it for a fortnight in the old brewhouse at Stanmere Court, as she counted everything, and had never meant to use it. She found the first letter with her thumb. The type was upside down and backwards, and the nick on its shank had to be felt for, like the edge of a stair in the dark; she set the line from left to right, with every letter facing the wrong way, and it took her forty minutes to say what she had said in Hertford Street in a quarter of one.

She set it in capitals, because it seemed to her that what she had to say was not a matter for the lower case. I AM PEREGRINE PRY. Nine lines, the width of a psalm. When she had set the last she stood holding the stick, in which the whole of it was lying the wrong way round, and found that her hands had stopped shaking some lines ago and she had not noticed.

Winifred reached the end of hers, stuck it, and turned. She read the stick the right way up, which is to say the wrong way round, as she had read everything since she was seventeen. Then she read it from the other end. She found two errors in the time it takes to say so: DBET for DEBT, and, in BROTHER’S, an E of the wrong fount, a size too small, which stood in the line like a child in a row of grown persons. She mentioned neither.

“Thank you, Miss Fell,” she said. She had gone, as she did when angry, extremely polite. “That is very exact. Lady Constance has been told?”

“This morning.”

“And she said?”

“That she had burned twenty-one letters, and I had posted one paper, and we should see which was the more ashamed.”

Something went across Winifred’s face and was put away. She had read a Florence postmark across a room in June; she did not say so. She was thinking, with the unfair clearness of the very angry, of her father, who had sat in this room on Saturday with the Crier over his face and said on Sunday at breakfast that he thought he would go to bed for a week; and of the bond on the house; and of the stick, which was Toby’s, and would make a very fair missile. She laid it down on the ledge.

“You did not walk two miles in the rain to set one stick,” said Winifred.

“No.” Agnes’s voice came out thin and she let it. “He writes to me on Fridays. A line only. On Friday he wrote: The 28th, madam. Six o’clock. Mr Sowerby will swear before an alderman on the 25th. I shall be obliged by a column on the compositor’s conscience. H.L.”

“The twenty-eighth is a Saturday.”

“The last before Michaelmas. There is to be a second number of the Crier, with the carter’s affidavit, that you saw the error at a quarter to five and let the cart go. It will be at the corners at six in the morning. I did not send the column.” She swallowed. “I do not think he knows yet why.”

“He has an eye for a title,” said Winifred. “On the compositor’s conscience.”

“He tells me what is true and useful, and nothing else. It is the most frightening habit in the world.”

“Yes.” Winifred looked at the Drip. “Yes, I have noticed.”

She stood so for the time it takes a pan to fall three times. Behind her, in the corner, Orme’s stick went on ticking at the case, deaf and perfect, setting someone’s sermon. Then she said, in a different voice, the voice of the shop, which asks what the job is:

“It is mine.”

“I beg your pardon?”

“I set it. I saw it at a quarter to five and I let it go, and Mr Sowerby saw me stand there. It is mine to tell, and he shall not tell it first. I shall tell it myself, in my own name, in a place where it will do the most harm, which is to me.” She almost smiled; it was not a kind smile, but it was the first. “And I shall set the correction.”

“The Gazette will not print a correction. Mr Underhill—”

“Mr Underhill edits the Gazette. Mrs Rudge owns it.”

“Mrs Rudge is at Bath.”

“Then I shall write to Bath.” Winifred took up a bodkin, looked at it, and put it down. “And there is the money. I cannot pay eleven hundred pounds in September, and I shall not be bought out of it, by anybody.”

“Miss Quarles keeps her father’s books,” said Agnes. “I may be—” She stopped. It was the sentence that had hanged her. She had said it for twelve years without noticing and for three days could not say it at all. She said it now, with deliberate dread, like a woman putting her hand back on a stove. “I may be quite wrong, but I do not think she has been asked.”

“No,” said Winifred. “She has not.”

“And there is the matter of the Gazette on the streets before six. The run takes the Albion and the Old Lady near three hours at the best, and it cannot be done short-handed. I counted, in the press-room, on my way through. The Albion wants two men at the bar, and you have one.” Agnes looked at her hands. “I may be quite wrong, but I think you ought to ask the Marquess to pull it.”

Winifred did not answer. She picked up the Duchess’s card, found a place for her thumb on the edge of it, and read it as though it had been in a foreign tongue.

“I should like,” said Agnes, “to read your proofs. I am very good at finding what is wrong with a thing in print. It was my profession.”

“Mr Ingram reads for the Gazette.”

“Mr Ingram has a quinsy.”

“He always has a quinsy.” But Winifred held out the card, across the frame, without looking up. “The third line,” she said. “Tell me what is wrong with it.”

Agnes took it. She read it once, with her bonnet in her left hand, and said, “There is a comma after honour that does not belong.” Winifred looked at it for a very long time, and took it out.

She wrote the letter that evening, at the kitchen table, when Mrs Hobday had gone up and Barnaby’s snores were coming down the speaking-tube in a rhythm like a slow press. It ran to eleven pages. It began Madam, On the sixth of June last the Gazette printed a paragraph that was false, and I set it. I have the honour to ask your leave to tell you how; it began upright, in the small square hand of the proof-margins, and grew smaller as it went, like a person going down a stair. It told the whole. It did not leave out the Drip, nor the cat, nor the cart, nor the arch. When she had signed it she did not read it over. She had a feeling that if she did, she should find something she wished to correct, and it would be the truth.

“I will take it,” said Agnes. “The Bath mail goes at eight from the coach office in Piccadilly. I beg your pardon, but I think you would rather it went by a person who knows what is in it.”

“Yes,” said Winifred, and gave it to her.

At half past six Miss Fell put the packet in her cloak, took up her pen-case, and went out through the arch of Hand and Pen Court into Paternoster Row. It was raining. She had her bonnet in her hand. She had meant to put it on at the corner, and at the corner she found that she had not.

She walked down the middle of the Row, between the dark shops with their lamps already lit, past the booksellers’ apprentices and the umbrella of a curate and a woman who sold chestnuts; and she looked, for the first time in two years, at every face she met. None of them knew her. The rain came down on the white streak at her temple and stood there in beads. She did not put up a hand to it.

chapters.title: A Brewer's Terms
chapters.html:
The dray-horse in the yard of the Black Bull Brewery was the size of a small church, and had much the same expression of settled disapproval. He stood in his shafts with his head down, a Suffolk the colour of wet bread, while two draymen in leather aprons rolled hogsheads up a plank behind him, and he regarded Winifred Pargeter as she came in through the gate as though she were a person who had not paid her pew-rent.

The smell had reached her a quarter of an hour before the brewery did. It had met her on London Bridge, and by the time she turned in at Bankside it was a hot brown sweetness of malt and wet horse and spent hops, which took hold of the back of the throat and invited it to stay for supper. It was the twelfth of September, a Thursday. It was drizzling, as a matter of course.

“That is Bishop,” said Verity Quarles, at the head of the counting-house stair. “He will not hurt you. He disapproves of everyone equally, and it is restful.”

The counting-house was a glass box at the head of the yard, with a stove, a high desk, and four walls of ledgers lettered on their backs in a hand like a row of barrels. Verity wore her brown dress. It had been to three routs and a flood, and had never, Winifred thought, been so well employed as it was now, with a pencil laid along the sleeve and the spectacles down on their chain. She took Winifred straight to the desk, without a word about the weather, as a good cook takes a visitor to the larder.

“Look,” she said. “Hops, Lady Day to Midsummer. Bought, forty-one pockets. Brewed, thirty-three. The other eight go out of the back gate on a cart to a gentleman in Deptford, who sells them back to the hop-factor at a third under, and gives Mr Halloran a commission for the introduction. Every month since February of last year. I make it eleven hundred pounds.”

Winifred counted down the column with one finger. She could not help it; a column of figures on a page was a line of type to her, and it had a measure. “The seventh entry is wrong.”

“The seventh entry is where he began to be careful. I have not told him.” Verity took off her spectacles. “I have told his clerk that I have mislaid a column. Mr Halloran has been so kind as to offer to help me find it.”

Winifred laughed, which she had not done in a fortnight, and found that it hurt in a place she had been keeping shut.

“Papa will deal with him in the spring,” said Verity. “I should like to be there. But that is not why you are here. You are here for plain terms, and Papa has been looking forward to it since Monday, and here he is.”

Sir Ephraim Quarles filled the door as a cask fills a cellar. He was broad and bald and sixty, with a face like a well-baked loaf and a voice that had been used to cross yards, and he took a stool, and set a mug of small beer on the ledger, and looked at Winifred without any appearance of being in a hurry. She counted four minutes by the counting-house clock, in which neither of them said anything much; and at the end of them she saw that she had been liked.

“Plain terms, Miss Pargeter. What do you want, how much, how long, and what do I get?”

“Twelve hundred pounds, Sir Ephraim, for three years, at six per cent.”

“Security?”

“The Albion, the stock, and my word.”

“I’d put ’em the other way about.”

“So would I. But my word is not in the inventory.”

“Hah.” He drank. “I’ll tell you what I get, then, and you tell me if it’s fair. You print every label this house sends out, for three years: Entire, Porter, Double Stout, the Christmas Ale. Handbills. Dray-tickets. At a fair price. I’ll not have it said I kept a printer out of charity. I keep a printer to print.”

“Mr Lovejoy has had them fifteen years.”

“He has. He sets a handsome label. I shall miss the bull.” Sir Ephraim set down the mug. “But I do not employ a man who printed my wife’s fainting fits in a gossip sheet. I’ve seen what the Crier said of Lady Quarles at the Waterloo rout, and I would not mind it if it were wrong. It was perfectly right. A man does not like to see his own opinion in the hands of Hector Lovejoy.” He leaned forward. “Is there a Marquess in this?”

“There is not.”

“Good. I distrust ’em. A man who has never asked a price is a man who has never been told one.” He took a paper from his waistcoat, a banker’s draft, already written, and blotted it on his sleeve. “Twelve hundred. It’s my own money, mind, not the brewery’s. The brewery is Verity’s in nine years, and I’ll not have Halloran’s fingers in it.”

“Papa,” said Verity.

“I do not say a thing I have not said to his face.”

“You have said nothing to his face. You have not noticed anything.”

“I’ve noticed that you’ve been unusually kind to him,” said Sir Ephraim, “and I’ve taken it for what it is.” He looked at his daughter with an expression that was very nearly the only soft one the counting-house had ever seen. Then the door opened.

Lady Quarles came in with a vinaigrette in one hand and a gown the colour of a fine claret, which had not been made for Bankside. She was fifty, and she came into the counting-house of her husband’s brewery as a swan comes into a stable-yard. “Ephraim, the carriage has been standing forty minutes in the smell. Miss Pargeter! My dear, I had no notion that you were come upon business.”

“Mamma,” said Verity, “Miss Pargeter is going to print our labels.”

“Labels?”

“Trade, my dear,” said Sir Ephraim. “Trade. Augusta. Trade.”

Lady Quarles went down gracefully, with her hand to her brow, upon the third ledger of the year 1811. The clerk, a Mr Pike, who had evidently been through this before, fanned her with a price list.

“She’ll come round at the sound of the kettle,” said Sir Ephraim, regarding his wife with tranquil approval. “She likes to be left. It’s her one accomplishment, and I’d not interrupt a woman at the head of her profession.”

It was at this point, as is the way of comedy, that someone knocked.

He came in with his hat in his hand, in an old brown coat with leather at the elbows, such as is worn by persons who buy hay; and he wore no waistcoat at all, which on Lord Rupert Tremayne amounted to a moral position. He looked at the party in the counting-house: at Sir Ephraim, at Winifred, at the lady on the floor with the price list going over her like a banner. “I have come at a bad moment,” he said. “I generally do. It is the only way I know of arriving at a good one.”

“Rupert,” said Verity.

“Miss Quarles.” He bowed. Then he looked for something to do with his hands, and tossed no guinea, there being none to toss. “I came to propose to you, and I find I do not know how it is done without a waistcoat.”

“Plain terms,” said Sir Ephraim, from his stool. “Have you a penny?”

“None, sir.”

“Good. It saves time.”

“Papa,” said Verity, “I will do this.” She put down her pencil. She had Rupert’s signet on her thumb, the gold one she had won from him at forfeits in Kent, and she turned it round, as Julian turned his, which Winifred noticed and said nothing about. “Say it, then.”

He said it, to his credit, standing quite still. “I owe two thousand three hundred pounds to eleven men and a glover. I can ride, dance, pick a horse, and tell you which of three will break its leg. I have been bored for nine years and find you the only thing that has stopped it. I do not want your brewery. I should be extremely bad at it. I should like to marry you, and I should rather like to be told what to do.”

“Eleven men and a glover,” said Verity.

“I forgot the glover. I wished to be honest.”

“I shall buy the paper. All of it, from the whole twelve, at five per cent. You will owe me instead of them, which is a convenience to your creditors and a great deal worse for you.” She was counting on her fingers. “And you will go on the drays.”

“The—”

“A month. Fourteen shillings a week, which is what Josh has, and Josh has a wife. I will not marry a man who believes that beer comes in barrels by Providence. If you are on the dray on the twelfth of October you may ask me again, and I will answer.”

“Am I not to be told the answer?”

“No.”

“Splendid.” Rupert went to the glass and looked out at the yard. “My dear girl. That is not a horse. That is a cathedral chapter.”

“His name is Bishop.”

“Of course it is,” said Rupert, and went out to be introduced.

When he had gone down the stair, with a cheer from the draymen at the bottom of it, Verity sat for a moment looking at her hands. “He will never forgive me for the barrels,” she said. “That is the foundation of a happy marriage. I read it in a book of Papa’s. It was about the Navy.”

Winifred came out into the yard with the draft in her glove at a quarter to twelve. It had stopped raining, which meant that it was merely dripping, and the whole brewery steamed gently like a horse. She was crossing to the gate, in the shadow of the weighing-room, when she saw who stood in its door.

Mr Lovejoy had his hat in front of him. He wore the snuff-coloured coat, and the glass on its ribbon, and a flat parcel of proofs under one arm, and his hands were scrubbed to the colour of boiled ham. He had printed the Quarles labels for fifteen years. He had come, she understood, for the second time that week, to be told by Sir Ephraim a thing he had been told on Monday, because he was a man who liked to hear a sentence twice, to see whether it kept.

“Miss Pargeter.”

“Mr Lovejoy.”

“I came with the proof of the Christmas Ale. A handsome bull. I cut the horns myself.” He looked at the parcel, and not at her. “Sir Ephraim was good enough to explain with great clearness that it will be set elsewhere.”

“I am sorry for it.”

“You are not, madam, and it would be a poor compliment to you if you were.” He bowed. “I allowed for Curzon Street. I did not think of Bankside. It is an oversight, and I make so few that I find I notice it.”

“I did not go to Curzon Street,” said Winifred.

“No. I perceive that.”

“There is still the matter of the carter.”

“I know about the carter, Mr Lovejoy. I shall be telling it myself.”

He did not answer at once. He looked at her as he looked at a page that had been given him to lay out, with his head a little on one side, working out what could be taken away and what must stay. It was not a look she had had from him before. She had had the other, the one that fell upon a nicked sort. It lasted about as long as it takes to say Great Primer.

“That is unusual,” he said at last.

“Yes.”

“I have not a rule for it.”

“I can discharge the notes tomorrow,” said Winifred. “In full, in coin, if you will name the hour. I should be glad to.”

“I do not doubt it.” He inclined his head, with real courtesy. “But notes payable at Michaelmas are payable at Michaelmas, madam. I could not think of taking yours a day sooner. It would be a discourtesy to the instrument.”

It was his right. It was the only unkindness he permitted himself, and she saw that he knew it was one, and that he took no pleasure in it, and that he would do it all the same, as a man dresses a wound he has himself been obliged to make. He put on his hat and went out through the gate, small and neat, with the proofs under his arm, past the church-sized horse, who did not look at him either.

They walked back over London Bridge, she and Verity, to the bankers’ in Lombard Street, with the river going out under the nineteen arches like a long brown thought. Winifred counted the arches. She always did.

“You miss him,” said Verity.

“Like a tooth.”

“I thought so. Teeth are a nuisance. One keeps putting one’s tongue in the place.” Verity walked as she did everything, in a straight line. “He sent me a note on Monday. One line. Is she well? J. I sent it back by the same boy with Ask her written on the bottom.”

“I told him not to come.”

“Then it is hardly surprising that he is not coming.”

“I am not surprised,” said Winifred. “That is the tooth.”

Messrs Garland and Pell counted twelve hundred pounds into a strongbox lent for the purpose by Sir Ephraim, an oak-and-iron affair with a brass bull’s head on the lid and a lock like a bishop’s. Winifred had asked for it in gold, in a form that could be counted aloud on a stone, and the clerk had said that gold was dear. Verity had said that so was a good name. At three the box went home to Hand and Pen Court upon the Black Bull dray, behind Bishop, with two draymen sitting on the lid and Verity on the shaft; the great horse leaned into Ludgate Hill like a church being moved, and the whole of the Row came to its windows.

Fairweather carried it up to the second floor in his arms, like an infant, and said “Aye.” Mrs Hobday had it put under her bed beside her hymn-book. “Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth,” she said, “where moth and rust doth corrupt. And meanwhile, under the bed.”

When they had all gone down, Winifred stood in the housekeeper’s room a minute with her hand on the lid. Twelve hundred pounds. She had not been given it. She had been given the chance to earn it back at a fair price, which was better, and she had gone and done the bargaining herself, and not one word of it had been in a Marquess’s voice. She was as nearly happy as she had been since the thirty-first of August, and she wanted, with a violence that surprised her, to tell someone.

She knew with perfect exactness who. He was at that hour in Curzon Street, two and a half miles off, thirty-five minutes by hackney in the rain; and she had asked him not to come.

chapters.title: The Quaker and the Clause
chapters.html:
A post-chaise from Bath came into Pomfret Yard at ten minutes to ten on the morning of the twenty-fourth of September, splashing a drayman, and out of it was lifted, by a postilion and a footman acting in some sort of consultation, a very small old woman in Quaker grey, like a parcel that has been marked This Side Up and is being treated accordingly.

“Thee may put me down,” said Mrs Rudge. “I am not a parcel, though I have travelled as one.”

She stood on the cobbles in the rain, seventy-two years old and four feet eleven, in a grey bonnet like a coal-scuttle with a white cap beneath it, her better ear turned toward the noise of the yard and a pencil standing out of her reticule like the hilt of a sword. She looked at the offices of the Morning Gazette, a long dark house with a bow window and a brass plate, as a woman looks at a child that has been left in the charge of servants. Then she went in by a back stair, and was not seen again until she was in her chair.

Winifred’s letter had reached her on the fifth. The answer, of one line, had reached Hand and Pen Court on the eighth: I shall come when my chest will let me. Do nothing until I do. K.R. Winifred had done nothing for sixteen days, with great skill, as other people do something. She had printed the Duchess’s cards and the first of the Black Bull labels. She had said the opening of her speech to the Drip some four hundred times.

They had come in a hackney, she and Barnaby, with his foot on the opposite seat. “Win,” he had said, at the corner of Fleet Street. “Whatever you say in there, say it in the order it happened.”

“It is the only order I know.”

“Your mother used to say that a thing was true when it came out in the order it happened. She said that lies come in order of convenience.” He blew his nose, a trumpet-call, and pushed his spectacles up. “I shall stop in the cab. I have been told to say nothing to anybody. I mean to say it to the horse.”

Mrs Rudge had sent for them both, and for a third. Winifred had sent word by Minton that she would tell it alone, and the third party had not argued. He had merely arrived at a quarter to ten, and sat down upon a bale of newsprint at the foot of the steps, under the lean-to, with his hat on his knee, since nobody had forbidden bales.

The counting-room of the Gazette had a stove, a ledger-desk, a hard chair, and a clock that was nine minutes fast on principle. In the hard chair, with her good ear to the room and her pencil in her lap, the proprietor was already seated. Mr Underhill stood before her, in a coat buttoned correctly for once, pink to the roots of his hair. Mr Ingram stood at the window in his muffler. On a stool at the far side, with a leather folder on one knee and the glass on its ribbon at his waistcoat, sat Mr Lovejoy, who had been invited by Mr Underhill, and who had come, as he went everywhere, early.

“Winifred Pargeter,” said Mrs Rudge. “Come in out of the wet. Ezekiel Underhill, thee is pink. Thee was pink in the fourth month of ‘ninety-seven, and I said then that it was a poor colour for a man who prints the truth.”

“Madam—”

“Presently. I would sooner hear thee last.” She turned the good ear a fraction. “Thee may begin.”

He began. His voice, which had been a great organ for nineteen years, came out in the upper register, like an organ with a mouse in it. “The position of the Gazette, madam, is a simple one, and I have set it out in a memorandum. By the ninth clause of the contract of 1812, any error of the press requiring a correction shall render the contract void and the bond of five hundred pounds forfeit. An error has been proved. It has been proved in a public print, and by the confession of the party. The contract is void, the bond is forfeit, and the house in Hand and Pen Court answers for it. Mr Lovejoy, with great public spirit, has been so good as to offer to take up the work at four-fifths of the late price.”

“I have drawn the heads, madam,” said Mr Lovejoy, rising an inch, “if you wish to see them.”

“Thee will keep them in thy folder, Hector Lovejoy. I have not come to be sold anything.” Mrs Rudge took up the pencil, which was the signal, as every clerk in the building knew, for the end of other people’s remarks. “Winifred Pargeter. Thee wrote me eleven pages. I have read them four times, with this, and made no mark on them, which is not my custom. I should like to hear thee say it. All of it. Ezekiel Underhill will be quiet, which will be good for him.”

So Winifred told it.

She told it in the order in which it had happened, which is the only order a compositor trusts. She told the Drip, and the copy that came in damp at five from a clerk in a fair hand, and the second Drip at eight, which blotted the name-line. She told the cat. She said that a page had fallen at eleven into pie, from a cord that she had told a boy of thirteen to reknot and had not looked to herself; that the boy had had a pie in one hand and the cat underfoot; that she had never asked him and he had never said; and that she would be obliged if the room would take the cord for hers. She told the heap on the stone, and the two lines of one measure that lay together in it, the Marquess’s name-line and her own advertisement for fair copying, with the W in it that had a nick in the left foot. She said that a compositor does not read; she sees letters, as a baker sees flour. She said that she had set what she saw.

Mr Underhill made a small noise, as of a man swallowing the word libel. Mrs Rudge’s pencil moved a quarter of an inch, and he stopped.

She told the sheet at twenty minutes to five, hung to dry since two; Fairweather’s heel of bread; her own name. She told the arithmetic. She had done it standing, in the time it takes to say it: a reset, a reprint of eleven hundred, a cart at nine; Clause 6 on one side of the scale and Clause 9 on the other. She gave the figures aloud and softened none of them, because in her experience a figure softened is a figure lied about. Mrs Rudge listened with her head down, and when Winifred reached the arch she looked up.

“How long was the cart in the arch?”

“Four minutes.”

“And what did thee think of, in the four minutes?”

“The bond. The house. My father.” Winifred stopped. She had not put this in the letter. “I did not think of the Marquess at all. He was a name on a copy-slip. It is the thing I am most ashamed of, madam: I thought of him as a measure.”

“And then?”

“I let it go.”

It was very quiet in the counting-room. The stove ticked. In the yard a cart went by, and a carter swore at a horse in the tone of a man who has seen a great many weeks go past in the rain.

“The compositor’s honesty is touching, madam,” said Mr Lovejoy, quite gently, “and arrives four months late.”

“Yes,” said Winifred.

She did not defend herself. She had considered it, and found that there was nothing to defend that she would care to have defended.

Mrs Rudge laid down her pencil. “Why now?”

“Because the Gazette is the only paper in London whose owner reads it with a pencil.”

The old woman looked at her for some seconds with clear, unhurried, unamused eyes, the eyes of a person to whom nothing has been said for forty years that she did not hear. Then she turned the good ear to Mr Underhill.

“Ezekiel Underhill, I have heard thee call the ninth clause the glory of this house. I have thought about it at Bath, which is a place made for the purpose. A newspaper that cannot say it was wrong cannot be trusted when it says it is right. I said that to thee in the sixth month, in this room, and thee took it for a remark upon the weather. The ninth clause is a rule that teaches printers to hide. It has taught one. It is struck.”

“Madam, the contract—”

“The contract is restored as of the sixth of the sixth month, without the clause, and the bond is returned. Write this in its place. An error of the press shall be corrected in the number next following, in type as large as the error was set in, and the printer who first reports it shall not be penalised. Write it, Ezekiel Underhill. I have a good ear for dictation and a poor one for argument.”

He wrote it. The pen shook slightly, and the room, with the tact of long habit, looked at the stove.

“And on Saturday,” said Mrs Rudge, “the Gazette will print an erratum. It will be the first in nineteen years. The compositor who made the error will set it, and sign it, in Great Primer. I do not wish it softened. I wish it to be where it will be seen.”

“The Gazette, madam, does not retract.” It came out with something of the old organ, but thin, like a note held after the bellows have been let go. “It clarifies.”

“Then thee will have the honour of doing it for the first time.” She took a folded sheet from her reticule. “And beside it will run a tenth letter from the Kentish Farmer, which came to me at Bath on the third. I have read it three times with this pencil, and found nothing in it that wants correcting, which has never happened to a Farmer before. It begins, For A Kentish Farmer read Julian, Marquess of Stanmere.”

There was a pause, in which the clock, nine minutes fast, struck the hour.

“The Farmer?” said Mr Underhill. “My Farmer is—”

“Thee never asked who he was, Ezekiel Underhill. Thee asked only whether he was sound.” Mrs Rudge folded the paper. “He is sitting on my bale in the wet, and I think it good for him. It runs, if the writer will let his name stand under it, and I have no doubt that he will.”

Mr Ingram looked at the ceiling with the face of a man who has kept a secret for eighteen months and is not certain whether to be relieved. Mr Lovejoy, on his stool, remarked “I did observe the commas,” to no one in particular; and then, because it was true and might be useful, he stood.

“It is only fair, madam, to tell the Gazette that the Crier will print Sowerby’s account on Saturday at six. The carter has sworn to it. I should not like you to hear it first from a hawker.”

“Print it, Hector Lovejoy.” Mrs Rudge did not raise her voice. “Thee has not told a lie in thirty years. I have watched.” She turned to the stove, the clock, and the editor, in that order. “Then the Gazette will be carted at a quarter past four, an hour before its time, and be on the streets before the Crier is cried. It has never been done.”

“Madam, it cannot—”

“It will be done by the Pargeters, Ezekiel Underhill, who have done a harder thing this morning. Thee may inform thy carters.”

Winifred came down the steps at eleven with her gloves in her hand. It was still raining, in the thin, discouraged way in which it had rained since May; and at the foot of the steps, on a bale of newsprint, with his hat on his knee and his hair stuck to his forehead, the Marquess of Stanmere got up. He had been there an hour and a quarter and looked it.

“Well?”

“I have been given until Saturday,” said Winifred, “to say that I was wrong, in type the size of a door.”

“Great Primer is eighteen points. It is rather smaller than a door.”

“You have not seen the paragraph.”

He opened his mouth and shut it. He had learned, in the last three weeks and at some expense, the exact moment at which a sentence of his began to be an arrangement, and he stood at the edge of it like a man at the edge of a pond. “May I—”

“Dick Sparrow has gone to Mr Lovejoy,” said Winifred. “We are short a pressman. The Albion wants two at the bar, and Fairweather will not do it with the boy standing on a box. You may pull it.”

“I should be honoured.”

“You will be paid nothing.”

“I had not hoped otherwise.”

“You signed it,” she said. It was the other matter, and it came out sideways. “The tenth. With your name.”

“You told me to, in July, in the brewhouse.” He turned the signet on his finger. “You were right. I am a little late in being told so.”

“I have not forgiven you.”

“I know.”

“I have forgiven the bar-pulling.”

She went past him across the yard, toward the pump, where a hackney stood with a gouty foot raised at its window and a horse being addressed in a low voice on the subject of Mrs Rudge; and she did not look back, having learned from her trade that the thing one looks back at is the thing one sets again.

He stayed where he was. On the bale beside him, where he had been sitting, lay a folded newspaper, someone’s Tuesday Gazette, left by a porter gone to his breakfast, and the rain, which had found it, was beginning to turn the inner sheet to pulp. It was an extremely small matter. It was a stranger’s property and worth sevenpence. He looked at it, and then he took off his coat, which was a good one, and laid it over the bale and the paper together, to keep the rain off.

chapters.title: The Saturday Number
chapters.html:
At two o’clock on the afternoon of Friday the twenty-seventh of September, three hours before it was due and thirteen before it was wanted, the copy arrived at Hand and Pen Court in a pile, and was laid on the imposing stone like the pieces of a puzzle that has been kept too long in its box.

Mrs Rudge had ordered it early. A newspaper that meant to be early in the streets, she had said, had best begin by being early in the shop. There was the news, in a clerk’s fair hand, grudging as a bill. There was Mr Underhill’s own notice, a paragraph of three lines on a correction which the Gazette “had been advised to make”, which Winifred set aside with the interest of a naturalist for an unusual beetle. There was a column headed A. FELL, on the Weald and the Subscription, which every margin in the shop would have known for a razor’s; the proprietor had sent for the writer in three words, Send the woman. There was the Farmer, in Minton’s fair copy, with a covering line in the Marquess’s own hand: The commas are mine. Please do not correct them. J.S. And there was the Erratum. Mrs Rudge had drafted it in pencil on a half-sheet, and her draft had stopped at The error was the compositor’s. Winifred had added the rest in the margin, the name, and what the name had seen, and what it had done about it; and against the addition the proprietor had written, in the same pencil, a single word: True.

The rain had come back at noon, as a creditor comes back. Barnaby had hung a bucket from a nail in the beam, directly under the broken slate, and was explaining to it that this was the last night.

By six the shop was as full as it had been on the night of the Misprint, and a good deal fuller of the right people. Orme sat in his corner, deaf and perfect, composing the Farmer in Pica with the rhythm of a metronome that has been told a secret. Fairweather stood by the Albion. Mrs Hobday came and went with the tea, saying “In the night-watches” to the kettle, and Toby sat on an upturned pail in his paper hat with a fresh pie in his lap, which he was keeping, he said, for later, in the tone of a man laying down wine.

At five the Marquess had come in with his hat in his hand.

“My lord,” Winifred had said.

“Miss Pargeter.”

It was the whole conversation, and the shop, which had its ears out like a field of hares, found it adequate. She had put a stick in his hand. “Set your name,” she said. “I will not set it for you.” And Julian, in Barnaby’s old apron, had gone to the case beside Orme’s, and got the J into the stick in the first half-minute, the right way up, which is to say the wrong way round, as he had not managed on the thirteenth of June. Orme looked across, without turning his head.

“Clerkenwell?”

“Harrow.”

“Hm.” The stick ticked on. “Someone’s been teaching you to hate a river.”

The Erratum was set between eight and ten. Winifred set the body of it with her mother’s brass stick, the thumb-rest bright and warm; Orme set the Gazette’s part; and at half past nine Toby, who had been given a line, stood at the upper case with a quad in his teeth and said to the type, so low that she had to lean to hear, “Miss. It were me.”

“What was, Toby?”

“The page.” His ears were scarlet. “I had a pie. Brevier come under, and I trod, and it went. I never said. I told her.” He jerked his head at the cat, who was washing herself on the Albion with the air of a person who has heard it before.

“I know,” said Winifred.

“You know?”

“I have known since the Thursday. You did not eat for two days, and you looked at the cat as though she had robbed you.” She did not stop setting. “The cord was mine to look to. A thing told is worth three that are found out. Set your line.”

He set it. It was the last, and has never before had occasion to do so, in nine words, and it took him eleven minutes and a good deal of nose; and when it was in the stick Winifred read it backwards and found it right, and said nothing, and he went on with his face wet and a more than ordinary dignity.

The company came in as the night went on. Verity arrived at ten with a hamper of porter and a ledger, to witness whatever Mr Lovejoy might bring, and sat down on a ream of paper with the ledger on her knee like a woman in a theatre who has paid for her seat. Rupert carried paper. He had been carrying barrels for fifteen days, and he came and went with a ream under each arm and the expression of a man to whom labour has been revealed by a miracle. At eleven two footmen of Ormsgill House, in claret and silver, with their calves in the rain, presented themselves in the court with a card on a salver: My footmen are idle. Send them to the corners. O. Mrs Hobday gave them tea in the scullery and a hymn. And at midnight Lady Constance Dyer arrived in a closed carriage with Blücher under her arm, and took the chair by the fire without a word, and sat in it like a monument to the principle of being present.

Agnes read the proofs. She sat at the proofing press with a pencil, her mittens off since ten, and her right hand blue to the second joint and quite plain to see. Lady Constance looked at it once, from the chair, and looked away. Agnes found a turned n in the Farmer and a comma in the second line of Mr Underhill, and she held up the proof of the Erratum to the lamp, and said, “Miss Pargeter. The W.”

It was there, in the signature, in Great Primer, in W. PARGETER: the hairline gap in the left foot, as plain as a crack in a cup. She had meant to replace it since March. A new sort was fourpence.

“I can go to the foundry in the morning,” said Agnes. “It would be a quarter of an hour.”

“It is the same W,” said Winifred. “It was in the Misprint. Let it stand.”

At ten minutes past one, with the formes locked and lying on the stone for their last look, a slate went.

It went with a sound like a cough, and then there was no longer a Drip; there was a rope of water the thickness of a wrist, falling from the roof onto the stone and the formes upon it. Winifred was across the room before the second quart. She had the oilcloth from the proofing press in her arms, and Julian, who had been at her elbow, took the other end without being told, and they spread it over the type and lay on it, as one lies over a child in a crowd, with their backs to the roof and their arms out to the corners, while the water drummed on their shoulders. It ran down her neck. It ran down his. He said nothing. His cheek was an inch from hers, on the wet oilcloth, and he stayed there, and did not arrange anything.

Two sorts had gone with the first rush: a Great Primer e and a full stop, in the third column. She found the holes with her bodkin under the oilcloth by the light of Toby’s lantern, and reset them by feel, one and then the other, as a person puts a stopper in a bottle in the dark. The water was in her ears. When she had done, she said “Quoins,” and he knew where they were.

At half past one the two presses began.

The Albion’s toggle collar cracked at two.

It cracked with a note like a plate. The bar went slack in Julian’s hands, and the whole iron frame took on a look of a man who has heard bad news. Barnaby was on his knees in front of it before anyone else had moved, with his spectacles on his forehead and his gouty foot out behind him, feeling the collar with fingers that knew it better than his own. “Cracked through,” he said. “It’s the cold. My cousin Ebenezer’s iron never liked a wet autumn. I want a collar of the right metal, and there’s nothing in the shop of the right metal, and the Old Lady cannot do the run alone. At a hundred and fifty an hour—”

“It cannot be done,” said Orme, from the corner, to the room.

Julian had already taken off his signet ring.

He did not do it as a gesture. He did it as a man takes off a glove to pick up something small. He turned it once on his finger, as he had turned it all his life when he was thinking, and drew it over the knuckle, and held it out to Barnaby, and said, “Will this do?” It was the Stanmere griffin, in eighteen-carat gold, that had been on the hand of six marquesses.

Barnaby weighed it in his palm. “My dear fellow, it’s soft. It’ll flatten. It ought to last two thousand pulls if you’re kind to it.” He fitted it into the gap with a hammer and a prayer. The griffin went into the iron like a coin into a slot; and the bar came taut again. “A very good ring,” said Barnaby, “for a very bad purpose.”

“Pull,” said Winifred.

He pulled.

Mr Lovejoy came in at half past two, with an umbrella furled in his hand like a rolled proof, and Mr Gribble behind him in the brown coat.

“Madam. Mr Pargeter. I regret the hour.” He did not look as though he regretted it. He looked as he had looked in June, small and clean, in the snuff-coloured coat, with the glass on its ribbon swinging against his waistcoat. “I have here a demand in form under the third clause. The sum of eleven hundred and forty pounds, with interest to this day, is payable on demand upon the loss of the Gazette contract, and I now demand it. I have not reckoned the interest. I thought it civil that we should do it together.”

“The law, Miss Pargeter,” said Mr Gribble, apologetically, to the oilcloth, “don’t allow me to lay a finger on the press before sunrise. I’d not wish it thought I’d tried.”

It was a very good stroke. It cost nothing and it took time. A demand must be received; the interest must be reckoned to the day; a receipt must be written; a signature, the signature of an old man with ink in the creases of his hands, must be fetched from the Albion, where it was inking. Every minute of it was a minute that the run did not run. The cart went at a quarter past four. At a hundred and fifty an hour, with the Old Lady, and the Albion held by a ring, it wanted every minute it had.

“I have reckoned it,” said Winifred.

“I beg your pardon?”

“One hundred and eighty-seven days at six per cent on seven hundred and forty pounds. Twenty-two pounds fifteen shillings.” She had turned and was speaking to the dark of the stair. “Rupert.”

Lord Rupert Tremayne came down with the Black Bull strongbox on his shoulder, like a man carrying a lamb, and set it on the oilcloth that covered the stone. Winifred took the key from the ribbon at her neck. She counted the money out in piles of twenty guineas, aloud, and Mr Lovejoy, who counted aloud when he handled money, counted it back, a pile behind her; so that for eleven minutes the composing room resounded with two voices, one dry and one soft, going up the scale together like a pair of sparrows on a stair. Nobody in the room had ever heard so much silence made out of numbers.

“One thousand, one hundred and sixty-two pounds, fifteen shillings,” said Winifred.

“I make it the same to a farthing, madam. You may keep the farthing.”

Verity wrote the receipt in her square upright hand. It was brought to Barnaby, who signed it with a hand that left its own thumb-mark in the margin, and then held the pen in the air.

“Hector,” he said, “my dear fellow. You had the best hands I ever had in the shop. I don’t believe I ever said.”

“No, sir.” Mr Lovejoy’s face did not move. The glass on its ribbon swung once. “You did not.”

“It’s a pity to say it at half past two in the morning, over a receipt.”

“I find it comes out when it comes, Mr Pargeter,” said Mr Lovejoy. He took the three cancelled notes and folded them, and put on his hat.

At the door he stopped. He stood there with his hand on the latch, looking back, with his head a little on one side, as a craftsman sizes a page; and the room, which had been about to breathe, did not. Then he came back across the floor to the line where the first sheets hung to dry, and lifted one with the tips of his fingers, and put up the glass.

“Madam. The word-spacing in your third column is uneven. At the ninth line there is a thick space where there should be a middle. No reader will notice it.” He lowered the glass. “I cannot bear it.”

Winifred looked at him. Then she stopped the Albion. She slackened the quoins at the corner, and opened line nine with a bodkin, and made it right, and locked it again; and the seven minutes it took were the most expensive in the history of the house, and nobody complained, and Fairweather said “Aye.” When she looked up Mr Lovejoy was nodding, once, as a man nods at a sum that has come out. He bowed to Barnaby, and to Mrs Hobday, and to the pug. He went out into the court. The rain shut behind him.

It is time to say what was on the sheet that he had held, since it was the object of all this and has not yet been seen. It had been headed, in Great Primer capitals, centred, with a rule beneath it, and it began at the top of the second page, where the Fashionable Intelligence usually was.

ERRATUM. In our number of Thursday the 6th of June, in the paragraph headed Marriage in High Life, for ‘the engagement between the Marquess of Stanmere and Miss W. Pargeter, of Paternoster Row, is entirely well founded, and that his Lordship is at present engaged to the lady’, read ‘the report of an engagement between the Marquess of Stanmere and Miss Quarles, daughter of Sir Ephraim Quarles, Bart., is entirely without foundation, and that his Lordship is at present engaged to no lady whatever.’ The error was the compositor’s. The compositor is W. Pargeter, who saw it before the sheets left her house and did not stop them. The Gazette begs the pardon of the Marquess of Stanmere, of Miss Quarles, and of its readers, and has never before had occasion to do so.

The Gazette of that Saturday was the only newspaper in London in which the Marquess of Stanmere was, at the hour of printing, correctly engaged to no lady whatever. By half past six that would have changed.

The last sheet came off at ten past four. The cart was in the arch. Sowerby was on the box in his oilskin, with Jehu’s ears laid back and his face like an old saddle left out in the rain; and Winifred, who had a clean apron and nothing else to change, climbed up beside him with the first copy folded on her knees.

He did not look at her. He was red to the ears.

“Miss. I only told the clerk what I seen. I wish to God I’d kept my tongue and my quart.”

“You said what was true,” said Winifred. “That is why it has been so difficult.”

He clicked to the horse. The cart went out under the arch, past the pump, into Paternoster Row, and this time she went with it.

The sun was a pale disc over the dome when she came back on foot from Pomfret Yard. It was not copper. It was merely there, the colour of a sixpence that has been in a pocket, and it lit the wet street without any warmth. The Gazette had been in the streets since half past five. At the corner of Ludgate Hill stood a footman of Ormsgill House in claret and silver, with his calves in the rain, crying “Erratum! The Gazette! Erratum!” in the voice in which he was accustomed to announce Her Grace’s carriage, and a crossing-sweeper had got a copy and was reading it aloud to a hackney-man, with his finger under the words. “She says she saw it and let it go.” “Well,” said the hackney-man. “She says it.” At six the Crier’s hawkers began to come into the Churchyard with their armfuls, and found the street full of people reading something else.

Hand and Pen Court was quiet. The lamps had burned down. Lady Constance slept upright in the chair by the fire with the pug on her knees and her trumpet on the floor; Mrs Hobday slept with the hymn-book on her chest; Brevier slept on the Albion, under the bar. In the kitchen, over the dregs of the tea, with the door shut and Mrs Hobday’s ear missing nothing from the scullery, the Marquess of Stanmere had already asked Barnaby Pargeter the question which that gentleman had been waiting to be asked since a bowl of broth in a tithe barn on the fifteenth of August; and had got his answer, which had been Ask her properly, my dear fellow, she’s had a great deal of the other thing.

She found him on the stairs that led up to the parlour. He sat with his coat off and his sleeves rolled, ink to the shoulder, a night’s grey on his face, with a bent ring in his hand. It had come out of the collar as an oval, with the griffin flattened to a smear. It would not go back on the finger it had come from.

“You have asked my father.”

“I asked his leave. He gave it.” He stood. “It is the twenty-eighth. Michaelmas is tomorrow. I counted fifty-five days in a hop garden, and there is one left, and I find I cannot do the last.”

“You are a day early.”

“In a man who has been three months late it seemed excusable. You said I was to ask you when you did not need me. You paid Mr Lovejoy out of your own box at half past two, and did not look round once to see whether I was there. I took that to be what you meant.” He held the ring. “I signed Article the Third before I loved you. I broke it afterwards. That is the whole of the defence, and I do not offer it as one.”

She stood quite still, with the Gazette’s grey light behind her.

“Miss Pargeter, will you marry me? By banns, at your church and at mine, on three Sundays, in the open, with your father to give you away, and nobody paying for anything but the people in it. I have drawn up no Articles. I could not think of a seventh that you would let me have.”

“It is the first time,” said Winifred, “that anyone has asked me, instead of arranging. I wished to have noticed it.”

“And?” said Julian. “I should like it noted that I do not at present know.”

“Yes,” said Winifred.

chapters.title: If Any of You Know Cause
chapters.html:
On Michaelmas Day, which fell that year upon a Sunday and rained, the clerk of St Vedast, Foster Lane, stood up in his box under the pulpit, at the end of the second lesson, and read the banns for the first time.

The notice of them had been taken on the Saturday, at ten minutes past four, in the dining-room of the Reverend Mr Lathom, who was at that moment at his dinner, and had been delivered by a printer of fifty-nine with a gouty foot in flannel and a boy of thirteen with his mouth full, both of whom had arrived at the door at a run, which for the printer was an achievement. Mr Lathom had taken it, and put down his fork, and had not stopped smiling since.

“I publish the Banns of Marriage,” said the clerk, in the voice of a man who has been reading them for thirty years and never until today been listened to, “between Julian, Marquess of Stanmere, of the parish of St George, Hanover Square, bachelor, and Winifred Pargeter, of this parish, spinster. If any of you know cause, or just impediment, why these two persons should not be joined together in holy Matrimony, ye are to declare it. This is the first time of asking.”

There followed the silence that the Prayer Book provides for and that nobody has ever entirely believed in. It was a wet silence. It had the rain on the leads in it, and a gutter of Sir Christopher Wren’s discharging into a bucket that had been put there for the purpose, and four hundred persons not coughing, which was three hundred and eighty more than St Vedast had held on a Michaelmas since the Peace. The reader, who knows of impediments enough to furnish a vestry, that the engagement was a mistake and was kept up as a lie and was ruined by a friend and mended by a Quaker, is requested to keep her seat. It is the one occasion in this book on which the reader’s silence is required.

Nobody spoke. In the Pargeter pew Barnaby wept steadily into a handkerchief, with his foot on a hassock, and looked about him for someone to tell it to. Mrs Hobday sang under her breath. Toby sat with his ears pink and an air of having personally arranged the Church of England. Lady Constance, who had come in a closed carriage with her trumpet, took it from her lap and put it on the pew beside her, which was the nearest she had ever come to being at the mercy of a sermon. And in the last pew of all, alone, in a snuff-coloured coat, with his hat on his knee and the glass on its ribbon at his waistcoat, sat Mr Hector Lovejoy, who had walked there from Ave Maria Lane, a distance of two hundred yards, and was looking at nothing in particular with every appearance of being at a funeral he approved.

He was waiting in the porch when she came out. The rain had thinned to a drift, and the Churchyard was full of persons being looked at; but he stood by himself against a pillar, small and neat, and when she came out on her father’s arm he stepped forward and gave her a flat parcel, wrapped in a half-sheet of the Gazette, about the size of a visiting card.

“Madam.”

She undid the paper. Inside lay a single capital W, cast in best type-metal, still bright, with its face as sharp as a pin and both feet whole.

“The old one has a cracked foot,” said Mr Lovejoy. “It is in the Pargeter fount. Your father cut the matrices in ‘eighty-two, and I dressed that fount for seven years, and I had it by heart. I should not like to think of it going out into the world in a state.” He bowed to her, and to Barnaby, who had stopped weeping in order to stare. “I wish you every happiness, Miss Pargeter. I have no doubt that you will have it. You have been exceedingly well set.”

He went away down Foster Lane in the rain, and did not look back. He did not mention the notes, or the Crier, or the labels, or Saturday. He had said what was true and useful, and he took it with him, as he took everything, in clean hands.

Saturday’s Gazette had sold out by nine, and been reprinted on the Monday, and by the day of the wedding its circulation stood at three thousand, a number at which Mr Underhill, who had once feared that the truth would ruin him, now looked with the haunted pride of a man who has been proved right by accident. The Crier’s account of Sowerby had been cried in the Churchyard at six, and nobody wanted it; the hawkers sold eleven, and one of those to Mr Lovejoy.

Mr Underhill had framed the Erratum in gilt, and hung it above the stove, and showed it to visitors with the air of a man who had always believed in it. Mrs Rudge, in the ninth month, had appointed Miss Agnes Fell to a weekly column under her own name, at a salary that would clear a lieutenant’s hosiery in two years; and Miss Quarles, who had a ledger and a purpose, had in the meantime bought the hosiery from Mr Lovejoy at par, and Mr Lovejoy had sold it with an alacrity that surprised nobody who knew that he disliked being owed money by persons he might meet in church.

The Duchess’s cards were on the stone. Dick Sparrow had come back on the Monday, in a clean neckcloth, and Fairweather had looked at the neckcloth for some time and said “Aye”, in a manner that left Mr Sparrow in no doubt about the neckcloth. And the Farmer’s name was now the Marquess’s, in every county in England, and the Weald Relief Subscription stood at nineteen hundred pounds.

The banns were read on the same three Sundays, the twenty-ninth of September and the sixth and thirteenth of October, in St Vedast and in St George’s, Hanover Square, to a silence of a different but equally expensive kind. On the fifteenth, which was a Tuesday, a post-chaise from Dover with the mud of three countries on it drew up at the door in Curzon Street, and a tall woman got out of it in a travelling-cloak.

He had been on the step since ten. Gantry had given up asking him to come in. She stood on the pavement with the rain on her hood, fifty-three years old, grey-eyed, with a mouth that had once said something to him and not been heard, and looked up at the house, and at the man on the step.

“You are taller,” said Cecilia, Marchioness of Stanmere.

“I was nine, madam,” said Julian. And then, because the word was on the paper somewhere in Lombard Street and he had crossed it out: “Mother.”

She looked at his nose. “Who did that?”

“A Greek verb.”

“Ah,” she said, and came up the steps.

In the hall, at the foot of the stair, Lady Constance Dyer stood with Blücher in her arms and her eyes shut. She had stood so for twenty minutes, by the clock. The two women regarded one another across the black-and-white marble, the one with her eyes shut and the other with her hood back, and the pug, who knew a great occasion when he smelled one, turned his single eye from the one to the other and began, quite quietly, to wag.

“Constance.”

Lady Constance opened her eyes. “Cecilia.” And then, with the exactness of her whole life: “I gave him the last.”

“You gave it to him.”

“In the end.”

“In the end will do,” said Cecilia.

It did not shine. The reader will have wished for sun on the seventeenth of October, and the narrator would be glad to supply it, having promised it; but he has undertaken not to lie, and the morning came up the colour of dishwater over the roofs of Foster Lane, with a wind off the river and a smell of wet slate. It stopped raining, however, for the length of the vows, which in the year 1816 amounted to very nearly the same thing.

Winifred went up the aisle on her father’s arm at eleven o’clock in a gown of dove-grey sarsenet, bought out of the Duchess’s cards at four and sixpence the yard from a man in Cheapside, which was the fourth gown of her life that she had paid for herself. She had her mother’s seed-pearl brooch at the throat and her mother’s brass rule through her hair. She wore gloves on neither hand. She had meant to wear the left one and had left it, at the last, upon the hall table, and Lady Constance had seen it lying there and said nothing, in a tone that could be heard in the street. The thumb was as God and Fairweather’s ink had made it, a clear blue-black to the ball. She carried it before her like a banner, and the church, which was full, had its first sight of a bride with a trade.

Barnaby had a new coat. He walked the length of the church with his spectacles pushed up on his forehead, where for the first time in her recollection he did not forget them, and he gave her away in the tone of a man handing over a very fine press. “Her mother,” he had said in the vestry, “would have said you’d improved the line.” Toby walked before them with the ring on a composing-stick tray, lined with baize, in a paper hat he had been made to remove and a collar that he had not. The ring was Naomi Lamb’s. It had been in Barnaby’s waistcoat pocket since the March of 1807, thin at the inner edge from nineteen years of lye. Brevier, in a hamper, was in the vestry; the church had been told that she was a hat.

They were all there. Orme, with his hand cupped to his better ear, had set the wedding card, and had pronounced it, backwards, perfectly plain. Fairweather, in a blue coat, carried his fiddle in a green baize bag on his knee, like an infant, to be played at the breakfast, badly and with devotion. Verity sat beside Rupert, who had a drayman’s arms and a gold signet on his own hand once more, as of Saturday the twelfth, on which day she had answered, to everyone’s satisfaction but his own surprise. Agnes sat behind them, with her bonnet in her lap. Minton sat very straight, with the stopped watch in his pocket and the sketchbook in the other. Dr Pym, who had been in the porch a quarter of an hour with a rain-gauge, was observed to look at the leads when the rain left off, and was heard to say, “That will be the rods,” and this time somebody laughed.
